on-anger_book-1.originalText: You have demanded of me, Novatus, that I should write how anger may be soothed, and it appears to me that you are right in feeling especial fear of this passion, which is above all others hideous and wild: for the others have some alloy of peace and quiet, but this consists wholly in action and the impulse of grief, raging with an utterly inhuman lust for arms, blood and tortures, careless of itself provided it hurts another, rushing upon the very point of the sword, and greedy for revenge even when it drags the avenger to ruin with itself. Some of the wisest of men have in consequence of this called anger a short madness: for it is equally devoid of self control, regardless of decorum, forgetful of kinship, obstinately engrossed in whatever it begins to do, deaf to reason and advice, excited by trifling causes, awkward at perceiving what is true and just, and very like a falling rock which breaks itself to pieces upon the very thing which it crushes.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: You asked me to write about how to calm anger, Novatus. I think you're right to be especially afraid of this emotion. It's the most hideous and savage of all emotions. Other emotions have some peace mixed in with them. But anger is pure action and impulse. It rages with an inhuman desire for weapons, blood, and torture. It doesn't care if it destroys itself as long as it hurts someone else. It rushes straight onto sword points. It craves revenge even when that revenge will destroy the person seeking it. Some of the wisest people have called anger "brief madness" — and they're right. Anger has no self-control. It ignores social rules. It forgets family bonds. It obsesses over whatever it starts doing. It can't hear reason or advice. Small things set it off. It can't tell right from wrong. It's like a falling boulder that shatters itself on whatever it crushes.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: That you may know that they whom anger possesses are not sane, look at their appearance; for as there are distinct symptoms which mark madmen, such as a bold and menacing air, a gloomy brow, a stern face, a hurried walk, restless hands, changed colour, quick and strongly-drawn breathing; the signs of angry men, too, are the same: their eyes blaze and sparkle, their whole face is a deep red with the blood which boils up from the bottom of their heart, their lips quiver, their teeth are set, their hair bristles and stands on end, their breath is laboured and hissing; their joints crack as they twist them about, they groan, bellow, and burst into scarcely intelligible talk, they often clap their hands together and stamp on the ground with their feet, and their whole body is highly-strung and plays those tricks which mark a distraught mind, so as to furnish an ugly and shocking picture of self-perversion and excitement.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: If you want to know that angry people have lost their minds, just look at them. Madmen have clear warning signs — a bold and threatening look, a dark frown, a harsh face, jerky movements, restless hands, a strange color, and quick, heavy breathing. Angry people show the exact same signs. Their eyes burn and flash. Their whole face turns deep red as blood rushes up from their heart. Their lips shake. They clench their teeth. Their hair stands on end. They breathe hard and make hissing sounds. Their joints crack as they twist around. They groan and roar and burst into words you can barely understand. They clap their hands and stomp their feet. Their whole body is wound tight and does all the crazy things that show a broken mind. It's an ugly and shocking picture of someone who has twisted themselves with excitement.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: You cannot tell whether this vice is more execrable or more disgusting. Other vices can be concealed and cherished in secret; anger shows itself openly and appears in the countenance, and the greater it is, the more plainly it boils forth. Do you not see how in all animals certain signs appear before they proceed to mischief, and how their entire bodies put off their usual quiet appearance and stir up their ferocity? Boars foam at the mouth and sharpen their teeth by rubbing them against trees, bulls toss their horns in the air and scatter the sand with blows of their feet, lions growl, the necks of enraged snakes swell, mad dogs have a sullen look—there is no animal so hateful and venomous by nature that it does not, when seized by anger, show additional fierceness. I know well that the other passions, can hardly be concealed, and that lust, fear, and boldness give signs of their presence and may be discovered beforehand, for there is no one of the stronger passions that does not affect the countenance: what then is the difference between them and anger? Why, that the other passions are visible, but that this is conspicuous.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: You can't decide if anger is more evil or more disgusting. Other vices can be hidden and nursed in private. But anger shows itself openly. It appears right on your face. The stronger it gets, the more clearly it bubbles up for everyone to see. Haven't you noticed how all animals give warning signs before they attack? Their whole bodies drop their usual calm look and stir up their wildness. Boars foam at the mouth and sharpen their tusks by rubbing them on trees. Bulls toss their horns in the air and kick up sand with their hooves. Lions growl. Angry snakes puff up their necks. Mad dogs get that menacing look. There's no animal so naturally hateful and poisonous that it doesn't show extra fierceness when anger takes hold. I know that other emotions can barely be hidden either. Lust, fear, and boldness all give themselves away. You can spot them coming. Every strong emotion affects how you look. So what's the difference between those emotions and anger? Simple: the other emotions are visible, but anger is impossible to miss.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Next, if you choose to view its results and the mischief that it does, no plague has cost the human race more dear: you will see slaughterings and poisonings, accusations and counter-accusations, sacking of cities, ruin of whole peoples, the persons of princes sold into slavery by auction, torches applied to roofs, and fires not merely confined within city-walls but making whole tracts of country glow with hostile flame. See the foundations of the most celebrated cities hardly now to be discerned; they were ruined by anger. See deserts extending for many miles without an inhabitant: they have been desolated by anger. See all the chiefs whom tradition mentions as instances of ill fate; anger stabbed one of them in his bed, struck down another, though he was protected by the sacred rights of hospitality, tore another to pieces in the very home of the laws and in sight of the crowded forum, bade one shed his own blood by the parricide hand of his son, another to have his royal throat cut by the hand of a slave, another to stretch out his limbs on the cross: and hitherto I am speaking merely of individual cases.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
Now, if you look at what anger actually does — at all the damage it causes — no disease has cost humanity more. You will see mass killings and poisonings. False accusations flying back and forth. Cities ransacked. Entire peoples destroyed. Rulers sold into slavery at public auctions. Buildings set on fire. Flames that don't stop at city walls but spread across whole regions like enemy armies.

Look at the ruins of the most famous cities — you can barely tell where they once stood. Anger destroyed them. Look at empty deserts stretching for miles without a single person living there. Anger made them wastelands. Think of all the leaders that history remembers for their terrible fates. Anger stabbed one in his bed. It struck down another even though he was a guest under sacred protection. It tore another apart right in the courthouse, in front of a crowd. It made one man die by his own son's hand. It had another king's throat cut by his slave. It nailed another to a cross. And I'm only talking about individual cases here.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: What, if you were to pass from the consideration of those single men against whom anger has broken out to view whole assemblies cut down by the sword, the people butchered by the soldiery let loose upon it, and whole nations condemned to death in one common ruin . . . .[1] as though by men who either freed themselves from our charge or despised our authority? Why, wherefore is the people angry with gladiators, and so unjust as to think itself wronged if they do not die cheerfully? It thinks itself scorned, and by looks, gestures, and excitement turns itself from a mere spectator into an adversary.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: What if you moved beyond thinking about individual victims of anger? What if you looked at entire crowds cut down by swords? What about whole populations butchered by soldiers turned loose on them? What about entire nations condemned to die together in one shared destruction? It's as if these people had either escaped our control or shown contempt for our authority. But why is the crowd angry with gladiators? Why is it so unfair that it feels wronged if the gladiators don't die happily? The crowd thinks it's being disrespected. Through their looks, gestures, and shouting, they transform themselves from mere spectators into enemies.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Everything of this sort is not anger, but the semblance of anger, like that of boys who want to beat the ground when they have fallen upon it, and who often do not even know why they are angry, but are merely angry without any reason or having received any injury, yet not without some semblance of injury received, or without some wish to exact a penalty for it. Thus they are deceived by the likeness of blows, and are appeased by the pretended tears of those who deprecate their wrath, and thus an unreal grief is healed by an unreal revenge.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: All of this isn't real anger — it's just the appearance of anger. It's like little boys who want to hit the ground when they fall down. They often don't even know why they're angry. They're just angry for no reason, even though no one hurt them. But they act as if someone did hurt them, and they want to punish someone for it. So they get fooled by what looks like real attacks. They calm down when people pretend to cry and beg for forgiveness. This fake hurt gets healed by fake revenge.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "We often are angry," says our adversary, "not with men who have hurt us, but with men who are going to hurt us: so you may be sure that anger is not born of injury." It is true that we are angry with those who are going to hurt us, but they do already hurt us in intention, and one who is going to do an injury is already doing it. "The weakest of men," argues he, "are often angry with the most powerful: so you may be sure that anger is not a desire to punish their antagonist—for men do not desire to punish him when they cannot hope to do so." In the first place, I spoke of a desire to inflict punishment, not a power to do so:
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "We often get angry," our opponent says, "not with people who have hurt us, but with people who are going to hurt us. So you can see that anger doesn't come from injury." It's true we get angry with those who are going to hurt us. But they already hurt us by intending to do it. Someone who plans to harm you is already harming you. "Weak people," he argues, "often get angry with powerful people. So you can see that anger isn't a desire to punish your enemy — because people don't want to punish someone when they have no hope of doing it." First of all, I said anger was a desire to inflict punishment, not the power to do it.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: now men desire even what they cannot obtain. In the next place, no one is so low in station as not to be able to hope to inflict punishment even upon the greatest of men: we all are powerful for mischief. Aristotle's definition differs little from mine: for he declares anger to be a desire to repay suffering. It would be a long task to examine the differences between his definition and mine: it may be urged against both of them that wild beasts become angry without being excited by injury, and without any idea of punishing others or requiting them with pain: for, even though they do these things, these are not what they aim at doing.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Now, people desire even what they can't get. And no one is so powerless that they can't hope to hurt even the most powerful person. We're all capable of causing harm. Aristotle's definition is close to mine. He says anger is the desire to pay back suffering. It would take too long to examine all the differences between his definition and mine. But here's an objection to both: wild animals get angry without being hurt first and without any plan to punish or hurt others in return. Sure, they do hurt others when angry, but that's not their goal.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: We must admit, however, that neither wild beasts nor any other creature except man is subject to anger: for, whilst anger is the foe of reason, it nevertheless does not arise in any place where reason cannot dwell. Wild beasts have impulses, fury, cruelty, combativeness: they have not anger any more than they have luxury: yet they indulge in some pleasures with less self-control than human beings. Do not believe the poet who says: "The boar his wrath forgets, the stag forgets the hounds. The bear forgets how 'midst the herd he leaped with frantic bounds."[2] When he speaks of beasts being angry he means that they are excited, roused up: for indeed they know no more how to be angry than they know how to pardon.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: We have to admit that only humans experience anger. Animals don't. Anger is the enemy of reason, and it can only exist where reason could live. Wild animals have impulses, fury, cruelty, and a fighting spirit. But they don't have anger any more than they have luxury. Though they do enjoy some pleasures with less self-control than we do. Don't believe the poet who wrote: 'The boar forgets his wrath, the stag forgets the hounds. The bear forgets how he leaped frantically among the herd.' When he talks about angry beasts, he just means they're excited or worked up. Animals know as little about being angry as they know about forgiveness.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Dumb creatures have not human feelings, but have certain impulses which resemble them: for if it were not so, if they could feel love and hate, they would likewise be capable of friendship and enmity, of disagreement and agreement. Some traces of these qualities exist even in them, though properly all of them, whether good or bad, belong to the human breast alone. To no creature besides man has been given wisdom, foresight, industry, and reflexion. To animals not only human virtues but even human vices are forbidden: their whole constitution, mental and bodily, is unlike that of human beings: in them the royal[3] and leading principle is drawn from another source, as, for instance, they possess a voice, yet not a clear one, but indistinct and incapable of forming words:
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Animals don't have human feelings, but they do have certain impulses that look similar. If animals could truly feel love and hate, they would also be able to form friendships and make enemies. They would have conflicts and agreements. You can see hints of these qualities in animals, but really all emotions — good and bad — belong only to humans. No creature except humans has been given wisdom, planning ahead, hard work, and deep thought. Animals are denied not just human virtues but even human vices. Their entire makeup, both mental and physical, is different from ours. In animals, the ruling and governing part of their nature comes from a different source. For example, they have voices, but not clear ones — their sounds are unclear and can't form actual words.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: a tongue, but one which is fettered and not sufficiently nimble for complex movements: so, too, they possess intellect, the greatest attribute of all, but in a rough and inexact condition. It is, consequently, able to grasp those visions and semblances which rouse it to action, but only in a cloudy and indistinct fashion. It follows from this that their impulses and outbreaks are violent, and that they do not feel fear, anxieties, grief, or anger, but some semblances of these feelings: wherefore they quickly drop them and adopt the converse of them: they graze after showing the most vehement rage and terror, and after frantic bellowing and plunging they straightway sink into quiet sleep.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Animals have a tongue, but it's clumsy and can't make complex sounds. They have intellect too — the greatest gift of all — but theirs is rough and unclear. They can sense things that move them to action, but only dimly and confusedly. That's why their impulses and outbursts are so violent. They don't actually feel fear, worry, grief, or anger — just pale copies of these emotions. So they drop these feelings quickly and swing to the opposite. A cow will graze peacefully right after showing wild rage and terror. After frantic bellowing and thrashing around, they fall straight into quiet sleep.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
What anger is has been sufficiently explained. The difference
between it and irascibility is evident: it is the same as that
between a drunken man and a drunkard; between a frightened man and
a coward. It is possible for an angry man not to be irascible; an
irascible man may sometimes not be angry. I shall omit the other
varieties of anger, which the Greeks distinguish by various names,
because we have no distinctive words for them in our language,
although we call men bitter, and harsh, and also peevish, frantic,
clamorous, surly, and fierce: all of which are different forms of
irascibility. Among these you may class sulkiness, a refined form
of irascibility; for there are some sorts of anger which go no
further than noise, while some are as lasting as they are common:
some are fierce in deed, but inclined to be sparing of words: some
expend themselves in bitter words and curses: some do not go beyond
complaining and turning one’s back: some are great, deep-seated,
and brood within a man: there are a thousand other forms of a
multiform evil.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: We've explained enough about what anger is. The difference between anger and being an angry person is clear. It's like the difference between a drunk man and a drunkard, or between a frightened man and a coward. You can be angry without being an angry person. And an angry person might not be angry right now. I'll skip the other types of anger that the Greeks give different names to. We don't have specific words for them in Latin, though we do call people bitter, harsh, peevish, frantic, loud, surly, and fierce. These are all different forms of being angry by nature. You can add sulkiness to this list — it's anger with a refined twist. Some kinds of anger are all noise and nothing else. Others last as long as they are common. Some are violent in action but use few words. Others spend themselves in bitter words and curses. Some never go beyond complaining and giving people the cold shoulder. Others are deep, serious, and fester inside a person. There are a thousand other forms of this many-faced evil.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
We have now finished our enquiry as to what anger is, whether
it exists in any other creature besides man, what the difference
is between it and irascibility, and how many forms it possesses.
Let us now enquire whether anger be in accordance with nature, and
whether it be useful and worth entertaining in some measure.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: We have now finished exploring what anger is. We've looked at whether any creatures besides humans feel it. We've examined the difference between anger and being quick-tempered. And we've covered the many forms anger takes. Now let's ask a different question: Is anger natural? Is it useful? Should we hold onto some amount of it?

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Whether it be according to nature will become evident if we consider
man’s nature, than which what is more gentle while it is in its
proper condition? Yet what is more cruel than anger? What is more
affectionate to others than man? Yet what is more savage against
them than anger? Mankind is born for mutual assistance, anger for
mutual ruin: the former loves society, the latter estrangement. The
one loves to do good, the other to do harm; the one to help even
strangers, the other to attack even its dearest friends.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: To find out if anger fits with human nature, we need to look at what humans are really like. What creature is gentler than a person in their natural state? Yet what is crueler than anger? What is more loving toward others than humanity? Yet what is more savage toward them than anger? People are born to help each other. Anger exists to destroy each other. Humanity loves connection. Anger loves isolation. One wants to do good. The other wants to do harm. One helps even strangers. The other attacks even our closest friends.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
The one
is ready even to sacrifice itself for the good of others, the other
to plunge into peril provided it drags others with it. Who, then,
can be more ignorant of nature than he who classes this cruel and
hurtful vice as belonging to her best and most polished work? Anger,
as we have said, is eager to punish; and that such a desire should
exist in man’s peaceful breast is least of all according to his
nature; for human life is founded on benefits and harmony, and is
bound together into an alliance for the common help of all, not by
terror, but by love towards one another.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: One person is ready to sacrifice themselves for others' good. The angry person will plunge into danger as long as they can drag others down with them. Who could be more ignorant of human nature than someone who thinks this cruel and harmful vice belongs to nature's best and most refined creation? Anger, as we've said, is eager to punish. But such a desire has no place in a human's peaceful heart — it goes against our very nature. Human life is built on kindness and harmony. We are bound together by an alliance meant to help everyone, not through fear, but through love for one another.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "What, then? Is not correction sometimes necessary?" Of course it is; but with discretion, not with anger; for it does not injure, but heals under the guise of injury. We char crooked spearshafts to straighten them, and force them by driving in wedges, not in order to break them, but to take the bends out of them; and, in like manner, by applying pain to the body or mind we correct dispositions which have been rendered crooked by vice. So the physician at first, when dealing with slight disorders, tries not to make much change in his patient's daily habits, to regulate his food, drink, and exercise, and to improve his health merely by altering the order in which he takes them.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "What then? Don't we sometimes need to correct people?" Of course we do. But we should correct with wisdom, not with anger. Correction doesn't harm — it heals by appearing to hurt. We heat crooked spear shafts to straighten them. We force them with wedges, not to break them, but to remove their bends. In the same way, we use pain on the body or mind to fix habits that vice has twisted out of shape. A doctor first tries gentle methods with minor illnesses. He adjusts his patient's food, drink, and exercise. He improves health just by changing the order of these daily habits.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: The next step is to see whether an alteration in their amount will be of service. If neither alteration of the order or of the amount is of use, he cuts off some and reduces others. If even this does not answer, he forbids food, and disburdens the body by fasting. If milder remedies have proved useless he opens a vein; if the extremities are injuring the body and infecting it with disease he lays his hands upon the limbs; yet none of his treatment is considered harsh if its result is to give health.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: The doctor's next step is to see if changing the amount of food or exercise helps. If changing the order or the amount doesn't work, he cuts some things out and reduces others. If that still doesn't work, he stops the patient from eating and lets the body rest through fasting. If gentler treatments fail, he opens a vein to let blood. If diseased limbs are hurting the body and spreading infection, he operates on them. But none of this treatment seems harsh when the result is good health.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Similarly, it is the duty of the chief administrator of the laws, or the ruler of a state, to correct ill-disposed men, as long as he is able, with words, and even with gentle ones, that he may persuade them to do what they ought, inspire them with a love of honour and justice, and cause them to hate vice and set store upon virtue. He must then pass on to severer language, still confining himself to advising and reprimanding; last of all he must betake himself to punishments, yet still making them slight and temporary.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: A ruler or judge has a similar duty. First, he should try to fix troubled people with words — gentle ones. He wants to persuade them to do the right thing. He wants them to love honor and justice, and hate vice while valuing virtue. If that doesn't work, he moves to harsher language. But he's still just advising and scolding. Only as a last resort does he turn to punishment. And even then, the punishments should be light and temporary.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: He ought to assign extreme punishments only to extreme crimes, that no one may die unless it be even to the criminal's own advantage that he should die. He will differ from the physician in one point alone; for whereas physicians render it easy to die for those to whom they cannot grant the boon of life, he will drive the condemned out of life with ignominy and disgrace, not because he takes pleasure in any man's being punished, for the wise man is far from such inhuman ferocity, but that they may be a warning to all men, and that, since they would not be useful when alive, the state may at any rate profit by their death.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: A ruler should use extreme punishments only for extreme crimes. No one should die unless their death would actually benefit even them. The ruler differs from a doctor in one way. Doctors make dying easy for patients they cannot save. But the ruler drives condemned criminals out of life with shame and disgrace. Not because he enjoys punishing people — a wise person is far from such cruelty. He does it so their fate warns everyone else. Since these criminals were useless while alive, at least the state can benefit from their deaths.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Man's nature is not, therefore, desirous of inflicting punishment; neither, therefore, is anger in accordance with man's nature, because that is desirous of inflicting punishment. I will also adduce Plato's argument—for what harm is there in using other men's arguments, so far as they are on our side? "A good man," says he, "does not do any hurt: it is only punishment which hurts. Punishment, therefore, does not accord with a good man: wherefore anger does not do so either, because punishment and anger accord one with another. If a good man takes no pleasure in punishment, he will also take no pleasure in that state of mind to which punishment gives pleasure: consequently anger is not natural to man."
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Human nature does not want to inflict punishment. So anger is not natural to humans, because anger does want to inflict punishment. I'll also use Plato's argument here — why not borrow from others when they support our point? "A good person," he says, "does not hurt anyone. Only punishment hurts people. So punishment does not fit with being a good person. Therefore anger doesn't fit either, because punishment and anger go hand in hand." If a good person takes no pleasure in punishment, then he also takes no pleasure in the mindset that enjoys punishment. This proves that anger is not natural to humans.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: May it not be that, although anger be not natural, it may be right to adopt it, because it often proves useful? It rouses the spirit and excites it; and courage does nothing grand in war without it, unless its flame be supplied from this source; this is the goad which stirs up bold men and sends them to encounter perils. Some therefore consider it to be best to control anger, not to banish it utterly, but to cut off its extravagances, and force it to keep within useful bounds, so as to retain that part of it without which action will become languid and all strength and activity of mind will die away.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: But wait — maybe anger isn't natural, but we should still use it because it's often helpful. Anger fires up the spirit and gets us excited. Courage can't do anything great in war without anger feeding its flame. Anger is the prod that stirs up brave people and sends them into danger. So some people think the best approach is to control anger, not get rid of it completely. They say we should cut off its worst parts and force it to stay within useful limits. That way we keep the part of anger that prevents action from becoming weak and lazy, and stops all our mental strength and energy from dying away.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: In the first place, it is easier to banish dangerous passions than to rule them; it is easier not to admit them than to keep them in order when admitted; for when they have established themselves in possession of the mind they are more powerful than the lawful ruler, and will in no wise permit themselves to be weakened or abridged. In the next place, Reason herself, who holds the reins, is only strong while she remains apart from the passions; if she mixes and befouls herself with them she becomes no longer able to restrain those whom she might once have cleared out of her path; for the mind, when once excited and shaken up, goes whither the passions drive it.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
First, it's easier to banish dangerous emotions than to control them. It's easier to keep them out than to manage them once they're in. When they take hold of your mind, they become stronger than your rational self. They won't let you weaken them or cut them back.

Second, reason itself — the part that's supposed to be in charge — only stays strong when it keeps away from the passions. If reason mixes with emotions and gets contaminated by them, it can no longer restrain what it once could have thrown out completely. Once your mind gets stirred up and shaken, it goes wherever the passions drag it.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: There are certain things whose beginnings lie in our own power, but which, when developed, drag us along by their own force and leave us no retreat. Those who have flung themselves over a precipice have no control over their movements, nor can they stop or slacken their pace when once started, for their own headlong and irremediable rashness has left no room for either reflexion or remorse, and they cannot help going to lengths which they might have avoided. So, also, the mind, when it has abandoned itself to anger, love, or any other passion, is unable to check itself: its own weight and the downward tendency of vices must needs carry the man off and hurl him into the lowest depth.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Some things start small and seem under our control. But once they grow, they drag us along with their own power. We can't retreat anymore. Think of people who jump off a cliff. Once they're falling, they can't control their movement. They can't stop or slow down. Their reckless choice has cut off all escape routes. There's no time left for thinking or regret. They have to go where they never wanted to end up. The mind works the same way. When it gives in to anger, love, or any other strong emotion, it loses the ability to stop itself. Its own weight and the pull of these destructive forces carry the person downward and hurl him into the depths.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
The best plan is to reject straightway the first incentives
to anger, to resist its very beginnings, and to take care not to
be betrayed into it: for if once it begins to carry us away, it is
hard to get back again into a healthy condition, because reason
goes for nothing when once passion has been admitted to the mind,
and has by our own free will been given a certain authority, it
will for the future do as much as it chooses, not only as much as
you will allow it. The enemy, I repeat, must be met and driven back
at the outermost frontier-line: for when he has once entered the
city and passed its gates, he will not allow his prisoners to set
bounds to his victory.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: The best plan is to reject the first signs of anger right away. Fight it from the very start. Don't let it trick you into giving in. Once anger starts carrying you away, it's hard to get back to a healthy state of mind. Why? Because reason becomes useless once you've let passion into your mind. Once you've given it authority by your own free choice, it will do whatever it wants — not just what you're willing to allow. The enemy must be met and driven back at the border. Once anger has entered your city and passed through the gates, it won't let you set any limits on its victory.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
The mind does not stand apart and view its
passions from without, so as not to permit them to advance further
than they ought, but it is itself changed into a passion, and is
therefore unable to check what once was useful and wholesome strength,
now that it has become degenerate and misapplied: for passion and
reason, as I said before, have not distinct and separate provinces,
but consist of the changes of the mind itself for better or for
worse. How then can reason recover itself when it is conquered and
held down by vices, when it has given way to anger? or how can it
extricate itself from a confused mixture, the greater part of which
consists of the lower qualities?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Your mind can't step back and watch its emotions from the outside. It can't say, "That's far enough" and stop them there. Instead, your mind becomes the emotion itself. Once that happens, it can't control what used to be healthy strength — now that this strength has turned corrupt and misdirected. Passion and reason don't live in separate rooms, as I said before. They are just the same mind changing for better or worse. So how can reason save itself once anger has beaten it down? How can it escape from this messy mixture when most of it is now made of the worst parts?

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
“But,” argues our adversary, “some
men when in anger control themselves.” Do they so far control
themselves that they do nothing which anger dictates, or some
what? If they do nothing thereof, it becomes evident that anger is
not essential to the conduct of affairs, although your sect advocated
it as possessing greater strength than reason . . . . Finally, I
ask, is anger stronger or weaker than reason? If stronger, how can
reason impose any check upon it, since it is only the less powerful
that obey: if weaker, then reason is competent to effect its ends
without anger, and does not need the help of a less powerful quality.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "But," our opponent argues, "some people control themselves when they're angry." Do they control themselves completely — doing nothing that anger tells them to do? Or only partly? If they do nothing anger demands, then anger clearly isn't necessary for handling life's business. Yet your school of philosophy promoted anger as being stronger than reason. Finally, I ask: is anger stronger or weaker than reason? If it's stronger, how can reason control it at all? Only the weaker force obeys the stronger one. If anger is weaker, then reason can accomplish its goals without anger's help. It doesn't need assistance from something less powerful.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
“But some angry men remain consistent and control themselves.” When
do they do so? It is when their anger is disappearing and leaving
them of its own accord, not when it was red-hot, for then it was
more powerful than they. What then? do not men, even in the height
of their anger, sometimes let their enemies go whole and unhurt,
and refrain from injuring them? “They do: but when do they do so?
It is when one passion overpowers another, and either fear or greed
gets the upper hand for a while. On such occasions, it is not thanks
to reason that anger is stilled, but owing to an untrustworthy and
fleeting truce between the passions.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "But some angry people stay consistent and control themselves." When do they do this? Only when their anger is already fading and leaving on its own — not when it was burning hot. When anger was at its peak, it was stronger than they were. What about this — don't people sometimes spare their enemies even when they're furious? Don't they hold back from hurting them? They do, but when? Only when one emotion overpowers another. Fear or greed takes control for a moment. When this happens, reason doesn't calm the anger. Instead, you get an unreliable and short-lived truce between competing passions.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
In the next place, anger has nothing useful in itself, and does
not rouse up the mind to warlike deeds: for a virtue, being
self-sufficient, never needs the assistance of a vice: whenever it
needs an impetuous effort, it does not become angry, but rises to
the occasion, and excites or soothes itself as far as it deems
requisite, just as the machines which hurl darts may be twisted to
a greater or lesser degree of tension at the manager’s pleasure.
“Anger,” says Aristotle, “is necessary, nor can any fight be won
without it, unless it fills the mind, and kindles up the spirit.
It must, however, be made use of, not as a general, but as a soldier,”
Now this is untrue; for if it listens to reason and follows whither
reason leads, it is no longer anger, whose characteristic is
obstinacy:
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
Anger has nothing useful in itself. It doesn't inspire the mind for battle. Virtue is self-sufficient — it never needs help from vice. When virtue needs forceful action, it doesn't get angry. Instead, it rises to meet the challenge. It excites or calms itself as needed, like those machines that launch spears — the operator can adjust the tension higher or lower as he chooses.

Aristotle says, "Anger is necessary. No battle can be won without it filling the mind and firing up the spirit. But anger should be used as a soldier, not as a general."

This is wrong. If anger listens to reason and follows where reason leads, it's no longer anger. The defining feature of anger is that it's stubborn.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
if, again, it is disobedient and will not be quiet when
ordered, but is carried away by its own wilful and headstrong
spirit, it is then as useless an aid to the mind as a soldier who
disregards the sounding of the retreat would be to a general. If,
therefore, anger allows limits to be imposed upon it, it must be
called by some other name, and ceases to be anger, which I understand
to be unbridled and unmanageable: and if it does not allow limits
to be imposed upon it, it is harmful and not to be counted among
aids: wherefore either anger is not anger, or it is useless: for
if any man demands the infliction of punishment, not because he is
eager for the punishment itself, but because it is right to inflict
it, he ought not to be counted as an angry man: that will be the
useful soldier, who knows how to obey orders: the passions cannot
obey any more than they can command.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: If anger refuses to listen and won't calm down when told to, but gets carried away by its own stubborn nature, then it's as useless to the mind as a soldier who ignores the retreat signal would be to his general. So if anger accepts limits, we should call it something else — because it's no longer anger. I define anger as wild and uncontrollable. And if anger won't accept limits, then it's harmful and shouldn't be counted as help. Either anger isn't really anger, or it's useless. If someone demands punishment not because they crave revenge, but because it's the right thing to do, that person isn't angry. That's the useful soldier — one who knows how to follow orders. The passions can't obey commands any more than they can give them.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
For this cause reason will never call to its aid blind and fierce
impulses, over whom she herself possesses no authority, and which
she never can restrain save by setting against them similar and
equally powerful passions, as for example, fear against anger, anger
against sloth, greed against timidity. May virtue never come to
such a pass, that reason should fly for aid to vices! The mind can
find no safe repose there, it must needs be shaken and tempest-tossed
if it be safe only because of its own defects, if it cannot be brave
without anger, diligent without greed, quiet without fear: such is
the despotism under which a man must live if he becomes the slave
of a passion. Are you not ashamed to put virtues under the patronage
of vices?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Reason will never call on blind and fierce impulses for help. Reason has no power over these impulses. She can only hold them back by fighting fire with fire — using fear against anger, anger against laziness, greed against cowardice. May virtue never fall so low that reason has to run to vices for help! The mind can't find peace that way. It will always be shaken and storm-tossed if it's only safe because of its own flaws. If it can't be brave without anger, hardworking without greed, or calm without fear, then what kind of life is that? That's the tyranny you live under when you become a slave to passion. Aren't you ashamed to put virtues under the protection of vices?

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Then, too, reason ceases to have any power if she can do
nothing without passion, and begins to be equal and like unto
passion; for what difference is there between them if passion without
reason be as rash as reason without passion is helpless? They are
both on the same level, if one cannot exist without the other. Yet
who could endure that passion should be made equal to reason? “Then,”
says our adversary, “passion is useful, provided it be moderate.”
Nay, only if it be useful by nature: but if it be disobedient
to authority and reason, al that we gain by its moderation is that
the less there is of it, the less harm it does: wherefore a moderate
passion is nothing but a moderate evil.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Besides, reason loses all its power if it can't do anything without passion. It becomes just as weak as passion itself. What's the difference between them if passion without reason is reckless, but reason without passion is helpless? They're both equally useless if one can't exist without the other. But who could accept making passion equal to reason? "Well," our opponent says, "passion is useful as long as it's kept moderate." No — only if it's naturally good to begin with. But if passion fights against authority and reason, then moderating it just means we get less harm from it. A moderate passion is still just a moderate evil.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "But," argues he, "against our enemies anger is necessary." In no case is it less necessary; since our attacks ought not to be disorderly, but regulated and under control. What, indeed, is it except anger, so ruinous to itself, that overthrows barbarians, who have so much more bodily strength than we, and are so much better able to endure fatigue? Gladiators, too, protect themselves by skill, but expose themselves to wounds when they are angry. Moreover, of what use is anger, when the same end can be arrived at by reason? Do you suppose that a hunter is angry with the beasts he kills? Yet he meets them when they attack him, and follows them when they flee from him, all of which is managed by reason without anger.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "But," someone argues, "we need anger when fighting our enemies." Actually, that's when we need it least. Our attacks should be planned and controlled, not wild and messy. What else but anger — which destroys itself — defeats barbarians who are much stronger than us and can handle pain better? Look at gladiators. They protect themselves with skill, but they get wounded when they lose their temper. Besides, why use anger when reason can do the same job? Do you think a hunter gets angry at the animals he kills? He fights them when they attack and chases them when they run. He does all this through reason, not anger.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: When so many thousands of Cimbri and Teutones poured over the Alps, what was it that caused them to perish so completely, that no messenger, only common rumour, carried the news of that great defeat to their homes, except that with them anger stood in the place of courage? and anger, although sometimes it overthrows and breaks to pieces whatever it meets, yet is more often its own destruction. Who can be braver than the Germans? who charge more boldly? who have more love of arms, among which they are born and bred, for which alone they care, to the neglect of everything else? Who can be more hardened to undergo every hardship, since a large part of them have no store of clothing for the body, no shelter from the continual rigour of the climate: yet Spaniards and Gauls, and even the unwarlike races of Asia and Syria cut them down before the main legion comes within sight, nothing but their own irascibility exposing them to death.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
When thousands of Cimbri and Teutones poured over the Alps, what caused them to be wiped out so completely? Why did no messenger return home — only vague rumors of their great defeat? It was because they used anger instead of courage. Anger sometimes destroys whatever it hits. But more often, it destroys itself.

Who can be braver than the Germans? Who charges harder into battle? Who loves weapons more? They're born and raised with arms. It's all they care about — they ignore everything else. Who can endure hardship better? Most of them have no warm clothes, no shelter from the freezing weather. Yet Spaniards and Gauls cut them down easily. Even the unwarlike people of Asia and Syria defeat them before the main Roman legion even shows up. Nothing kills them except their own rage.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Give but intelligence to those minds, and discipline to those bodies of theirs, which now are ignorant of vicious refinements, luxury, and wealth,—to say nothing more, we should certainly be obliged to go back to the ancient Roman habits of life. By what did Fabius restore the shattered forces of the state, except by knowing how to delay and spin out time, which angry men know not how to do? The empire, which then was at its last gasp, would have perished if Fabius had been as daring as anger urged him to be: but he took thought about the condition of affairs, and after counting his force, no part of which could be lost without everything being lost with it, he laid aside thoughts of grief and revenge, turning his sole attention to what was profitable and to making the most of his opportunities, and conquered his anger before he conquered Hannibal.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Give these German minds some intelligence and discipline to their bodies. Right now they know nothing of corruption, luxury, and wealth. If you did that — we would have to return to the old Roman way of life. How did Fabius restore Rome's broken forces? By knowing how to delay and take time — something angry men cannot do. The empire was dying then. It would have collapsed if Fabius had been as reckless as his anger wanted him to be. But he thought carefully about the situation. He counted his forces and knew that losing any part meant losing everything. So he set aside thoughts of grief and revenge. He focused only on what was useful and making the most of his chances. He conquered his anger before he conquered Hannibal.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: What did Scipio do? Did he not leave behind Hannibal and the Carthaginian army, and all with whom he had a right to be angry, and carry over the war into Africa with such deliberation that he made his enemies think him luxurious and lazy? What did the second Scipio do? Did he not remain a long, long time before Numantia, and bear with calmness the reproach to himself and to his country that Numantia took longer to conquer than Carthage? By blockading and investing his enemies, he brought them to such straits that they perished by their own swords. Anger, therefore, is not useful even in wars or battles: for it is prone to rashness, and while trying to bring others into danger, does not guard itself against danger. The most trustworthy virtue is that which long and carefully considers itself, controls itself, and slowly and deliberately brings itself to the front.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: What did Scipio do? He left Hannibal and the Carthaginian army behind — all the people he had good reason to be angry with. Instead, he moved the war to Africa. He did this so carefully that his enemies thought he was lazy and soft. What about the second Scipio? He stayed outside Numantia for a very long time. He calmly endured criticism — people blamed both him and Rome for taking longer to conquer Numantia than it had taken to conquer Carthage. But by surrounding his enemies and cutting off their supplies, he forced them into such desperation that they killed themselves with their own swords. So anger is useless even in wars and battles. It makes you reckless. While you're trying to put others in danger, you forget to protect yourself. The most reliable strength comes from thinking long and hard, staying in control, and moving forward slowly and deliberately.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "What, then," asks our adversary, "is a good man not to be angry if he sees his father murdered or his mother outraged?" No, he will not be angry, but will avenge them, or protect them. Why do you fear that filial piety will not prove a sufficient spur to him even without anger? You may as well say—"What then? When a good man sees his father or his son being cut down, I suppose he will not weep or faint," as we see women do whenever any trifling rumour of danger reaches them. The good man will do his duty without disturbance or fear, and he will perform the duty of a good man, so as to do nothing unworthy of a man. My father will be murdered: then I will defend him: he has been slain, then I will avenge him, not because I am grieved, but because it is my duty.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "What then?" our opponent asks. "Should a good man not get angry if he sees his father murdered or his mother attacked?" No, he won't be angry, but he will take revenge or protect them. Why do you worry that love for his family won't be enough motivation without anger? You might as well ask — "What then? When a good man sees his father or son being killed, I suppose he won't weep or faint?" like we see women do whenever they hear even small rumors of danger. The good man will do his duty without panic or fear. He will act like a good man should, doing nothing unworthy of a man. If my father is being murdered, I will defend him. If he has been killed, I will avenge him — not because I'm upset, but because it's my duty.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "Good men are made angry by injuries done to their friends." When you say this, Theophrastus, you seek to throw discredit upon more manly maxims; you leave the judge and appeal to the mob: because every one is angry when such things befall his own friends, you suppose that men will decide that it is their duty to do what they do: for as a rule every man considers a passion which he recognises to be a righteous one. But he does the same thing if the hot water is not ready for his drink, if a glass be broken, or his shoe splashed with mud. It is not filial piety, but weakness of mind that produces this anger, as children weep when they lose their parents, just as they do when they lose their toys. To feel anger on behalf of one's friends does not show a loving, but a weak mind: it is admirable and worthy conduct to stand forth as the defender of one's parents, children, friends, and countrymen, at the call of duty itself, acting of one's own free will, forming a deliberate judgment, and looking forward to the future, not in an impulsive, frenzied fashion.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
Theophrastus argues that "good men get angry when their friends are wronged." When you say this, you're trying to discredit stronger principles. You abandon sound reasoning and appeal to the crowd instead. Since everyone gets angry when bad things happen to their friends, you assume people will decide this anger is justified. After all, we usually think our familiar emotions are righteous ones.

But this same person gets angry if his bath water isn't hot enough, if someone breaks his cup, or if mud splashes on his shoe. This isn't love or devotion — it's mental weakness. It's like children who cry just as hard when they lose their parents as when they lose their toys.

Getting angry for your friends doesn't show a loving heart. It shows a weak mind. What's truly admirable is standing up for your parents, children, friends, and fellow citizens because duty calls you to do so. You act from your own free choice. You think it through carefully and plan ahead. You don't just react in a wild, frenzied way.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: No passion is more eager for revenge than anger, and for that very reason it is unapt to obtain it: being over hasty and frantic, like almost all desires, it hinders itself in the attainment of its own object, and therefore has never been useful either in peace or war: for it makes peace like war, and when in arms forgets that Mars belongs to neither side, and falls into the power of the enemy, because it is not in its own. In the next place, vices ought not to be received into common use because on some occasions they have effected somewhat: for so also fevers are good for certain kinds of ill-health, but nevertheless it is better to be altogether free from them: it is a hateful mode of cure to owe one's health to disease. Similarly, although anger, like poison, or falling headlong, or being shipwrecked, may have unexpectedly done good, yet it ought not on that account to be classed as wholesome, for poisons have often proved good for the health.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
No emotion craves revenge more than anger does. But that's exactly why anger is so bad at getting revenge. Anger is too rushed and wild, like most strong desires. It gets in its own way and blocks what it's trying to achieve. That's why anger has never been useful in peace or war. It turns peace into war. And when you're actually fighting, anger makes you forget that luck can go either way. You lose control and hand victory to your enemy.

Besides, we shouldn't accept bad habits just because they sometimes work out. Fevers can help cure certain diseases, but it's still better to never get a fever at all. It's a terrible way to get healthy — needing a disease to cure you. The same goes for anger. Sure, anger might accidentally help sometimes, like poison or falling off a cliff or getting shipwrecked. But that doesn't make anger good for you. After all, even poison can sometimes improve your health.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Moreover, qualities which we ought to possess become better and more desirable the more extensive they are: if justice is a good thing, no one will say that it would be better if any part were subtracted from it; if bravery is a good thing, no one would wish it to be in any way curtailed: consequently the greater anger is, the better it is, for who ever objected to a good thing being increased? But it is not expedient that anger should be increased: therefore it is not expedient that it should exist at all, for that which grows bad by increase cannot be a good thing.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Besides, good qualities become better and more valuable when they grow stronger. If justice is good, no one would say we should have less of it. If courage is good, no one would want to reduce it. So if anger were truly good, then more anger would be better. But who has ever complained about having too much of a genuinely good thing? Yet we know that increasing anger makes things worse, not better. This proves that anger isn't good at all. Anything that becomes harmful when you have more of it was never truly good in the first place.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "Anger is useful," says our adversary, "because it makes men more ready to fight." According to that mode of reasoning, then, drunkenness also is a good thing, for it makes men insolent and daring, and many use their weapons better when the worse for liquor: nay, according to that reasoning, also, you may call frenzy and madness essential to strength, because madness often makes men stronger. Why, does not fear often by the rule of contraries make men bolder, and does not the terror of death rouse up even arrant cowards to join battle?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "Anger is useful," our opponent argues, "because it makes men more ready to fight." By that logic, drunkenness is also good — it makes people bold and reckless. Many fighters perform better when drunk. Following the same reasoning, you could say madness is essential for strength, since crazy people are often stronger. Why not praise fear too? Fear sometimes makes cowards brave by forcing them into battle when they're terrified of death.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Yet anger, drunkenness, fear, and the like, are base and temporary incitements to action, and can furnish no arms to virtue, which has no need of vices, although they may at times be of some little assistance to sluggish and cowardly minds. No man becomes braver through anger, except one who without anger would not have been brave at all: anger does not therefore come to assist courage, but to take its place. What are we to say to the argument that, if anger were a good thing it would attach itself to all the best men? Yet the most irascible of creatures are infants, old men, and sick people. Every weakling is naturally prone to complaint.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: But anger, drunkenness, fear, and similar emotions are crude and short-lived motivators. They can't provide real weapons to virtue, which doesn't need vices to help it — even though these emotions might occasionally help lazy and cowardly minds. No one becomes braver through anger, except someone who wouldn't be brave at all without it. So anger doesn't come to help courage — it comes to replace it. What should we say to the argument that if anger were good, it would attach itself to all the best people? Yet the most quick-tempered creatures are babies, old men, and sick people. Every weak person is naturally prone to complaining.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
It is impossible, says Theophrastus, for a good man not to be
angry with bad men. By this reasoning, the better a man is, the
more irascible he will be: yet will he not rather be more tranquil,
more free from passions, and hating no one: indeed, what reason has
he for hating sinners, since it is error that leads them into such
crimes? now it does not become a sensible man to hate the erring,
since if so he will hate himself: let him think how many things he
does contrary to good morals, how much of what he has done stands
in need of pardon, and he will soon become angry with himself also,
for no righteous judge pronounces a different judgment in his own
case and in that of others.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Theophrastus says it's impossible for a good man not to get angry with bad men. If that were true, then the better a person is, the angrier he would be. But wouldn't he actually be calmer, more peaceful, and hate no one? Why would he hate sinners when it's their mistakes that lead them to crime? A wise person shouldn't hate people who make mistakes. If he did, he'd have to hate himself too. Let him think about how many things he does wrong, how much he needs forgiveness himself. Soon he'd be angry with himself as well. No fair judge applies different standards to his own case than to others'.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
No one, I affirm, will be found who can
acquit himself. Every one when he calls himself innocent looks
rather to external witnesses than to his own conscience. How much
more philanthropic it is to deal with the erring in a gentle and
fatherly spirit, and to call them into the right course instead of
hunting them down? When a man is wandering about our fields because
he has lost his way, it is better to place him on the right path
than to drive him away.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: No one can honestly say they are completely innocent. When people claim they've done nothing wrong, they look to other people for approval rather than examining their own conscience. How much kinder it is to treat people who make mistakes with gentleness and a fatherly spirit. Guide them back to the right path instead of attacking them. When someone is wandering lost in your fields, it's better to show them the way than to chase them off.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: The sinner ought, therefore, to be corrected both by warning and by force, both by gentle and harsh means, and may be made a better man both towards himself and others by chastisement, but not by anger: for who is angry with the patient whose wounds he is tending? "But they cannot be corrected, and there is nothing in them that is gentle or that admits of good hope." Then let them be removed from mortal society, if they are likely to deprave every one with whom they come in contact, and let them cease to be bad men in the only way in which they can: yet let this be done without hatred: for what reason have I for hating the man to whom I am doing the greatest good, since I am rescuing him from himself?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: So people who do wrong should be corrected — sometimes with gentle warnings, sometimes with firm action. We might need to use both kind and harsh methods to make them better for themselves and others. But we should never act from anger. After all, do doctors get angry with patients when they're treating their wounds? "But some people can't be corrected. They're hopeless — there's nothing good left in them." Fine. Then remove them from society if they're going to corrupt everyone around them. Let them stop being bad in the only way they can. But do this without hatred. Why should I hate someone I'm actually helping? I'm saving them from themselves.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Does a man hate his own limbs when he cuts them off? That is not an act of anger, but a lamentable method of healing. We knock mad dogs on the head, we slaughter fierce and savage bulls, and we doom scabby sheep to the knife, lest they should infect our flocks: we destroy monstrous births, and we also drown our children if they are born weakly or unnaturally formed; to separate what is useless from what is sound is an act, not of anger, but of reason. Nothing becomes one who inflicts punishment less than anger, because the punishment has all the more power to work reformation if the sentence be pronounced with deliberate judgment. This is why Socrates said to the slave, "I would strike you, were I not angry." He put off the correction of the slave to a calmer season; at the moment, he corrected himself. Who can boast that he has his passions, under control, when Socrates did not dare to trust himself to his anger?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
Does a man hate his own limbs when he cuts them off? That's not anger — it's a sad but necessary cure. We put down rabid dogs. We slaughter wild bulls. We kill diseased sheep before they infect the herd. We destroy monsters when they're born, and we even drown our own children if they're born too weak or deformed. Separating what's harmful from what's healthy isn't anger — it's reason.

Nothing hurts punishment more than anger. Punishment works better when it comes from careful thought, not emotion. That's why Socrates told his slave, "I would hit you if I weren't angry." He waited for a calmer moment to correct the slave. Right then, he corrected himself instead. Who can claim to control their emotions when even Socrates didn't trust himself when he was angry?

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
We do not, therefore, need an angry chastiser to punish the
erring and wicked: for since anger is a crime of the mind, it is
not right that sins should be punished by sin. “What! am I not to
be angry with a robber, or a poisoner?” No: for I am not angry with
myself when I bleed myself. I apply all kinds of punishment as
remedies. You are as yet only in the first stage of error, and do
not go wrong seriously, although you do so often: then I will try
to amend you by a reprimand given first in private and then in
public.[4] You, again, have gone too far to be restored to
virtue by words alone; you must be kept in order by disgrace. For
the next, some stronger measure is required, something that he can
feel must be branded upon him; you, sir, shall be sent into exile
and to a desert place. The next man’s thorough villany needs harsher
remedies: chains and public imprisonment must be applied to him.
You, lastly, have an incurably vicious mind, and add crime to crime:
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: So we don't need an angry person to punish those who do wrong. Since anger is itself a mental crime, it's wrong to punish sins with sin. "What! Should I not be angry with a robber or a poisoner?" No — I'm not angry with myself when I draw my own blood for medical treatment. I use all kinds of punishment as medicine. You are still in the early stage of error. You don't sin seriously, though you do it often. I'll try to fix you with a private warning first, then a public one. You have gone too far to be restored by words alone. You must be controlled through shame. The next person needs something stronger — something that will leave a lasting mark. You, sir, will be sent into exile to a remote place. The next man's complete wickedness needs harsher medicine: chains and public prison. You, finally, have a mind that cannot be cured. You pile crime upon crime.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
you have come to such a pass, that you are not influenced by the
arguments which are never wanting to recommend evil, but sin itself
is to you a sufficient reason for sinning: you have so steeped your
whole heart in wickedness, that wickedness cannot be taken from you
without bringing your heart with it. Wretched man! you have long
sought to die; we will do you good service, we will take away that
madness from which you suffer, and to you who have so long lived a
misery to yourself and to others, we will give the only good thing
which remains, that is, death.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: You have reached the point where you don't even need bad reasons to do evil anymore. Sin itself is reason enough for you to sin. You have soaked your whole heart in wickedness so completely that we can't remove the evil without destroying you entirely. You miserable man! You have wanted to die for a long time. We will do you a favor. We will take away the madness you suffer from. You have been a misery to yourself and everyone else for so long. We will give you the only good thing left for you — death.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Why should I be angry with a man
just when I am doing him good: sometimes the truest form of compassion
is to put a man to death. If I were a skilled and learned physician,
and were to enter a hospital, or a rich[5] man’s house, I should
not have prescribed the same treatment for all the patients who
were suffering from various diseases. I see different kinds of vice
in the vast number of different minds, and am called in to heal the
whole body of citizens: let us seek for the remedies proper for
each disease.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Why should I be angry with someone when I'm actually helping them? Sometimes the kindest thing you can do is put someone to death. If I were a skilled doctor entering a hospital or a wealthy person's home, I wouldn't give the same treatment to every patient with different diseases. I see many kinds of vice in all these different minds, and I've been called to heal the entire community. Let's find the right cure for each disease.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
This man may be cured by his own sense of honour,
that one by travel, that one by pain, that one by want, that one
by the sword. If, therefore, it becomes my duty as a magistrate to
put on black[6] robes, and summon an assembly by the sound of a
trumpet,[7] I shall walk to the seat of judgment not in a rage
or in a hostile spirit, but with the countenance of a judge; I shall
pronounce the formal sentence in a grave and gentle rather than a
furious voice, and shall bid them proceed sternly, yet not
angrily. Even when I command a criminal to be beheaded, when I sew
a parricide up in a sack, when I send a man to be punished by
military law, when I fling a traitor or public enemy down the
Tarpeian Rock, I shall be free from anger, and shall look and feel
just as though I were crushing snakes and other venomous creatures.
“Anger is necessary to enable us to punish.” What? do you think
that the law is angry with men whom it does not know, whom it has
never seen, who it hopes will never exist?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: One person might be cured by appealing to his sense of honor. Another might need to travel and see the world. Another might need to experience pain, poverty, or even death. So when I put on my judge's robes and call court to session with the trumpet, I won't walk to my seat filled with rage or hatred. I'll have the calm face of a judge. I'll speak the formal sentence in a serious but gentle voice — stern, but not angry. Even when I order someone beheaded, or sew a murderer into a sack, or send someone to military punishment, or throw a traitor off the Tarpeian Rock — I'll be free from anger. I'll feel like I'm just crushing snakes and poisonous creatures. "But anger is necessary for punishment!" Really? Do you think the law itself is angry with people it doesn't know, has never seen, and hopes will never exist?

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
We ought, therefore, to
adopt the law’s frame of mind, which does not become angry, but
merely defines offences: for, if it is right for a good man to be
angry at wicked crimes, it will also be right for him to be moved
with envy at the prosperity of wicked men: what, indeed, is more
scandalous than that in some cases the very men, for whose deserts
no fortune could be found bad enough, should flourish and actually
be the spoiled children of success? Yet he will see their affluence
without envy, just as he sees their crimes without anger: a good
judge condemns wrongful acts, but does not hate them. “What then?
when the wise man is dealing with something of this kind, will his
mind not be affected by it and become excited beyond its usual
wont?” I admit that it will: he will experience a slight and trifling
emotion; for, as Zeno says, “Even in the mind of the wise man, a
scar remains after the wound is quite healed.” He will, therefore,
feel certain hints and semblances of passions; but he will be free
from the passions themselves.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: So we should think like the law thinks. The law doesn't get angry — it just defines what counts as wrongdoing. If it's right for a good person to get angry at wicked crimes, then it would also be right for him to feel envious when wicked people prosper. And what could be more outrageous? Sometimes the very people who deserve the worst possible fate are the ones who flourish and get spoiled by success. Yet a good person will see their wealth without envy, just as he sees their crimes without anger. A good judge condemns wrong acts but doesn't hate them. "But wait — when the wise man deals with this kind of thing, won't his mind be affected? Won't he get stirred up more than usual?" I admit he will. He'll feel a slight, small emotion. As Zeno says, "Even in the wise man's mind, a scar remains after the wound has completely healed." So he'll feel certain hints and shadows of emotion. But he'll be free from the emotions themselves.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Aristotle says that "certain passions, if one makes a proper use of them, act as arms": which would be true if, like weapons of war, they could be taken up or laid aside at the pleasure of their wielder. These arms, which Aristotle assigns to virtue, fight of their own accord, do not wait to be seized by the hand, and possess a man instead of being possessed by him. We have no need of external weapons, nature has equipped us sufficiently by giving us reason. She has bestowed this weapon upon us, which is strong, imperishable, and obedient to our will, not uncertain or capable of being turned against its master. Reason suffices by itself not merely to take thought for the future, but to manage our affairs: what, then, can be more foolish than for reason to beg anger for protection, that is, for what is certain to beg of what is uncertain? what is trustworthy of what is faithless? what is whole of what is sick?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Aristotle says that certain emotions, if used properly, can act like weapons. This might be true if emotions were like real weapons — something you could pick up or put down whenever you wanted. But these emotional 'weapons' that Aristotle gives to virtue fight on their own. They don't wait for you to grab them. They possess you instead of you possessing them. We don't need external weapons. Nature has already equipped us perfectly by giving us reason. She gave us this weapon that is strong, lasting, and obedient to our will. It's not unreliable or likely to turn against us. Reason alone is enough not just to plan for the future, but to handle all our problems. So what could be more foolish than for reason to beg anger for protection? Why would something reliable ask for help from something unreliable? Why would something trustworthy depend on something faithless? Why would something healthy rely on something sick?

on-anger_book-1.originalText: What, indeed? since reason is far more powerful by itself even in performing those operations in which the help of anger seems especially needful: for when reason has decided that a particular thing should be done, she perseveres in doing it; not being able to find anything better than herself to exchange with. She, therefore, abides by her purpose when it has once been formed; whereas anger is often overcome by pity: for it possesses no firm strength, but merely swells like an empty bladder, and makes a violent beginning, just like the winds which rise from the earth and are caused by rivers and marshes, which blow furiously without any continuance: anger begins with a mighty rush, and then falls away, becoming fatigued too soon: that which but lately thought of nothing but cruelty and novel forms of torture, is become quite softened and gentle when the time comes for punishment to be inflicted.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Actually, reason is far more powerful on its own, even in situations where anger seems most useful. When reason decides something should be done, it sticks with it. It can't find anything better than itself to trade places with. So once reason makes up its mind, it stays committed. But anger often gets overcome by pity. Anger has no real strength — it just puffs up like an empty balloon and makes a big show at first. It's like winds that rise from rivers and swamps. They blow hard but don't last. Anger starts with a huge rush, then collapses and gets tired too quickly. The same anger that was just thinking about cruelty and new ways to torture someone becomes soft and gentle when it's actually time to punish.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Passion soon cools, whereas reason is always consistent: yet even in cases where anger has continued to burn, it often happens that although there may be many who deserve to die, yet after the death of two or three it ceases to slay. Its first onset is fierce, just as the teeth of snakes when first roused from their lair are venomous, but become harmless after repeated bites have exhausted their poison. Consequently those who are equally guilty are not equally punished, and often he who has done less is punished more, because he fell in the way of anger when it was fresher. It is altogether irregular; at one time it runs into undue excess, at another it falls short of its duty: for it indulges its own feelings and gives sentence according to its caprices, will not listen to evidence, allows the defence no opportunity of being heard, clings to what it has wrongly assumed, and will not suffer its opinion to be wrested from it, even when it is a mistaken one.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Passion cools off quickly, but reason stays consistent. Even when anger keeps burning, it often stops killing after two or three deaths, even though many more people deserve to die. Anger's first attack is fierce. It's like a snake fresh from its den — its bite is most poisonous at first, but becomes harmless after it bites repeatedly and uses up its venom. So people who are equally guilty don't get punished equally. Often the person who did less wrong gets punished more, just because he crossed anger's path when it was still fresh. Anger is completely unpredictable. Sometimes it goes too far, sometimes it doesn't go far enough. It follows its own feelings and makes decisions based on its moods. It won't listen to evidence. It won't let the defense speak. It clings to whatever it assumed was true, even when it's wrong. And it won't let anyone change its mind, even when it made a mistake.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Reason gives each side time to plead; moreover, she herself
demands adjournment, that she may have sufficient scope for the
discovery of the truth; whereas anger is in a hurry: reason wishes
to give a just decision; anger wishes its decision to be thought
just: reason looks no further than the matter in hand; anger is
excited by empty matters hovering on the outskirts of the case: it
is irritated by anything approaching to a confident demeanour, a
loud voice, an unrestrained speech, dainty apparel, high-flown
pleading, or popularity with the public. It often condemns a man
because it dislikes his patron;
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Reason gives both sides time to make their case. It asks for more time to find the truth. But anger is always in a rush. Reason wants to make a fair decision.
