Anger just wants its decision to look fair. Reason focuses only on the facts that matter. Anger gets worked up over meaningless details that have nothing to do with the case. It gets annoyed by confident behavior, loud voices, bold speech, fancy clothes, dramatic arguments, or popularity with the crowd. It often condemns a person just because it doesn't like their lawyer.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
it loves and maintains error even
when truth is staring it in the face. It hates to be proved wrong,
and thinks it more honourable to persevere in a mistaken line of
conduct than to retract it. I remember Gnaeus Piso, a man who was
free from many vices, yet of a perverse disposition, and one who
mistook harshness for consistency. In his anger he ordered a soldier
to be led off to execution because he had returned from furlough
without his comrade, as though he must have murdered him if he could
not show him. When the man asked for time for search, he would not
grant it:
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Anger loves its mistakes and clings to them even when the truth is obvious. It hates being proven wrong. It thinks it's more honorable to stick with a bad decision than to admit error. I remember Gnaeus Piso, a man who avoided many vices but had a twisted nature. He confused cruelty with being consistent. In his anger, he ordered a soldier to be executed because the man returned from leave without his companion. Piso assumed the soldier must have killed his friend if he couldn't produce him. When the soldier begged for time to search for his missing comrade, Piso refused.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
the condemned man was brought outside the rampart, and
was just offering his neck to the axe, when suddenly there appeared
his comrade who was thought to be slain. Hereupon the centurion in
charge of the execution bade the guardsman sheathe his sword, and
led the condemned man back to Piso, to restore to him the
innocence which Fortune had restored to the soldier. They were led
into his presence by their fellow soldiers amid the great joy of
the whole camp, embracing one another and accompanied by a vast
crowd. Piso mounted the tribunal in a fury and ordered them both
to be executed, both him who had not murdered and him who had not
been slain.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: The condemned soldier was brought outside the camp walls. He was about to put his neck on the execution block when suddenly his missing comrade appeared — the one everyone thought was dead. The centurion in charge of the execution told the guardsman to put away his sword. He led the condemned man back to Piso to restore his innocence, since Fortune had restored the missing soldier to life. The whole camp celebrated as fellow soldiers led both men to Piso. They embraced each other, followed by a huge crowd of cheering soldiers. Piso climbed onto his judgment platform in a rage and ordered both men executed — the one who hadn't murdered anyone and the one who hadn't been killed.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
What could be more unworthy than this? Because one was
proved to be innocent, two perished. Piso even added a third: for
he actually ordered the centurion, who had brought back the condemned
man, to be put to death. Three men were set up to die in the same
place because one was innocent. O, how clever is anger at inventing
reasons for its frenzy! “You,” it says, “I order to be executed,
because you have been condemned to death: you, because you have
been the cause of your comrade’s condemnation, and you, because
when ordered to put him to death you disobeyed your general.” He
discovered the means of charging them with three crimes, because
he could find no crime in them.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: What could be more unfair than this? Because one man was proven innocent, two men died. Piso even added a third victim. He ordered the centurion who had brought back the condemned man to be executed too. Three men were sentenced to die in the same spot because one was innocent. Look how clever anger is at finding excuses for its madness! "You," anger says, "I order you executed because you were condemned to death. You, because you caused your friend's death sentence. And you, because you disobeyed your general when he told you to kill him." Piso found ways to charge them with three different crimes because he couldn't find any real crime in them.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Irascibility, I say, has this fault—it is loth to be ruled: it is angry with the truth itself, if it comes to light against its will: it assails those whom it has marked for its victims with shouting and riotous noise and gesticulation of the entire body, together with reproaches and curses. Not thus does reason act: but if it must be so, she silently and quietly wipes out whole households, destroys entire families of the enemies of the state, together with their wives and children, throws down their very dwellings, levels them with the ground, and roots out the names of those who are the foes of liberty. This she does without grinding her teeth or shaking her head, or doing anything unbecoming to a judge, whose countenance ought to be especially calm and composed at the time when he is pronouncing an important sentence.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Anger has this terrible flaw — it refuses to be controlled. It gets angry at the truth itself when the truth comes out against its wishes. It attacks its victims with shouting, wild noise, and wild gestures of the whole body. It hurls insults and curses. Reason doesn't act this way. When reason must destroy people, it quietly wipes out whole families. It destroys entire households of enemies of the state, along with their wives and children. It tears down their homes, levels them to the ground, and erases the very names of those who threaten freedom. But reason does all this without grinding its teeth or shaking its head. It does nothing unfit for a judge, whose face should be especially calm and composed when pronouncing an important sentence.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "What need is there," asks Hieronymus, "for you to bite your own lips when you want to strike some one?" What would he have said, had he seen a proconsul leap down from the tribunal, snatch the fasces from the lictor, and tear his own clothes because those of others were not torn as fast as he wished. Why need you upset the table, throw down the drinking cups, knock yourself against the columns, tear your hair, smite your thigh and your breast? How vehement do you suppose anger to be, if it thus turns back upon itself, because it cannot find vent on another as fast as it wishes? Such men, therefore, are held back by the bystanders and are begged to become reconciled with themselves.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "Why do you bite your own lips when you want to hit someone?" asks Hieronymus. What would he have said if he had seen a Roman governor jump down from his judgment seat, grab the ceremonial rods from his attendant, and rip his own clothes because other people's weren't being torn fast enough for his liking? Why do you need to flip the table, throw down the cups, bang yourself against the pillars, pull your hair, and beat your thighs and chest? How violent do you think anger must be if it turns on itself this way — just because it can't attack others as quickly as it wants? People like this have to be held back by bystanders and begged to make peace with themselves.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: But he who while free from anger assigns to each man the penalty which he deserves, does none of these things. He often lets a man go after detecting his crime, if his penitence for what he has done gives good hope for the future, if he perceives that the man's wickedness is not deeply rooted in his mind, but is only, as the saying is, skin-deep. He will grant impunity in cases where it will hurt neither the receiver nor the giver. In some cases he will punish great crimes more leniently than lesser ones, if the former were the result of momentary impulse, not of cruelty, while the latter were instinct with secret, underhand, long-practised craftiness. The same fault, committed by two separate men, will not be visited by him with the same penalty, if the one was guilty of it through carelessness, the other with a premeditated intention of doing mischief.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: But a person who stays calm while deciding what punishment someone deserves acts very differently. They often let someone go free after catching them in a crime — if the person shows real regret and seems likely to change. They can tell when someone's badness isn't deep-rooted, but just surface-level, as people say. They'll show mercy when it won't harm either the criminal or society. Sometimes they'll punish major crimes more gently than minor ones. A serious crime might have been a momentary lapse, while a small crime might show long-practiced sneakiness and cruelty. When two people commit the same offense, this judge won't give them the same punishment. One person might have acted carelessly, while the other planned to cause harm.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: In all dealing with crime he will remember that the one form of punishment is meant to make bad men better, and the other to put them out of the way. In either case he will look to the future, not to the past: for, as Plato says, "no wise man punishes any one because he has sinned, but that he may sin no more: for what is past cannot be recalled, but what is to come may be checked." Those, too, whom he wishes to make examples of the ill success of wickedness, he executes publicly, not merely in order that they themselves may die, but that by dying they may deter others from doing likewise. You see how free from any mental disturbance a man ought to be who has to weigh and consider all this, when he deals with a matter which ought to be handled with the utmost care, I mean, the power of life and death. The sword of justice is ill-placed in the hands of an angry man.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: When dealing with crime, the judge will remember that punishment has two purposes. One is to make bad people better. The other is to remove them from society. Either way, he looks to the future, not the past. As Plato says, "No wise man punishes someone because they sinned, but so they won't sin again. The past cannot be undone, but the future can be changed." Some criminals he executes publicly. Not just so they die, but so their death will warn others not to follow their path. You can see how calm and clear-headed a man must be when he weighs all these factors. He's dealing with matters of life and death — decisions that require the utmost care. Justice wielded by an angry man is dangerous.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Neither ought it to be believed that anger contributes anything to magnanimity: what it gives is not magnanimity but vain glory. The increase which disease produces in bodies swollen with morbid humours is not healthy growth, but bloated corpulence. All those whose madness raises them above human considerations, believe themselves to be inspired with high and sublime ideas; but there is no solid ground beneath, and what is built without foundation is liable to collapse in ruin. Anger has no ground to stand upon, and does not rise from a firm and enduring foundation, but is a windy, empty quality, as far removed from true magnanimity as fool-hardiness from courage, boastfulness from confidence, gloom from austerity, cruelty from strictness. There is, I say, a great difference between a lofty and a proud mind: anger brings about nothing grand or beautiful.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Don't think that anger makes you brave or noble. What it gives you isn't true greatness — it's just empty pride. When disease makes a body swell up, that's not healthy growth. It's just bloating. People who let madness lift them above normal human concerns think they're having deep, elevated thoughts. But there's nothing solid underneath. What you build without a foundation will collapse. Anger has no foundation to stand on. It doesn't grow from anything firm or lasting. It's just windy emptiness. Anger is as far from true greatness as recklessness is from real courage, as bragging is from confidence, as moodiness is from discipline, as cruelty is from being strict. There's a huge difference between having a noble mind and just being proud. Anger never creates anything grand or beautiful.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: On the other hand, to be constantly irritated seems to me to be the part of a languid and unhappy mind, conscious of its own feebleness, like folk with diseased bodies covered with sores, who cry out at the lightest touch. Anger, therefore, is a vice which for the most part affects women and children. "Yet it affects men also." Because many men, too, have womanish or childish intellects. "But what are we to say? do not some words fall from angry men which appear to flow from a great mind?" Yes, to those who know not what true greatness is: as, for example, that foul and hateful saying, "Let them hate me, provided they fear me," which you may be sure was written in Sulla's time.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: On the other hand, getting constantly irritated seems to me like the mark of a weak and miserable mind. It shows you're aware of your own weakness. It's like people with diseased bodies covered in sores who scream at the slightest touch. So anger is mostly a vice that affects women and children. "But it affects men too." That's because many men have minds like women or children. "But what should we say? Don't some words from angry men seem to come from a great mind?" Yes, they do — to people who don't know what true greatness actually is. For example, that disgusting and hateful saying: "Let them hate me, as long as they fear me." You can be sure that was written during Sulla's time.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: I know not which was the worse of the two things he wished for, that he might be hated or that he might be feared. It occurs to his mind that some day people will curse him, plot against him, crush him: what prayer does he add to this? May all the gods curse him—for discovering a cure for hate so worthy of it. "Let them hate." How? "Provided they obey me?" No! "Provided they approve of me?" No! How then? "Provided they fear me!" I would not even be loved upon such terms. Do you imagine that this was a very spirited saying? You are wrong: this is not greatness, but monstrosity.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: I don't know which was worse — wanting to be hated or wanting to be feared. He knows that someday people will curse him, plot against him, and destroy him. And what does he pray for? May the gods curse him for finding such a twisted solution to hatred! "Let them hate me." How? "As long as they obey me?" No! "As long as they approve of me?" No! Then how? "As long as they fear me!" I wouldn't even want to be loved on those terms. Do you think this was a bold, heroic statement? You're wrong. This isn't greatness — it's monstrous.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: You should not believe the words of angry men, whose speech is very loud and menacing, while their mind within them is as timid as possible: nor need you suppose that the most eloquent of men, Titus Livius, was right in describing somebody as being "of a great rather than a good disposition." The things cannot be separated: he must either be good or else he cannot be great, because I take greatness of mind to mean that it is unshaken, sound throughout, firm and uniform to its very foundation; such as cannot exist in evil dispositions. Such dispositions may be terrible, frantic, and destructive, but cannot possess greatness; because greatness rests upon goodness, and owes its strength to it.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Don't believe angry people when they shout and make threats. Their words sound loud and scary, but inside they're actually cowards. And don't think the great historian Titus Livy was right when he described someone as having "a great spirit rather than a good one." You can't separate these things. A person must be good, or they can't be great. True greatness of mind means being unshaken, sound all the way through, firm and consistent right down to the foundation. Evil people can't have this kind of greatness. They might be terrifying, wild, and destructive — but they can't be great. Greatness rests on goodness and gets its strength from it.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "Yet by speech, action, and all outward show they will make one think them great." True, they will say something which you may think shows a great spirit, like Gaius Caesar, who when angry with heaven because it interfered with his ballet-dancers, whom he imitated more carefully than he attended to them when they acted, and because it frightened his revels by its thunders, surely ill-directed, challenged Jove to fight, and that to the death, shouting the Homeric verse:— "Carry me off, or I will carry thee!" How great was his madness! He must have believed either that he could not be hurt even by Jupiter himself, or that he could hurt even Jupiter itself. I imagine that this saying of his had no small weight in nerving the minds of the conspirators for their task: for it seemed to be the height of endurance to bear one who could not bear Jupiter.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "But they'll use their words, actions, and outward behavior to make you think they're great." True enough. They'll say things that seem to show a great spirit. Take Gaius Caesar, for example. When he got angry at the heavens for interfering with his ballet dancers — whom he copied more carefully than he watched when they performed — and for scaring his parties with thunder that was surely misdirected, he challenged Jupiter to a fight to the death. He shouted the line from Homer: "Carry me off, or I will carry you!" What complete madness! He must have believed either that Jupiter himself couldn't hurt him, or that he could hurt Jupiter. I suspect this saying of his played no small part in giving the conspirators the courage they needed for their task. It seemed unbearable to put up with someone who couldn't even put up with Jupiter.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
There is therefore nothing great or noble in anger, even when
it seems to be powerful and to contemn both gods and men alike. Any
one who thinks that anger produces greatness of mind, would think
that luxury produces it: such a man wishes to rest on ivory, to be
clothed with purple, and roofed with gold; to remove lands, embank
seas, hasten the course of rivers, suspend woods in the air. He
would think that avarice shows greatness of mind: for the avaricious
man broods over heaps of gold and silver, treats whole provinces
as merely fields on his estate, and has larger tracts of country
under the charge of single bailiffs than those which consuls once
drew lots to administer.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: There is nothing great or noble about anger, even when it seems powerful and scorns both gods and people. Anyone who thinks anger creates greatness of mind would also think luxury creates it. Such a person wants to rest on ivory, wear purple clothes, and live under golden roofs. He wants to move entire lands, build dikes in the sea, change the course of rivers, and hang forests in the air. He would think greed shows greatness of mind too. The greedy man sits on piles of gold and silver. He treats whole provinces like fields on his personal estate. He has single managers overseeing larger territories than consuls once governed by lottery.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
He would think that lust shows greatness
of mind: for the lustful man swims across straits, castrates troops
of boys, and puts himself within reach of the swords of injured
husbands with complete scorn of death. Ambition, too, he would think
shows greatness of mind: for the ambitious man is not content with
office once a year, but, if possible, would fill the calendar of
dignities with his name alone, and cover the whole world with his
titles. It matters nothing to what heights or lengths these passions
may proceed: they are narrow, pitiable, grovelling. Virtue alone
is lofty and sublime, nor is anything great which is not at the
same time tranquil.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: He would think that lust shows greatness of mind too. The lustful man swims across dangerous waters, mutilates groups of young men, and faces the swords of angry husbands without fear of death. He would also think ambition shows greatness of mind. The ambitious person isn't satisfied with holding office once a year. If he could, he would fill every position with his own name and cover the whole world with his titles. It doesn't matter how high or far these passions reach. They are all narrow, pitiful, and low. Only virtue is truly lofty and noble. Nothing is great unless it is also peaceful.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
My first book, Novatus, had a more abundant subject: for carriages
roll easily down hill:[1] now we must proceed to drier matters. The
question before us is whether anger arises from deliberate choice
or from impulse, that is, whether it acts of its own accord or like
the greater part of those passions which spring up within us without
our knowledge. It is necessary for our debate to stoop to the
consideration of these matters, in order that it may afterwards be
able to rise to loftier themes; for likewise in our bodies the parts
which are first set in order are the bones, sinews, and joints,
which are by no means fair to see, albeit they are the foundation
of our frame and essential to its life: next to them come the parts
of which all beauty of face and appearance consists; and after
these, colour, which above all else charms the eye, is applied last
of all, when the rest of the body is complete.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: My first book, Novatus, had an easier topic to write about. Carriages roll downhill without effort. Now we must tackle drier, harder material. The question before us is this: Does anger come from deliberate choice or from impulse? Does it act on its own, or is it like most passions that spring up inside us without our knowledge? We need to examine these basic matters first. Only then can we rise to higher themes. Think of the human body. First we set the bones, tendons, and joints in place. These parts aren't beautiful to look at, but they're the foundation of our frame and essential to life. Next come the parts that create all the beauty of face and appearance. Finally, color is applied last of all — the thing that charms the eye most — but only after the rest of the body is complete.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
There is no doubt
that anger is roused by the appearance of an injury being done:
but the question before us is, whether anger straightway follows
the appearance, and springs up without assistance from the mind,
or whether it is roused with the sympathy of the mind. Our (the
Stoics’) opinion is, that anger can venture upon nothing by itself,
without the approval of mind: for to conceive the idea of a wrong
having been done, to long to avenge it, and to join the two
propositions, that we ought not to have been injured and that it
is our duty to avenge our injuries, cannot belong to a mere impulse
which is excited without our consent. That impulse is a simple act;
this is a complex one, and composed of several parts. The man
understands something to have happened: he becomes indignant thereat:
he condemns the deed; and he avenges it. All these things cannot
be done without his mind agreeing to those matters which touched
him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
Everyone agrees that anger starts when we think someone has wronged us. But here's the key question: Does anger follow immediately after that thought? Or does it need our mind's permission first?

We Stoics believe anger cannot act on its own without the mind's approval. Think about what happens: We believe we've been wronged. We want revenge. We decide that we shouldn't have been hurt and that we must strike back. This isn't just a simple impulse that happens without our say-so. It's actually complex, made up of several parts.

Here's what really happens: A person sees what happened. He gets outraged. He judges the action as wrong. Then he seeks revenge. None of these steps can happen unless his mind agrees to be affected by what touched him.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Whither, say you, does this inquiry tend? That we may know what
anger is: for if it springs up against our will, it never will yield
to reason: because all the motions which take place without our
volition are beyond our control and unavoidable, such as shivering
when cold water is poured over us, or shrinking when we are touched
in certain places. Men’s hair rises up at bad news, their faces
blush at indecent words, and they are seized with dizziness when
looking down a precipice; and as it is not in our power to prevent
any of these things, no reasoning can prevent their taking place.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Where is this discussion heading, you ask? We need to understand what anger really is. If anger happens against our will, then reason will never be able to control it. All the reactions that happen without our choice are beyond our control. We can't avoid them. Think about shivering when cold water hits you. Or flinching when someone touches a sensitive spot. Your hair stands up at terrible news. Your face turns red at dirty jokes. You get dizzy looking down a cliff. We have no power to stop any of these things. No amount of reasoning can prevent them from happening.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
But anger can be put to flight by wise maxims; for it is a voluntary
defect of the mind, and not one of those things which are evolved
by the conditions of human life, and which, therefore, may happen
even to the wisest of us. Among these and in the first place must
be ranked that thrill of the mind which seizes us at the thought
of wrongdoing. We feel this even when witnessing the mimic scenes
of the stage, or when reading about things that happened long ago.
We often feel angry with Clodius for banishing Cicero, and
with Antonius for murdering him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: But anger can be driven away by wise thinking. Anger is a choice we make with our minds — it's not one of those things that just happen because we're human. Even the wisest people experience those automatic reactions. The first example is that gut feeling we get when we think about something wrong happening. We feel this even when watching plays or reading about things that happened long ago. We often get angry at Clodius for exiling Cicero, and at Antonius for killing him.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Who is not indignant with the wars
of Marius, the proscriptions of Sulla? who is not enraged against
Theodotus and Achillas and the boy king who dared to commit a more
than boyish crime?[2] Sometimes songs excite us, and quickened
rhythm and the martial noise of trumpets; so, too, shocking pictures
and the dreadful sight of tortures, however well deserved, affect
our minds. Hence it is that we smile when others are smiling, that
a crowd of mourners makes us sad, and that we take a glowing interest
in another’s battles;
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Who doesn't feel outraged by Marius's wars or Sulla's mass executions? Who isn't furious at Theodotus, Achillas, and that boy king who committed a crime far worse than anything you'd expect from a child? Sometimes music stirs us up — a fast beat or the warlike sound of trumpets. Disturbing paintings and horrible scenes of torture affect our minds too, even when the punishment is deserved. This is why we smile when others smile. A crowd of mourners makes us sad. We get caught up in other people's fights.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
all of which feelings are not anger, any more
than that which clouds our brow at the sight of a stage shipwreck
is sadness, or what we feel, when we read how Hannibal after Cannae
beset the walls of Rome, can be called fear. All these are emotions
of minds which are loth to be moved, and are not passions, but
rudiments which may grow into passions. So, too, a soldier starts
at the sound of a trumpet, although he may be dressed as a civilian
and in the midst of a profound peace, and camp horses prick up their
ears at the clash of arms. It is said that Alexander, when Xenophantus
was singing, laid his hand upon his weapons.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: None of these feelings are actual anger. When we frown at a shipwreck on stage, that's not real sadness. When we read about Hannibal attacking Rome after his victory at Cannae, what we feel isn't true fear. These are just stirrings in minds that don't want to be disturbed. They're not real passions — they're seeds that could grow into passions. A soldier will jump at the sound of a trumpet even when he's in civilian clothes during peacetime. War horses perk up their ears when they hear weapons clashing. They say that when Xenophantus was singing, Alexander reached for his sword.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
None of these things which casually influence the mind deserve
to be called passions: the mind, if I may so express it, rather
suffers passions to act upon itself than forms them. A passion,
therefore, consists not in being affected by the sights which are
presented to us, but in giving way to our feelings and following
up these chance promptings: for whoever imagines that paleness,
bursting into tears, lustful feelings, deep sighs, sudden flashes
of the eyes, and so forth, are signs of passion and betray the
state of the mind, is mistaken, and does not understand that these
are merely impulses of the body. Consequently, the bravest of men
often turns pale while he is putting on his armour; when the signal
for battle is given, the knees of the boldest soldier shake for a
moment; the heart even of a great general leaps into his mouth just
before the lines clash together, and the hands and feet even of the
most eloquent orator grow stiff and cold while he is preparing to
begin his speech. Anger must not merely move, but break out of
bounds, being an impulse:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: None of these random reactions deserve to be called emotions. The mind doesn't create them — it just lets them happen to it. Real emotion isn't about being affected by what we see. It's about giving in to those feelings and following wherever they lead. Anyone who thinks that going pale, crying, feeling lust, sighing deeply, or having your eyes flash means you're emotional doesn't understand how this works. These are just physical reactions. That's why the bravest warrior often goes pale while putting on his armor. When the battle horn sounds, even the boldest soldier's knees shake for a moment. A great general's heart pounds right before armies clash. The most gifted speaker's hands and feet go cold and stiff before a speech begins. Anger doesn't just stir — it breaks free and takes control. It's an impulse that:

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
now, no impulse can take place without
the consent of the mind: for it cannot be that we should deal with
revenge and punishment without the mind being cognisant of them. A
man may think himself injured, may wish to avenge his wrongs, and
then may be persuaded by some reason or other to give up his intention
and calm down: I do not call that anger, it is an emotion of the
mind which is under the control of reason. Anger is that which goes
beyond reason and carries her away with it: wherefore the first
confusion of a man’s mind when struck by what seems an injury is
no more anger than the apparent injury itself: it is the subsequent
mad rush, which not only receives the impression of the apparent
injury, but acts upon it as true, that is anger, being an exciting
of the mind to revenge, which proceeds from choice and deliberate
resolve. There never has been any doubt that fear produces flight,
and anger a rush forward; consider, therefore, whether you suppose
that anything can be either sought or avoided without the participation
of the mind.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: No impulse can happen without the mind's approval. We cannot deal with revenge and punishment without the mind knowing about it. A man might think he has been wronged. He might want to get back at someone. Then he might be talked out of it and calm down. I would not call that anger. That is just a feeling that reason can control. Real anger goes beyond reason and drags reason along with it. So the first shock a person feels when they think they have been hurt is not anger yet. Neither is the seeming injury itself. The anger is what comes next — the wild rush that not only receives the impression of being hurt, but treats it as true and acts on it. That is anger: an excitement of the mind toward revenge that comes from choice and deliberate decision. No one has ever doubted that fear makes us run away, and anger makes us rush forward. Think about this: do you believe anything can be sought or avoided without the mind taking part?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Furthermore, that you may know in what manner passions begin
and swell and gain spirit, learn that the first emotion is involuntary,
and is, as it were, a preparation for a passion, and a threatening
of one. The next is combined with a wish, though not an obstinate
one, as, for example, “It is my duty to avenge myself, because I
have been injured,” or “It is right that this man should be
punished, because he has committed a crime.” The third emotion is
already beyond our control, because it overrides reason, and wishes
to avenge itself, not if it be its duty, but whether or no. We are
not able by means of reason to escape from that first impression
on the mind, any more than we can escape from those things which
we have mentioned as occurring to the body: we cannot prevent other
people’s yawns temping us to yawn:[3] we cannot help winking when
fingers are suddenly darted at our eyes. Reason is unable to overcome
these habits, which perhaps might be weakened by practice and
constant watchfulness: they differ from an emotion which is brought
into existence and brought to an end by a deliberate mental act.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: To understand how passions begin, grow, and take hold, you need to know there are three stages. The first emotion is automatic. It's like a warning that passion might be coming. The second stage combines with a wish, though not a stubborn one. For example: "I should get revenge because someone hurt me," or "This person should be punished because they committed a crime." The third emotion is already out of our control. It overrides reason and wants revenge whether it's right or not. We can't use reason to escape that first mental impression, just like we can't escape certain body reactions. We can't stop ourselves from yawning when others yawn. We can't help blinking when fingers suddenly dart toward our eyes. Reason can't overcome these habits. Maybe practice and constant attention could weaken them. But they're different from an emotion that starts and ends through deliberate mental action.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
We must also enquire whether those whose cruelty knows no bounds,
and who delight in shedding human blood, are angry when they kill
people from whom they have received no injury, and who they themselves
do not think have done them any injury; such as were Apollodorus
or Phalaris. This is not anger, it is ferocity: for it does not do
hurt because it has received injury: but is even willing to receive
injury, provided it may do hurt. It does not long to inflict stripes
and mangle bodies to avenge its wrongs, but for its own pleasure.
What then are we to say? This evil takes its rise from anger; for
anger, after it has by long use and indulgence made a man forget
mercy, and driven all feelings of human fellowship from his mind,
passes finally into cruelty. Such men therefore laugh, rejoice,
enjoy themselves greatly, and are as unlike as possible in countenance
to angry men, since cruelty is their relaxation.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We should also ask about people whose cruelty has no limits. These are the ones who enjoy spilling human blood. Are they angry when they kill people who never hurt them — people they don't even think wronged them? Think of tyrants like Apollodorus or Phalaris. This isn't anger. It's pure savagery. They don't hurt others because they were hurt first. They're willing to be hurt themselves if it means they get to hurt someone else. They don't want to beat and torture people to get revenge. They do it for fun. So what's going on here? This evil actually starts with anger. When anger gets fed and pampered for a long time, it makes a person forget mercy. It drives out all sense of human connection. Finally, it turns into cruelty. Men like this laugh and smile and have a great time. They look nothing like angry people, because cruelty has become their entertainment.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
It is said that
when Hannibal saw a trench full of human blood, he exclaimed, “O,
what a beauteous sight!” How much more beautiful would he have
thought it, if it had filled a river or a lake? Why should we wonder
that you should be charmed with this sight above all others, you
who were born in bloodshed and brought up amid slaughter from a
child? Fortune will follow you and favour your cruelty for twenty
years, and will display to you everywhere the sight that you love.
You will behold it both at Trasumene and at Cannae, and lastly at
your own city of Carthage. Volesus, who not long ago, under the
Emperor Augustus, was proconsul of Asia Minor, after he had one day
beheaded three hundred persons, strutted out among the corpses with
a haughty air, as though he had performed some grand and notable
exploit, and exclaimed in Greek, “What a kingly action!” What would
this man have done, had he been really a king? This was not anger,
but a greater and an incurable disease.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: They say that when Hannibal saw a ditch filled with human blood, he cried out, "What a beautiful sight!" How much more beautiful would he have thought it if the blood had filled a river or a lake? Why should we be surprised that you find this sight so charming? After all, you were born into violence and raised on slaughter from childhood. Fortune will smile on you and reward your cruelty for twenty years. It will show you this sight you love everywhere you go. You'll see it at Trasimene and at Cannae, and finally at your own city of Carthage. Take Volesus, who served as governor of Asia Minor under Emperor Augustus not long ago. After he beheaded three hundred people in one day, he strutted around among the corpses looking proud. He acted as if he had done something grand and remarkable, shouting in Greek, "What a kingly deed!" What would this man have done if he had actually been a king? This wasn't anger — it was something worse and beyond cure.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“Virtue,” argues our adversary, “ought to be angry with what
is base, just as she approves of what is honourable.” What should
we think if he said that virtue ought to be both mean and great;
yet this is what he means, when he wants her to be raised and
lowered, because joy at a good action is grand and glorious, while
anger at another’s sin is base and befits a narrow mind: and virtue
will never be guilty of imitating vice while she is repressing it;
she considers anger to deserve punishment for itself, since it often
is even more criminal than the faults which which it is angry. To
rejoice and be glad is the proper and natural function of virtue:
it is as much beneath her dignity to be angry, as to mourn:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "Virtue," our opponent argues, "should be angry at what is wrong, just as she approves of what is right." What would we think if he said virtue should be both small and great? Yet this is what he means when he wants her to be raised up and brought low. Joy at a good deed is noble and glorious. But anger at someone else's sin is petty and shows a narrow mind. Virtue will never stoop to copying vice while trying to stop it. She believes anger itself deserves punishment, since it is often worse than the wrongs it gets angry about. To rejoice and be glad is virtue's proper and natural job. Being angry is as beneath her dignity as mourning would be.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
now,
sorrow is the companion of anger, and all anger ends in sorrow,
either from remorse or from failure. Secondly, if it be the part
of the wise man to be angry with sins, he will be more angry the
greater they are, and will often be angry: from which it follows
that the wise man will not only be angry but irascible. Yet
if we do not believe that great and frequent anger can find any
place in the wise man’s mind, why should we not set him altogether
free from this passion? for there can be no limit, if he ought to
be angry in proportion to what every man does: because he will
either be unjust if he is equally angry at unequal crimes, or he
will be the most irascible of men, if he blazes into wrath as often
as crimes deserve his anger.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Now, sorrow always comes with anger. All anger ends in sorrow — either because you regret what you did, or because you failed to get what you wanted. Second, if wise people should be angry at sins, then they'll be angrier when the sins are worse. They'll be angry all the time. This means wise people wouldn't just get angry — they'd be angry people by nature. But we don't believe that constant, intense anger belongs in a wise person's mind. So why not free them from this emotion entirely? There can be no middle ground here. If wise people should be angry in proportion to what everyone does wrong, then they'll either be unfair (getting equally angry at different crimes) or they'll be the angriest people alive (raging every time someone does something that deserves anger).

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
What, too, can be more unworthy of the wise man, than that his
passions should depend upon the wickedness of others? If so, the
great Socrates will no longer be able to return home with the same
expression of countenance with which he set out. Moreover, if it
be the duty of the wise man to be angry at base deeds, and to be
excited and saddened at crimes, then is there nothing more unhappy
than the wise man, for all his life will be spent in anger and
grief. What moment will there be at which he will not see something
deserving of blame? whenever he leaves his house, he will be obliged
to walk among men who are criminals, misers, spendthrifts, profligates,
and who are happy in being so:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: What could be more unworthy of a wise person than letting their emotions depend on how wicked other people are? If that were true, then great Socrates could never come home with the same calm expression he had when he left. Besides, if wise people must get angry at bad behavior and get upset and sad about crimes, then no one would be more miserable than the wise. Their entire life would be spent angry and grieving. What moment would they have when they don't see something worth condemning? Every time they leave their house, they'd have to walk among criminals, greedy people, wasteful people, corrupt people — and people who are happy being that way.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
he can turn his eyes in no direction
without their finding something to shock them. He will faint, if
he demands anger from himself as often as reason calls for it. All
these thousands who are hurrying to the law courts at break of day,
how base are their causes, and how much baser their advocates? One
impugns his father’s will, when he would have done better to deserve
it; another appears as the accuser of his mother; a third comes to
inform against a man for committing the very crime of which he
himself is yet more notoriously guilty. The judge, too, is chosen
to condemn men for doing what he himself has done, and the audience
takes the wrong side, led astray by the fine voice of the pleader.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: He can't look anywhere without seeing something that shocks him. He'll collapse from exhaustion if he gets angry every time reason tells him to. Look at all those thousands rushing to the law courts at dawn. Their cases are shameful, and their lawyers are even worse. One person challenges his father's will when he should have earned his inheritance honestly. Another accuses his own mother. A third informs on someone for the exact crime he himself is more obviously guilty of. The judge is chosen to condemn people for doing what he himself has done. And the audience sides with whoever has the prettier voice.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Why need I dwell upon individual cases? Be assured, when you
see the Forum crowded with a multitude, the Saepta[4] swarming
with people, or the great Circus, in which the greater part of the
people find room to show themselves at once, that among them there
are as many vices as there are men. Among those whom you see in the
garb of peace there is no peace: for a small profit any one of them
will attempt the ruin of another: no one can gain anything save by
another’s loss. They hate the fortunate and despise the unfortunate:
they grudgingly endure the great, and oppress the small:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Why focus on specific examples? Just look around. When you see the Forum packed with crowds, the voting grounds swarming with people, or the great Circus where most of the city gathers at once — know this: there are as many vices as there are people. These folks may wear peaceful clothes, but there's no peace in their hearts. For a small profit, any one of them will try to destroy another person. No one can win unless someone else loses. They hate successful people and look down on the unfortunate. They resent those above them and crush those below.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
they are
fired by divers lusts: they would wreck everything for the sake of
a little pleasure or plunder: they live as though they were in a
school of gladiators, fighting with the same people with whom they
live: it is like a society of wild beasts, save that beasts are
tame with one another, and refrain from biting their own species,
whereas men tear one another, and gorge themselves upon one another.
They differ from dumb animals in this alone, that the latter are
tame with those who feed them, whereas the rage of the former preys
on those very persons by whom they were brought up.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: They burn with all kinds of desires. They would destroy everything for a bit of pleasure or profit. They live like gladiators in training — fighting with the same people they share their lives with. It's like a pack of wild animals, except that animals are gentle with their own kind and don't attack their own species. But humans tear each other apart and devour one another. Here's the one difference between us and dumb animals: animals are tame with those who feed them, but human rage turns on the very people who raised us.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: The wise man will never cease to be angry, if he once begins, so full is every place of vices and crimes. More evil is done than can be healed by punishment: men seem engaged in a vast race of wickedness. Every day there is greater eagerness to sin, less modesty. Throwing aside all reverence for what is better and more just, lust rushes whithersoever it thinks fit, and crimes are no longer committed by stealth, they take place before our eyes, and wickedness has become so general and gained such a footing in everyone's breast that innocence is no longer rare, but no longer exists. Do men break the law singly, or a few at a time? Nay, they rise in all quarters at once, as though obeying some universal signal, to wipe out the boundaries of right and wrong.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: A wise person would never stop being angry if they started. Every place is so full of vice and crime. More evil happens than punishment can ever fix. People seem caught up in a huge competition to see who can be most wicked. Each day brings more eagerness to sin and less shame. People have thrown aside all respect for what is good and just. Desire rushes wherever it wants to go. Crimes aren't even hidden anymore — they happen right in front of us. Wickedness has become so common and taken such deep root in everyone's heart that innocence isn't just rare anymore. It doesn't exist at all. Do people break the law one by one, or just a few at a time? No. They all rise up at once, as if responding to some universal signal, to destroy the line between right and wrong.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: "Host is not safe from guest, Father-in-law from son; but seldom love Exists 'twixt brothers; wives long to destroy Their husbands, husbands long to slay their wives, Stepmothers deadly aconite prepare And child-heirs wonder when their sires will die." And how small a part of men's crimes are these! The poet has not described one people divided into two hostile camps, parents and children enrolled on opposite sides, Rome set on fire by the hand of a Roman, troops of fierce horsemen scouring the country to track out the hiding-places of the proscribed, wells defiled with poison, plagues created by human hands, trenches dug by children round their beleaguered parents, crowded prisons, conflagrations that consume whole cities, gloomy tyrannies, secret plots to establish despotisms and ruin peoples, and men glorying in those deeds which, as long as it was possible to repress them, were counted as crimes—I mean rape, debauchery, and lust .
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Hosts aren't safe from their guests. Fathers-in-law aren't safe from their sons-in-law. Brothers rarely love each other. Wives want to kill their husbands. Husbands want to kill their wives. Stepmothers prepare deadly poison. Children wonder when their parents will finally die. But these are just a tiny part of human crimes! The poet hasn't even described nations splitting into two enemy camps, with parents and children fighting on opposite sides. Or Rome being burned down by Romans themselves. Or cavalry hunting down outlaws in hiding. Or wells poisoned on purpose. Or plagues created by human hands. Or children digging trenches around their own besieged parents. Or packed prisons, cities burning to the ground, dark tyrannies, secret plots to set up dictatorships and destroy entire peoples. And men taking pride in acts that used to be called crimes — rape, corruption, and lust.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: . . . . Add to these, public acts of national bad faith, broken treaties, everything that cannot defend itself carried off as plunder by the stronger, knaveries, thefts, frauds, and disownings of debt such as three of our present law-courts would not suffice to deal with. If you want the wise man to be as angry as the atrocity of men's crimes requires, he must not merely be angry, but must go mad with rage.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Add to these public acts of national betrayal, broken treaties, and the strong stealing everything they can from those who cannot defend themselves. Add fraud, theft, swindling, and people refusing to pay their debts — crimes so numerous that three of our current courts couldn't handle them all. If you want the wise man to be as angry as human wickedness deserves, he wouldn't just be angry. He would go completely insane with rage.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
You will rather think that we should not be angry with people’s
faults; for what shall we say of one who is angry with those who
stumble in the dark, or with deaf people who cannot hear his orders,
or with children, because they forget their duty and interest
themselves in the games and silly jokes of their companions? What
shall we say if you choose to be angry with weaklings for being
sick, for growing old, or becoming fatigued? Among the other
misfortunes of humanity is this, that men’s intellects are confused,
and they not only cannot help going wrong, but love to go wrong.
To avoid being angry with individuals, you must pardon the whole
mass, you must grant forgiveness to the entire human race. If you
are angry with young and old men because they do wrong, you will
be angry with infants also, for they soon will do wrong. Does any
one become angry with children, who are too young to comprehend
distinctions?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: You'll realize we shouldn't get angry at people's faults. Would you get angry at someone who stumbles in the dark? Or at deaf people who can't hear your orders? Or at children who forget their duties because they're distracted by games and silly jokes with their friends? Would you get angry at weak people for being sick, growing old, or getting tired? Here's another misfortune of being human: our minds are confused. We can't help making mistakes, and we actually love making mistakes. To avoid getting angry at individuals, you have to forgive everyone. You have to forgive the entire human race. If you get angry at young and old people for doing wrong, you might as well get angry at babies too — they'll do wrong soon enough. Does anyone get angry at children who are too young to understand right from wrong?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Yet, to be a human being is a greater and a better
excuse than to be a child. Thus are we born, as creatures liable
to as many disorders of the mind as of the body; not dull and
slow-witted, but making a bad use of our keenness of wit, and leading
one another into vice by our example. He who follows others who
have started before him on the wrong road is surely excusable for
having wandered on[6] the highway. A general’s severity may be shown
in the case of individual deserters; but where a whole army deserts,
it must needs be pardoned. What is it that puts a stop to the wise
man’s anger? It is the number of sinners. He perceives how unjust
and how dangerous it is to be angry with vices which all men share.
Heraclitcus, whenever he came out of doors and beheld around him
such a number of men who were living wretchedly, nay, rather perishing
wretchedly, used to weep:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Being human is an even better excuse than being a child. This is how we were born — with minds just as prone to disorders as our bodies. We aren't dull or slow. We're sharp, but we use that sharpness badly. We lead each other astray by our example. If someone follows others who started down the wrong path first, you can hardly blame them for getting lost on the highway. A general might punish individual deserters harshly, but when the whole army deserts, he has to forgive them all. What stops the wise person from getting angry? The sheer number of sinners. He realizes how unfair and dangerous it is to be angry about vices that everyone shares. Heraclitus used to weep whenever he went outside. He would see so many people living miserably — no, actually dying miserably:

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
he pitied all those who met him joyous
and happy. He was of a gentle but too weak disposition: and he
himself was one of those for whom he ought to have wept. Democritus,
on the other hand, is said never to have appeared in public without
laughing; so little did men’s serious occupations appear serious
to him. What room is there for anger? Everything ought either to
move us to tears or to laughter. The wise man will not be angry
with sinners. Why not? Because he knows that no one is born
wise, but becomes so: he knows that very few wise men are produced
in any age, because he thoroughly understands the circumstances of
human life. Now, no sane man is angry with nature: for what should
we say if a man chose to be surprised that fruit did not hang on
the thickets of a forest, or to wonder at bushes and thorns not
being covered with some useful berry? No one is angry when nature
excuses a defect.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Heraclitus pitied everyone he met who seemed joyful and happy. He had a gentle heart, but it was too weak. He was actually one of the people he should have wept for. Democritus took the opposite approach — he never appeared in public without laughing. He found human affairs so ridiculous that nothing seemed serious to him. Where does this leave room for anger? Everything should either make us cry or make us laugh. A wise person won't get angry at sinners. Why not? Because he knows that no one is born wise — wisdom must be earned. He knows that very few people in any generation actually become wise. He understands what human life is really like. No reasonable person gets angry at nature. What would you think of someone who was shocked that wild forest bushes don't grow fruit, or amazed that thorny shrubs don't produce useful berries? No one gets mad when nature has a built-in limitation.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
The wise man, therefore, being tranquil, and
dealing candidly with mistakes, not an enemy to but an improver of
sinners, will go abroad every day in the following frame of mind:—”Many
men will meet me who are drunkards, lustful, ungrateful, greedy,
and excited by the frenzy of ambition.” He will view all these as
benignly as a physician does his patients. When a man’s ship leaks
freely through its opened seams, does he become angry with the
sailors or the ship itself? No; instead of that, he tries to remedy
it: he shuts out some water, bales out some other, closes all the
holes that he can see, and by ceaseless labour counteracts those
which are out of sight and which let water into the hold; nor does
he relax his efforts because as much water as he pumps out runs in
again. We need a long-breathed struggle against permanent and
prolific evils; not, indeed, to quell them, but merely to prevent
their overpowering us.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: The wise man stays calm and deals honestly with mistakes. He's not an enemy of sinners — he tries to improve them. He goes out each day thinking: 'I'll meet many people today who are drunks, perverts, ingrates, greedy types, and power-hungry maniacs.' He views them all as kindly as a doctor views his patients. When a ship is taking on water through cracked boards, does the captain get angry at the sailors or the ship? No. He tries to fix it. He plugs some holes, bails out water, seals what he can see, and keeps working to stop the leaks he can't see. He doesn't give up just because water keeps pouring in as fast as he pumps it out. We need a long, steady fight against evils that never go away. Not to destroy them completely, but just to keep them from destroying us.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: "Anger," says our opponent, "is useful, because it avoids contempt, and because it frightens bad men." Now, in the first place, if anger is strong in proportion to its threats, it is hateful for the same reason that it is terrible: and it is more dangerous to be hated than to be despised. If, again, it is without strength, it is much more exposed to contempt, and cannot avoid ridicule; for what is more flat than anger when it breaks out into meaningless ravings? Moreover, because some things are somewhat terrible, they are not on that account desirable: nor does wisdom wish it to be said of the wise man, as it is of a wild beast, that the fear which he inspires is as a weapon to him. Why, do we not fear fever, gout, consuming ulcers? and is there, for that reason, any good in them? nay; on the other hand, they are all despised and thought to be foul and base, and are for this very reason feared. So, too, anger is in itself hideous and by no means to be feared; yet it is feared by many, just as a hideous mask is feared by children.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "Anger is useful," our opponent argues, "because it prevents people from looking down on you. It scares bad people away." But here's the problem with this reasoning. First, if anger gets its power from threats, then people hate it for the same reason they fear it. And being hated is more dangerous than being despised. Second, if anger has no real strength behind it, it becomes even more ridiculous. Nothing looks sillier than someone having a meaningless tantrum. Just because something is scary doesn't make it good. We don't want people to say about a wise person what they say about a wild animal — that fear is his only weapon. After all, we fear fever, gout, and painful sores. Does that make them good? Of course not. We despise these things as ugly and vile, and that's exactly why we fear them. Anger works the same way. It's hideous and shouldn't be feared at all. Yet many people do fear it — just like children are afraid of ugly masks.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: How can we answer the fact that terror always works back to him who inspired it, and that no one is feared who is himself at peace? At this point it is well that you should remember that verse of Laberius, which, when pronounced in the theatre during the height of the civil war, caught the fancy of the whole people as though it expressed the national feeling:— "He must fear many, whom so many fear." Thus has nature ordained, that whatever becomes great by causing fear to others is not free from fear itself. How disturbed lions are at the faintest noises! How excited those fiercest of beasts become at strange shadows, voices, or smells! Whatever is a terror to others, fears for itself.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Besides, terror always comes back to haunt the person who creates it. No one who lives in peace ever needs to be feared. Here's a line from the playwright Laberius that really struck home during our civil war. When actors spoke it on stage, the whole audience erupted because it captured exactly how everyone felt: "The person whom many fear must himself fear many." This is how nature works. Whatever grows powerful by making others afraid can never be free from fear itself. Watch how lions jump at the smallest sounds. See how the fiercest wild animals get spooked by unfamiliar shadows, voices, or smells. Whatever terrifies others is always terrified for itself.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: There can be no reason, therefore, for any wise man to wish to be feared, and no one need think that anger is anything great because it strikes terror, since even the most despicable things are feared, as, for example, noxious vermin whose bite is venomous: and since a string set with feathers stops the largest herds of wild beasts and guides them into traps, it is no wonder that from its effect it should be named a "Scarer."[7] Foolish creatures are frightened by foolish things: the movement of chariots and the sight of their wheels turning round drives lions back into their cage: elephants are frightened at the cries of pigs: and so also we fear anger just as children fear the dark, or wild beasts fear red feathers: it has in itself nothing solid or valiant, but it affects feeble minds.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: So there's no reason why any wise person would want to be feared. And don't think anger is powerful just because it scares people. Even the most pathetic things can be frightening — like poisonous bugs whose bite can kill you. A simple string with feathers attached can stop entire herds of wild animals and drive them into traps. That's why they call it a "scarer." Foolish creatures get scared by foolish things. The sound of chariots and sight of spinning wheels drives lions back into their cages. Elephants run from squealing pigs. We fear anger the same way children fear the dark or wild animals fear red feathers. Anger has nothing solid or brave about it. It only works on weak minds.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: "Wickedness," says our adversary, "must be removed from the system of nature, if you wish to remove anger: neither of which things can be done." In the first place, it is possible for a man not to be cold, although according to the system of nature it may be winter-time, nor yet to suffer from heat, although it be summer according to the almanac. He may be protected against the inclement time of the year by dwelling in a favoured spot, or he may have so trained his body to endurance that it feels neither heat nor cold. Next, reverse this saying:—You must remove anger from your mind before you can take virtue into the same, because vices and virtues cannot combine, and none can at the same time be both an angry man and a good man, any more than he can be both sick and well.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "You can't remove wickedness from the world," our opponent argues, "so you can't remove anger either. And neither one is possible anyway." First, this is wrong. A person can avoid being cold even in winter, or avoid overheating even in summer. They might live somewhere with better weather, or they might train their body to handle extreme temperatures. Now flip this argument around: You must remove anger from your mind before you can let virtue in. Vices and virtues cannot coexist. No one can be both angry and good at the same time — any more than someone can be both sick and healthy.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: "It is not possible," says he, "to remove anger altogether from the mind, nor does human nature admit of it." Yet there is nothing so hard and difficult that the mind of man cannot overcome it, and with which unremitting study will not render him familiar, nor are there any passions so fierce and independent that they cannot be tamed by discipline. The mind can carry out whatever orders it gives itself: some have succeeded in never smiling: some have forbidden themselves wine, sexual intercourse, or even drink of all kinds. Some, who are satisfied with short hours of rest, have learned to watch for long periods without weariness. Men have learned to run upon the thinnest ropes even when slanting, to carry huge burdens, scarcely within the compass of human strength, or to dive to enormous depths and suffer themselves to remain under the sea without any chance of drawing breath.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "You can't completely remove anger from the mind," our opponent says. "Human nature won't allow it." But there's nothing so hard that the human mind can't overcome it. With constant practice, you can master anything. No passion is too wild to be tamed by discipline. The mind can do whatever it commands itself to do. Some people have trained themselves never to smile. Others have given up wine, sex, or even all drinks. Some people are happy with just a few hours of sleep and have learned to stay awake for long periods without getting tired. People have learned to run on thin ropes, even when they're tilted. They carry enormous weights that seem beyond human strength. They dive to incredible depths and hold their breath underwater for impossible amounts of time.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: There are a thousand other instances in which application has conquered all obstacles, and proved that nothing which the mind has set itself to endure is difficult. The men whom I have just mentioned gain either no reward or one that is unworthy of their unwearied application; for what great thing does a man gain by applying his intellect to walking upon a tight rope? or to placing great burdens upon his shoulders? or to keeping sleep from his eyes? or to reaching the bottom of the sea? and yet their patient labour brings all these things to pass for a trifling reward. Shall not we then call in the aid of patience, we whom such a prize awaits, the unbroken calm of a happy life? How great a blessing is it to escape from anger, that chief of all evils, and therewith from frenzy, ferocity, cruelty, and madness, its attendants?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: There are thousands of other examples where practice has overcome every obstacle. These examples prove that nothing is difficult when the mind decides to endure it. The people I just mentioned get little or no reward for their endless effort. What great thing does someone gain by learning to walk on a tightrope? Or by carrying heavy weights on their shoulders? Or by staying awake for days? Or by diving to the bottom of the sea? Yet their patient work makes all these things possible — for almost nothing in return. So shouldn't we use that same patience? After all, we have a much greater prize waiting for us: the unbroken calm of a happy life. What a blessing it would be to escape from anger, the worst of all evils, and escape from the frenzy, violence, cruelty, and madness that come with it.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
There is no reason why we should seek to defend such a passion
as this or excuse its excesses by declaring it to be either useful
or unavoidable. What vice, indeed, is without its defenders? yet
this is no reason why you should declare anger to be ineradicable.
The evils from which we suffer are curable, and since we were born
with a natural bias towards good, nature herself will help us if
we try to amend our lives. Nor is the path to virtue steep and
rough, as some think it to be: it may be reached on level ground.
This is no untrue tale which I come to tell you: the road to happiness
is easy; do you only enter upon it with good luck and the good help
of the gods themselves. It is much harder to do what you are doing.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: There's no reason to defend anger or excuse its extremes by calling it useful or unavoidable. Every vice has its defenders — but that doesn't mean you should accept anger as permanent. The problems we face can be healed. Since we were born with a natural pull toward good, nature herself will help us if we try to improve our lives. The path to virtue isn't steep and rough like some people think. You can reach it on level ground. This isn't a fairy tale I'm telling you. The road to happiness is easy. Just start walking it with good fortune and the gods' blessing. What you're doing now — staying angry — is much harder work.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
What is more restful than a mind at peace, and what more toilsome
than anger? What is more at leisure than clemency, what fuller of
business than cruelty? Modesty keeps holiday while vice is overwhelmed
with work. In fine, the culture of any of the virtues is easy, while
vices require a great expense. Anger ought to be removed from our
minds: even those who say that it ought to be kept low admit this
to some extent: let it be got rid of altogether; there is nothing
to be gained by it. Without it we can more easily and more justly
put an end to crime, punish bad men, and amend their lives.
The wise man will do his duty in all things without the help of any
evil passion, and will use no auxiliaries which require watching
narrowly lest they get beyond his control.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: What feels better than a peaceful mind? And what's more exhausting than anger? What's more relaxing than showing mercy? What's busier than being cruel? Good people can take it easy, while wicked people exhaust themselves with their schemes. In short, any virtue is easy to practice, while vices cost you dearly. We should remove anger from our minds completely. Even people who say we should just keep anger under control are admitting it's a problem — so let's get rid of it entirely. There's no benefit to keeping it around. Without anger, we can stop crimes more easily and more fairly. We can punish wrongdoers and help them change their ways. A wise person will do what's right without needing any destructive emotion to help. They won't rely on forces that might spin out of control.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Anger, then, must never become a habit with us, but we may
sometimes affect to be angry when we wish to rouse up the dull minds
of those whom we address, just as we rouse up horses who are slow
at starting with goads and firebrands. We must sometimes apply fear
to persons upon whom reason makes no impression: yet to be angry
is of no more use than to grieve or to be afraid. “What? do not
circumstances arise which provoke us to anger?” Yes: but at those
times above all others we ought to choke down our wrath. Nor is it
difficult to conquer our spirit, seeing that athletes, who devote
their whole attention to the basest parts of themselves, nevertheless
are able to endure blows and pain, in order to exhaust the strength
of the striker, and do not strike when anger bids them, but when
opportunity invites them.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Anger should never become a habit. But sometimes we can pretend to be angry when we need to wake up people who aren't listening to us. Think of how we use goads and torches to get slow horses moving. Sometimes we need to use fear on people who won't listen to reason. But actually being angry is no more useful than grieving or being afraid. "But don't things happen that make us angry?" Yes, they do. But those are exactly the times when we should control our anger most. It's not that hard to master our emotions. Look at athletes — they focus on the lowest parts of themselves, yet they can endure blows and pain to wear out their opponent. They don't strike when anger tells them to. They strike when the right moment comes.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
It is said that Pyrrhus, the most celebrated
trainer for gymnastic contests, used habitually to impress upon his
pupils not to lose their tempers: for anger spoils their science,
and thinks only how it can hurt: so that often reason counsels
patience while anger counsels revenge, and we, who might have
survived our first misfortunes, are exposed to worse ones. Some
have been driven into exile by their impatience of a single
contemptuous word, have been plunged into the deepest miseries
because they would not endure the most trifling wrong in silence,
and have brought upon themselves the yoke of slavery because they
were too proud to give up the least part of their entire liberty.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Pyrrhus was the most famous trainer for athletic competitions. He always told his students not to lose their tempers. Anger ruins their skill, he said, and only thinks about causing harm. Reason often tells us to be patient, while anger demands revenge. People who could have survived their first troubles end up facing worse ones because of their anger. Some have been driven into exile by a single insulting word. They couldn't bear to ignore even the smallest offense in silence, so they were plunged into deep misery. Others brought slavery upon themselves because they were too proud to give up even a tiny piece of their freedom.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“That you may be sure,” says our opponent, “that anger has in
it something noble, pray look at the free nations, such as the
Germans and Scythians, who are especially prone to anger.” The
reason of this is that stout and daring intellects are liable
to anger before they are tamed by discipline; for some passions
engraft themselves upon the better class of dispositions only, just
as good land, even when waste, grows strong brushwood, and the trees
are tall which stand upon a fertile soil. In like manner, dispositions
which are naturally bold produce irritability, and, being hot and
fiery, have no mean or trivial qualities, but their energy is
misdirected, as happens with all those who without training come
to the front by their natural advantages alone, whose minds, unless
they be brought under control, degenerate from a courageous temper
into habits of rashness and reckless daring.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "To prove that anger has something noble about it," our opponent argues, "just look at free nations like the Germans and Scythians — they're especially prone to anger." Here's the real reason for this: strong and bold minds are naturally inclined to anger before discipline tames them. Some passions only take root in better types of character. It's like how even wasteland, if the soil is rich, grows thick brush and tall trees. In the same way, naturally bold personalities produce quick tempers. Being hot and fiery, they have nothing small or petty about them. But their energy goes in the wrong direction. This happens with all people who rely on natural gifts alone without proper training. Unless their minds are brought under control, they slide from courage into recklessness and wild recklessness.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“What? are not milder
spirits linked with gentler vices, such as tenderness of heart,
love, and bashfulness?” Yes, and therefore I can often point out
to you a good disposition by its own faults: yet their being the
proofs of a superior nature does not prevent their being vices.
Moreover, all those nations which are free because they are wild,
like lions or wolves, cannot command any more than they can obey:
for the strength of their intellect is not civilized, but fierce
and unmanageable: now, no one is able to rule unless he is also
able to be ruled. Consequently, the empire of the world has almost
always remained in the hands of those nations who enjoy a milder
climate. Those who dwell near the frozen north have uncivilized
tempers—
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "What about gentler spirits?" you ask. "Don't they have milder vices — like being too tender-hearted, or too loving, or too shy?" Yes, they do. And I can often tell you have a good nature by looking at your particular faults. But just because these flaws show you have a noble spirit doesn't mean they aren't still flaws. Besides, all those nations that are free because they are wild — like lions or wolves — can't command others any more than they can obey. Their mental strength isn't civilized. It's fierce and uncontrollable. No one can rule unless he can also be ruled. That's why the world's empires have almost always stayed in the hands of nations with milder climates. People who live near the frozen north have uncivilized temperaments —

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“Just on the model of their native skies,”

as the poet has it.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "Just like the harsh skies they were born under," as the poet says.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Those animals, urges our opponent, are held to be the most
generous who have large capacity for anger. He is mistaken when he
holds up creatures who act from impulse instead of reason as patterns
for men to follow, because in man reason takes the place of impulse.
Yet even with animals, all do not alike profit by the same thing.
Anger is of use to lions, timidity to stags, boldness to hawks,
flight to doves. What if I declare that it is not even true that
the best animals are the most prone to anger? I may suppose that
wild beasts, who gain their food by rapine, are better the angrier
they are;
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Some people argue that animals with the strongest capacity for anger are the most noble. But this person is wrong to hold up creatures who act on instinct as examples for humans to follow. Humans have reason instead of instinct. Even among animals, not all benefit from the same traits. Lions benefit from anger. Deer benefit from timidity. Hawks benefit from boldness. Doves benefit from flight. But what if I told you that it's not even true that the best animals are the angriest? I suppose wild beasts who hunt for food might be better hunters when they're angrier.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
but I should praise oxen and horses who obey the rein for
their patience. What reason, however, have you for referring mankind
to such wretched models, when you have the universe and God, whom
he alone of animals imitates because he alone comprehends Him? “The
most irritable men,” says he, “are thought to be the most straightforward
