of all.” Yes, because they are compared with swindlers and sharpers,
and appear to be simple because they are outspoken. I should not
call such men simple, but heedless. We give this title of “simple”
to all fools, gluttons, spendthrifts, and men whose vices lie on
the surface.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: But I would praise oxen and horses for their patience in following the reins. Why would you use such terrible examples for humans anyway? You have the universe and God as models. Humans are the only animals who can imitate God because we're the only ones who can understand Him. "The most irritable people," my opponent says, "are thought to be the most honest." Yes, but only when you compare them to con artists and cheaters. They seem simple because they speak their minds. But I wouldn't call these people simple — I'd call them careless. We use the word "simple" for all kinds of fools: gluttons, spendthrifts, and people whose flaws are obvious to everyone.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“An orator,” says our opponent, “sometimes speaks better,
when he is angry.” Not so, but when he pretends to be angry: for
so also actors bring down the house by their playing, not when they
are really angry, but when they act the angry man well: and in like
manner, in addressing a jury or a popular assembly, or in any other
position in which the minds of others have to be influenced at our
pleasure, we must ourselves pretend to feel anger, fear, or pity
before we can make others feel them, and often the pretence of
passion will do what the passion itself could not have done. “The
mind which does not feel anger,” says he, “is feeble.” True, if it
has nothing stronger than anger to support it. A man ought to be
neither robber nor victim, neither tender-hearted nor cruel. The
former belongs to an over-weak mind, the latter to an over-hard
one. Let the wise man be moderate, and when things have to be done
somewhat briskly, let him call force, not anger, to his aid.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "An orator," says our opponent, "sometimes speaks better when he is angry." Not so, but when he pretends to be angry. Actors bring down the house with their performance, not when they are really angry, but when they act the angry man well. In the same way, when addressing a jury or a crowd, or in any situation where we need to influence other people's minds, we must pretend to feel anger, fear, or pity before we can make others feel them. Often the pretence of passion will do what real passion could not have done. "The mind which does not feel anger," says he, "is feeble." True, if it has nothing stronger than anger to support it. A man ought to be neither robber nor victim, neither tender-hearted nor cruel. The former belongs to an over-weak mind, the latter to an over-hard one. Let the wise man be moderate. When things have to be done somewhat briskly, let him call on force, not anger, to help him.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Now that we have discussed the questions propounded concerning
anger, let us pass on to the consideration of its remedies.
These, I imagine, are two-fold: the one class preventing our becoming
angry, the other preventing our doing wrong when we are angry. As
with the body we adopt a certain regimen to keep ourselves in health,
and use different rules to bring back health when lost, so likewise
we must repel anger in one fashion and quench it in another. That
we may avoid it, certain general rules of conduct which apply to
all men’s lives must be impressed upon us. We may divide these into
such as are of use during the education of the young and in after-life.

Education ought to be carried on with the greatest and most salutary
assiduity: for it is easy to mould minds while they are still tender,
but it is difficult to uproot vices which have grown up with
ourselves.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
Now that we've covered the questions about anger, let's move on to its remedies. I think there are two kinds: one prevents us from getting angry in the first place, and the other stops us from doing harm when we are angry. Just like we follow certain habits to stay healthy and use different treatments when we get sick, we need one approach to ward off anger and another to put it out once it starts. To avoid anger entirely, we need to learn some basic life principles that work for everyone. We can split these into lessons for young people and lessons for adults.

Education should be done with great care and attention. It's easy to shape minds while they're still soft, but it's hard to pull out bad habits that have grown up with us.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: A hot mind is naturally the most prone to anger: for as there are four elements,[8] consisting of fire, air, earth, and water, so there are powers corresponding and equivalent to each of these, namely, hot, cold, dry, and moist. Now the mixture of the elements is the cause of the diversities of lands and of animals, of bodies and of character, and our dispositions incline to one or the other of these according as the strength of each element prevails in us. Hence it is that we call some regions wet or dry, warm or cold. The same distinctions apply likewise to animals and mankind; it makes a great difference how much moisture or heat a man contains; his character will partake of whichever element has the largest share in him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: People with hot temperaments are naturally the most likely to get angry. Think of it this way: there are four basic elements — fire, air, earth, and water. Each has its own quality: hot, cold, dry, or wet. The mix of these elements creates all the differences we see in places, animals, bodies, and personalities. We lean toward whichever element is strongest in us. That's why we call some regions wet or dry, warm or cold. The same applies to animals and people. How much moisture or heat you have makes a huge difference. Your personality will reflect whatever element dominates in you.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: A warm temper of mind will make men prone to anger; for fire is full of movement and vigour; a mixture of coldness makes men cowards, for cold is sluggish and contracted. Because of this, some of our Stoics think that anger is excited in our breasts by the boiling of the blood round the heart: indeed, that place is assigned to anger for no other reason than because the breast is the warmest part of the whole body. Those who have more moisture in them become angry by slow degrees, because they have no heat ready at hand, but it has to be obtained by movement; wherefore the anger of women and children is sharp rather than strong, and arises on lighter provocation. At dry times of life anger is violent and powerful, yet without increase, and adding little to itself, because as heat dies away cold takes its place.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: People with warm temperaments are naturally prone to anger. Fire is full of movement and energy. A cold mixture makes people cowards, because cold is sluggish and tight. Because of this, some of our Stoic philosophers think that anger is stirred up in our chests by the boiling of blood around the heart. They assign anger to that location for one reason only — the chest is the warmest part of the whole body. People who have more moisture in them get angry slowly, because they don't have heat ready to use. They have to build it up through movement. That's why the anger of women and children is sharp rather than strong, and starts over small things. In the dry periods of life, anger is violent and powerful, but it doesn't grow. It adds little to itself, because as heat dies away, cold takes its place.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Old men are testy and full of complaints, as also are sick people and convalescents, and all whose store of heat has been consumed by weariness or loss of blood. Those who are wasted by thirst or hunger are in the same condition, as also are those whose frame is naturally bloodless and faints from want of generous diet. Wine kindles anger, because it increases heat; according to each man's disposition, some fly into a passion when they are heavily drunk, some when they are slightly drunk: nor is there any other reason than this why yellow-haired, ruddy-complexioned people should be excessively passionate, seeing that they are naturally of the colour which others put on during anger; for their blood is hot and easily set in motion.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Old men are cranky and full of complaints. So are sick people and those recovering from illness. Anyone whose inner heat has been drained by exhaustion or blood loss gets angry easily. People wasted by thirst or hunger are the same way. So are those who are naturally pale and weak from poor nutrition. Wine stirs up anger because it increases heat in the body. Some people get furious when heavily drunk, others when just slightly drunk. This explains why blonde, red-faced people are so quick to anger. They naturally have the color that everyone else turns when angry. Their blood runs hot and moves easily.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
But just as nature makes some men prone to anger, so there are
many other causes which have the same power as nature. Some are
brought into this condition by disease or bodily injury, others by
hard work, long watching, nights of anxiety, ardent longings, and
love: and everything else which is hurtful to the body or the spirit
inclines the distempered mind to find fault. All these, however,
are but the beginning and causes of anger. Habit of mind has very
great power, and, if it be harsh, increases the disorder. As
for nature, it is difficult to alter it, nor may we change the
mixture of the elements which was formed once for all at our birth:
yet knowledge will be so far of service, that we should keep wine
out of the reach of hot-tempered men, which Plato thinks ought also
to be forbidden to boys, so that fire be not made fiercer. Neither
should such men be over-fed:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Just as nature makes some people quick to anger, many other things can have the same effect. Disease or injury can make people angry. So can hard work, sleepless nights, worry, strong desires, and love. Anything that hurts your body or spirit makes your troubled mind more likely to complain. But these are just the starting points and causes of anger. Your habits matter most. If you have harsh habits, they make the problem worse. It's hard to change your nature. You can't alter the mix of elements that formed you at birth. But knowledge helps. We should keep wine away from hot-tempered people. Plato thought we should also keep it from boys, so we don't add fire to fire. These people shouldn't overeat either.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
for if so, their bodies will swell,
and their minds will swell with them. Such men ought to take exercise,
stopping short, however, of fatigue, in order that their natural
heat may be abated, but not exhausted, and their excess of fiery
spirit may be worked off. Games also will be useful: for moderate
pleasure relieves the mind and brings it to a proper balance. With
those temperaments which incline to moisture, or dryness and
stiffness, there is no danger of anger, but there is fear of greater
vices, such as cowardice, moroseness, despair, and suspiciousness:
such dispositions therefore ought to be softened, comforted, and
restored to cheerfulness: and since we must make use of different
remedies for anger and for sullenness, and these two vices require
not only unlike, but absolutely opposite modes of treatment, let
us always attack that one of them which is gaining the mastery.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: If they do overeat, their bodies will grow heavy and their minds will become heavy too. Hot-tempered people should exercise, but not to the point of exhaustion. This will cool their natural heat without draining them completely, and burn off their excess fiery energy. Games will help too — moderate pleasure calms the mind and brings it back into balance. People with different temperaments — those who tend toward moisture, dryness, or stiffness — don't struggle with anger. But they face bigger problems like cowardice, gloominess, despair, and suspicion. These types need to be softened, comforted, and cheered up. Since anger and sullenness need completely different remedies — in fact, opposite treatments — we should always focus on whichever problem is winning at the moment.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: It is, I assure you, of the greatest service to boys that they should be soundly brought up, yet to regulate their education is difficult, because it is our duty to be careful neither to cherish a habit of anger in them, nor to blunt the edge of their spirit. This needs careful watching, for both qualities, both those which are to be encouraged, and those which are to be checked, are fed by the same things; and even a careful watcher may be deceived by their likeness. A boy's spirit is increased by freedom and depressed by slavery: it rises when praised, and is led to conceive great expectations of itself: yet this same treatment produces arrogance and quickness of temper: we must therefore guide him between these two extremes, using the curb at one time and the spur at another.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Raising boys properly is incredibly important, I assure you. But it's also very difficult. We need to be careful not to teach them anger, but we also can't crush their spirit. This requires constant attention. The things that build character and the things that create problems are often fed by the same treatment. Even careful parents can be fooled by how similar they look. A boy's spirit grows when he has freedom and gets crushed when he's controlled too much. He rises when you praise him and starts to expect great things from himself. But this same treatment can also make him arrogant and quick to anger. So we have to guide him between these two extremes. Sometimes we need to hold him back, sometimes we need to push him forward.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: He must undergo no servile or degrading treatment; he never must beg abjectly for anything, nor must he gain anything by begging; let him rather receive it for his own sake, for his past good behaviour, or for his promises of future good conduct. In contests with his comrades we ought not to allow him to become sulky or fly into a passion: let us see that he be on friendly terms with those whom he contends with, so that in the struggle itself he may learn to wish not to hurt his antagonist but to conquer him: whenever he has gained the day or done something praiseworthy, we should allow him to enjoy his victory, but not to rush into transports of delight: for joy leads to exultation, and exultation leads to swaggering and excessive self-esteem.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Don't let a child be treated like a servant or be humiliated. He should never have to grovel for anything or get what he wants by begging. Instead, give him things because he deserves them — for who he is, for good behavior he's already shown, or because he promises to do better. When he competes with other children, don't let him sulk or throw tantrums. Make sure he stays friends with his competitors. That way, during the contest itself, he learns to want victory without wanting to hurt his opponent. When he wins or does something good, let him enjoy his success — but don't let him get carried away. Joy turns into gloating, and gloating turns into arrogance and thinking too highly of yourself.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: We ought to allow him some relaxation, yet not yield him up to laziness and sloth, and we ought to keep him far beyond the reach of luxury, for nothing makes children more prone to anger than a soft and fond bringing-up, so that the more only children are indulged, and the more liberty is given to orphans, the more they are corrupted. He to whom nothing is ever denied, will not be able to endure a rebuff, whose anxious mother always wipes away his tears, whose _paedagogus_ is made to pay for his shortcomings. Do you not observe how a man's anger becomes more violent as he rises in station? This shows itself especially in those that are rich and noble, or in great place, when the favouring gale has roused all the most empty and trivial passions of their minds. Prosperity fosters anger, when a man's proud ears are surrounded by a mob of flatterers, saying, "That man answer you! you do not act according to your dignity, you lower yourself." And so forth, with all the language which can hardly be resisted even by healthy and originally well-principled minds.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We should let him relax, but not give in to laziness. Keep him away from luxury. Nothing makes children more prone to anger than soft, indulgent parenting. The more you spoil an only child or give freedom to orphans, the more you corrupt them. A child who is never told "no" won't be able to handle rejection. His worried mother always wipes his tears. His tutor gets punished for the child's mistakes. Haven't you noticed how people's anger gets worse as they gain power? You see this especially in the rich, the noble, and those in high positions. When good fortune lifts them up, it stirs all the emptiest passions in their minds. Success feeds anger. Proud ears get surrounded by crowds of flatterers saying things like "How dare he talk to you that way! You're not acting with proper dignity. You're lowering yourself." And so on — language that even healthy, well-principled minds can barely resist.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Flattery, then, must be kept well out of the way of children. Let a child hear the truth, and sometimes fear it: let him always reverence it. Let him rise in the presence of his elders. Let him obtain nothing by flying into a passion: let him be given when he is quiet what was refused him when he cried for it: let him behold, but not make use of his father's wealth: let him be reproved for what he does wrong. It will be advantageous to furnish boys with even-tempered teachers and _paedagogi_: what is soft and unformed clings to what is near, and takes its shape:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Keep flatterers away from children. Let a child hear the truth, and sometimes be afraid of it. But let him always respect it. Make him stand up when adults enter the room. Don't give him anything when he throws a tantrum. Give him what he wants only when he's calm and quiet. Let him see his father's wealth, but not spend it freely. Correct him when he does something wrong. It helps to give boys teachers and tutors who stay calm and even-tempered. Young minds are soft and unformed — they stick to whatever is nearby and copy its shape.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: the habits of young men reproduce those of their nurses and _paedagogi_. Once, a boy who was brought up in Plato's house went home to his parents, and, on seeing his father shouting with passion, said, "I never saw any one at Plato's house act like that." I doubt not that he learned to imitate his father sooner than he learned to imitate Plato. Above all, let his food be scanty, his dress not costly, and of the same fashion as that of his comrades: if you begin by putting him on a level with many others, he will not be angry when some one is compared with him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Young people copy the habits of their nurses and teachers. A boy who grew up in Plato's house once went home to his parents. When he saw his father yelling in anger, he said, "I never saw anyone at Plato's house act like that." I bet he learned to copy his father faster than he learned to copy Plato. Most importantly, give your child simple food and plain clothes — the same as his friends wear. If you start by treating him like everyone else, he won't get angry when someone compares him to others.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
These precepts, however, apply to our children: in ourselves
the accident of birth and our education no longer admits of either
mistakes or advice; we must deal with what follows. Now we ought
to fight against the first causes of evil: the cause of anger is
the belief that we are injured; this belief, therefore, should not
be lightly entertained. We ought not to fly into a rage even when
the injury appears to be open and distinct: for some false things
bear the semblance of truth. We should always allow some time to
elapse, for time discloses the truth. Let not our ears be easily
lent to calumnious talk:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: These rules work for our children. But for ourselves, it's too late — our birth circumstances and upbringing can't be changed. We must work with what we have now. We need to fight against the root causes of evil. Anger comes from believing we've been wronged. So we shouldn't be quick to believe that. We shouldn't fly into a rage even when an injury seems obvious and clear. Some false things look like truth. We should always let some time pass first. Time reveals what really happened. Don't be quick to listen to gossip and accusations.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
let us know and be on our guard against
this fault of human nature, that we are willing to believe what we
are unwilling to listen to, and that we become angry before we have
formed our opinion. What shall I say? we are influenced not
merely by calumnies but by suspicions, and at the very look and
smile of others we may fly into a rage with innocent persons because
we put the worst construction upon it. We ought, therefore, to plead
the cause of the absent against ourselves, and to keep our anger
in abeyance: for a punishment which has been postponed may yet be
inflicted, but when once inflicted cannot be recalled.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Let's recognize and guard against this human flaw: we're quick to believe bad things we don't want to hear, and we get angry before we've even figured out what really happened. What's worse? We're influenced not just by gossip but by mere suspicions. We might fly into a rage at innocent people just because of how they looked at us or smiled — putting the worst possible spin on everything. So we should defend absent people against our own suspicions. Keep your anger on hold. A punishment that's delayed can still be given later. But once you've punished someone, you can never take it back.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Every one knows the story of the tyrannicide who, being
caught before he had accomplished his task, and being tortured by
Hippias to make him betray his accomplices, named the friends of
the tyrant who stood around, and every one to whom he knew the
tyrant’s safety was especially dear. As the tyrant ordered each man
to be slain as he was named, at last the man, being asked if any
one else remained, said, “You remain alone, for I have left no one
else alive to whom you are dear.” Anger had made the tyrant lend
his assistance to the tyrant-slayer, and cut down his guards with
his own sword. How far more spirited was Alexander, who after reading
his mother’s letter warning him to beware of poison from his physician
Philip, nevertheless drank undismayed the medicine which Philip
gave him!
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Everyone knows the story of the would-be assassin who was caught before he could kill the tyrant. Hippias tortured him to make him reveal his accomplices. The assassin named all the tyrant's friends who were standing around — everyone he knew the tyrant trusted most. As the tyrant ordered each person killed, the assassin was finally asked if anyone else remained. He said, "Only you are left. I've killed everyone else who cared about you." The tyrant's anger had turned him into the assassin's helper. He used his own sword to cut down his own guards. How much braver was Alexander! His mother wrote warning him that his doctor Philip might poison him. But Alexander still drank the medicine Philip gave him without fear.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
He felt more confidence in his friend: he deserved that
his friend should be innocent, and deserved that his conduct should
make him innocent. I praise Alexander’s doing this all the more
because he was above all men prone to anger; but the rarer moderation
is among kings, the more it deserves to be praised. The great Gaius
Caesar, who proved such a merciful conqueror in the civil war, did
the same thing; he burned a packet of letters addressed to Gnaeus
Pompeius by persons who had been thought to be either neutrals or
on the other side. Though he was never violent in his anger, yet
he preferred to put it out of his power to be angry: he thought
that the kindest way to pardon each of them was not to know what
his offence had been.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Alexander trusted his friend completely. He deserved to have an innocent friend, and his trust helped make his friend innocent. I admire Alexander's choice even more because he was naturally quick to anger. The rarer self-control is among kings, the more we should praise it. The great Julius Caesar, who showed such mercy when he won the civil war, did something similar. He burned a bundle of letters that people had sent to Pompey — people who had claimed to be neutral or on Caesar's side. Caesar was never violent in his anger. But he chose to make it impossible for himself to get angry. He thought the kindest way to forgive people was simply not to know what they had done wrong.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Readiness to believe what we hear causes very great mischief;
we ought often not even to listen, because in some cases it is
better to be deceived than to suspect deceit. We ought to free our
minds of suspicion and mistrust, those most untrustworthy causes
of anger. “This man’s greeting was far from civil; that one would
not receive my kiss; one cut short a story I had begun to tell;
another did not ask me to dinner; another seemed to view me with
aversion.” Suspicion will never lack grounds: what we want is
straightforwardness, and a kindly interpretation of things. Let us
believe nothing unless it forces itself upon our sight and is
unmistakable, and let us reprove ourselves for being too ready to
believe, as often as our suspicions prove to be groundless: for
this discipline will render us habitually slow to believe what we
hear.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Being too quick to believe what we hear causes huge problems. Often we shouldn't even listen, because sometimes it's better to be fooled than to live in constant suspicion. We need to clear our minds of suspicion and mistrust — they're the worst triggers for anger. "That person's greeting was cold. This one wouldn't let me kiss them. Someone cut me off when I was telling a story. Another person didn't invite me to dinner. That one looked at me with disgust." Suspicion always finds something to feed on. What we need instead is honesty and a generous way of seeing things. Let's believe nothing unless we see it clearly with our own eyes and can't mistake it. And whenever our suspicions turn out to be wrong, let's criticize ourselves for jumping to conclusions too quickly. This practice will train us to be slow to believe rumors.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Another consequence of this will be, that we shall not be exasperated by the slightest and most contemptible trifles. It is mere madness to be put out of temper because a slave is not quick, because the water we are going to drink is lukewarm, or because our couch is disarranged or our table carelessly laid. A man must be in a miserably bad state of health if he shrinks from a gentle breath of wind; his eyes must be diseased if they are distressed by the sight of white clothing; he must be broken down with debauchery if he feels pain at seeing another man work.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Another benefit of this approach is that tiny, worthless things won't make us furious. It's pure madness to get angry because a servant is slow, or because your drink is lukewarm, or because your bed is messy or your table wasn't set properly. A man must be in terrible health if a gentle breeze makes him wince. His eyes must be diseased if white clothing hurts them. He must be completely worn out by excess if watching someone else work causes him pain.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: It is said that there was one Mindyrides, a citizen of Sybaris, who one day seeing a man digging and vigorously brandishing a mattock, complained that the sight made him weary, and forbade the man to work where he could see him. The same man complained that he had suffered from the rose-leaves upon which he lay being folded double. When pleasures have corrupted both the body and the mind, nothing seems endurable, not indeed because it is hard, but because he who has to bear it is soft: for why should we be driven to frenzy by any one's coughing and sneezing, or by a fly not being driven away with sufficient care, or by a dog's hanging about us, or a key dropping from a careless servant's hand?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: There's a story about a man named Mindyrides from the city of Sybaris. One day he saw someone digging and swinging a pickaxe hard. He complained that just watching made him tired. He told the man to stop working where he could see him. This same man also complained that he couldn't sleep because the rose petals under him were folded wrong. When pleasure corrupts both your body and mind, nothing feels bearable. It's not because things are actually hard — it's because you've become too soft. Why should someone's cough or sneeze drive us crazy? Or a fly that isn't swatted quickly enough? Or a dog hanging around us? Or a servant dropping a key?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Will one whose ears are agonised by the noise of a bench being dragged along the floor be able to endure with unruffled mind the rude language of party strife, and the abuse which speakers in the forum or the senate house heap upon their opponents? Will he who is angry with his slave for icing his drink badly, be able to endure hunger, or the thirst of a long march in summer? Nothing, therefore, nourishes anger more than excessive and dissatisfied luxury: the mind ought to be hardened by rough treatment, so as not to feel any blow that is not severe.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Can someone who gets upset by the sound of a bench scraping across the floor handle the harsh words of political debates? Can they deal with the insults that speakers hurl at each other in courts and government buildings? If you get angry at your servant for not chilling your drink properly, how will you handle real hunger or thirst during a long summer march? Nothing feeds anger more than too much luxury and constantly wanting more comfort. Your mind needs to be toughened by rough experiences. That way, only truly severe blows will hurt you.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: We are angry, either with those who can, or with those who cannot do us an injury. To the latter class belong some inanimate things, such as a book, which we often throw away when it is written in letters too small for us to read, or tear up when it is full of mistakes, or clothes which we destroy because we do not like them. How foolish to be angry with such things as these, which neither deserve nor feel our anger! "But of course it is their makers who really affront us." I answer that, in the first place, we often become angry before making this distinction clear in our minds, and secondly, perhaps even the makers might put forward some reasonable excuses: one of them, it may be, could not make them any better than he did, and it is not through any disrespect to you that he was unskilled in his trade: another may have done his work so without any intention of insulting you: and, finally, what can be more crazy than to discharge upon things the ill-feeling which one has accumulated against persons?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We get angry with two kinds of things: those that can hurt us and those that cannot. The second group includes objects like books. We throw away a book when the letters are too small to read. We tear up one that's full of mistakes. We destroy clothes we don't like. How foolish it is to be angry with things that neither deserve nor feel our anger! "But of course it's really their makers who offend us." I say this: First, we often get angry before we think clearly about this. Second, maybe the makers have good reasons for their work. One craftsman might not have been able to do better than he did. His lack of skill wasn't meant to disrespect you. Another did his work with no intention of insulting you. And finally, what could be crazier than taking out your anger at people on lifeless objects?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Yet as it is the act of a madman to be angry with inanimate objects, so also is it to be angry with dumb animals, which can do us no wrong because they are not able to form a purpose; and we cannot call anything a wrong unless it be done intentionally. They are, therefore, able to hurt us, just as a sword or a stone may do so, but they are not able to do us a wrong. Yet some men think themselves insulted when the same horses which are docile with one rider are restive with another, as though it were through their deliberate choice, and not through habit and cleverness of handling that some horses are more easily managed by some men than by others. And as it is foolish to be angry with them, so it is to be angry with children, and with men who have little more sense than children: for all these sins, before a just judge, ignorance would be as effective an excuse as innocence.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: It's crazy to be angry with objects that can't think. But it's just as crazy to be angry with animals. Animals can't wrong you because they can't plan to hurt you. We can only call something a wrong if it's done on purpose. Animals can hurt us, sure — like a sword or stone can hurt us. But they can't actually wrong us. Yet some people feel insulted when horses that obey one rider won't obey them. They act like the horse chose to be difficult, instead of understanding that some riders are just better at handling horses through practice and skill. And just as it's foolish to be angry with animals, it's foolish to be angry with children or with adults who think like children. Before any fair judge, ignorance would excuse all these mistakes just as much as innocence would.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
There are some things which are unable to hurt us, and whose
power is exclusively beneficial and salutary, as, for example, the
immortal gods, who neither wish nor are able to do harm: for their
temperament is naturally gentle and tranquil, and no more likely
to wrong others than to wrong themselves. Foolish people who know
not the truth hold them answerable for storms at sea, excessive
rain, and long winters, whereas all the while these phenomena by
which we suffer or profit take place without any reference whatever
to us: it is not for our sake that the universe causes summer and
winter to succeed one another; these have a law of their own,
according to which their divine functions are performed. We think
too much of ourselves, when we imagine that we are worthy to have
such prodigious revolutions effected for our sake:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Some things cannot hurt us at all. Their power is only helpful and healing — like the immortal gods, who neither want to harm us nor can harm us. Their nature is gentle and peaceful. They are no more likely to wrong others than to wrong themselves. Foolish people who don't understand the truth blame the gods for storms at sea, too much rain, and long winters. But these things that help us or hurt us happen without any thought of us at all. The universe doesn't create summer and winter for our sake. These seasons follow their own laws. The gods perform their divine work according to those laws. We think too highly of ourselves when we imagine we are important enough to have such massive forces working just for us.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
so, then, none
of these things take place in order to do us an injury, nay, on the
contrary, they all tend to our benefit. I have said that there are
some things which cannot hurt us, and some which would not. To the
latter class belong good men in authority, good parents, teachers,
and judges whose punishments ought to be submitted to by us in the
same spirit in which we undergo the surgeon’s knife, abstinence
from food, and such like things which hurt us for our benefit.
Suppose that we are being punished; let us think not only of what
we suffer, but of what we have done: let us sit in judgement on our
past life. Provided we are willing to tell ourselves the truth, we
shall certainly decide that our crimes deserve a harder measure
than they have received.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: So none of these natural events happen to hurt us. In fact, they all help us in some way. I said there are some things that cannot hurt us, and some that would not hurt us. Good people in positions of power belong to this second group — good parents, teachers, and judges. We should accept their punishments the same way we accept a surgeon's knife or going without food. These things hurt us, but they help us too. If we are being punished, let's think about what we did, not just what we're suffering. Let's look honestly at our past behavior. If we're willing to tell ourselves the truth, we'll realize our wrongdoing deserves harsher punishment than we actually received.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: If we desire to be impartial judges of all that takes place, we must first convince ourselves of this, that no one of us is faultless: for it is from this that most of our indignation proceeds. "I have not sinned, I have done no wrong." Say, rather, you do not admit that you have done any wrong. We are infuriated at being reproved, either by reprimand or actual chastisement, although we are sinning at that very time, by adding insolence and obstinacy to our wrong-doings. Who is there that can declare himself to have broken no laws?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: If we want to judge situations fairly, we must first accept this truth: none of us is perfect. Most of our anger comes from forgetting this fact. When something happens to us, we think, "I haven't done anything wrong. I don't deserve this." But really, we just refuse to admit our mistakes. We get furious when someone corrects us or punishes us, even though we're making things worse by being stubborn and defiant. Who can honestly say they've never broken any rules?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Even if there be such a man, what a stinted innocence it is, merely to be innocent by the letter of the law. How much further do the rules of duty extend than those of the law! how many things which are not to be found in the statute book, are demanded by filial feeling, kindness, generosity, equity, and honour? Yet we are not able to warrant ourselves even to come under that first narrowest definition of innocence: we have done what was wrong, thought what was wrong, wished for what was wrong, and encouraged what was wrong: in some cases we have only remained innocent because we did not succeed.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Even if someone could claim they never broke a law, what a narrow kind of innocence that would be. Being legal is just the bare minimum. The rules of right and wrong go much further than written laws. How many things does the law say nothing about, but love for family, kindness, generosity, fairness, and honor demand? Yet we can't even meet that narrow legal standard of innocence. We have done wrong things, thought wrong things, wanted wrong things, and encouraged wrong things. Sometimes we stayed innocent only because we failed to carry out our bad plans.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: When we think of this, let us deal more justly with sinners, and believe that those who scold us are right: in any case let us not be angry with ourselves (for with whom shall we not be angry, if we are angry even with our own selves?), and least of all with the gods: for whatever we suffer befalls us not by any ordinance of theirs but of the common law of all flesh. "But diseases and pains attack us." Well, people who live in a crazy dwelling must have some way of escape from it. Some one will be said to have spoken ill of you: think whether you did not first speak ill of him:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: When we think about how flawed we all are, we should judge sinners more fairly. We should believe that people who criticize us might be right. And we definitely shouldn't be angry with ourselves — if we get angry with ourselves, who won't we be angry with? Most of all, we shouldn't be angry with the gods. Whatever we suffer doesn't come from some divine decree. It comes from the basic conditions of being human. "But diseases and pain attack us!" Well, people who live in a rickety house need an escape route. Someone might speak badly of you. Ask yourself: didn't you speak badly of him first?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: think of how many persons you have yourself spoken ill. Let us not, I say, suppose that others are doing us a wrong, but are repaying one which we have done them, that some are acting with good intentions, some under compulsion, some in ignorance, and let us believe that even he who does so intentionally and knowingly did not wrong us merely for the sake of wronging us, but was led into doing so by the attraction of saying something witty, or did whatever he did, not out of any spite against us, but because he himself could not succeed unless he pushed us back.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Think of how many people you have bad-mouthed yourself. Don't assume others are wronging you. Maybe they're just paying you back for something you did to them first. Some people act with good intentions. Some are forced into it. Some don't know any better. Even when someone hurts you on purpose, they probably weren't trying to hurt you just for the sake of it. Maybe they wanted to make a clever joke. Or maybe they did what they did because they couldn't succeed without pushing you down.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: We are often offended by flattery even while it is being lavished upon us: yet whoever recalls to his mind how often he himself has been the victim of undeserved suspicion, how often fortune has given his true service an appearance of wrong-doing, how many persons he has begun by hating and ended by loving, will be able to keep himself from becoming angry straightway, especially if he silently says to himself when each offence is committed: "I have done this very thing myself." Where, however, will you find so impartial a judge? The same man who lusts after everyone's wife, and thinks that a woman's belonging to someone else is a sufficient reason for adoring her, will not allow any one else to look at his own wife. No man expects such exact fidelity as a traitor: the perjurer himself takes vengeance of him who breaks his word:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We often get offended even by compliments and praise. But think about this: remember how often people have been suspicious of you for no good reason. Think about how often luck made your good deeds look bad. Think about all the people you first hated but later came to love. If you remember these things, you won't get angry so quickly. When someone offends you, quietly tell yourself: "I have done this very thing myself." But where will you find someone fair enough to do this? The same man who wants every other man's wife — who finds a woman more attractive just because she belongs to someone else — won't let anyone even look at his own wife. No one demands more loyalty than a traitor does. Even a person who breaks promises gets angry when others break their word.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: the pettifogging lawyer is most indignant at an action being brought against him: the man who is reckless of his own chastity cannot endure any attempt upon that of his slaves. We have other men's vices before our eyes, and our own behind our backs: hence it is that a father, who is worse than his son, blames the latter for giving extravagant feasts, and disapproves of the least sign of luxury in another, although he was wont to set no bounds to it in his own case; hence it is that despots are angry with homicides, and thefts are punished by those who despoil temples. A great part of mankind is not angry with sins, but with sinners. Regard to our own selves will make us more moderate, if we inquire of ourselves:—have we ever committed any crime of this sort? have we ever fallen into this kind of error? is it for our interest that we should condemn this conduct?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: The crooked lawyer gets most upset when someone sues him. The man who sleeps around can't stand it when someone tries to seduce his slaves. We see other people's flaws clearly, but we're blind to our own. That's why a father who's worse than his son will criticize the boy for throwing expensive parties. He'll condemn any luxury in others, even though he never set limits on his own spending. That's why dictators get angry at murderers, and why thieves punish people who rob temples. Most people aren't angry at sins — they're angry at sinners. We'd be more reasonable if we asked ourselves: Have I ever done something like this? Have I made this same mistake? Does it really help me to condemn this behavior?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence, but that it may form a right judgment about it: if it delays, it will come to an end. Do not attempt to quell it all at once, for its first impulses are fierce; by plucking away its parts we shall remove the whole. We are made angry by some things which we learn at second-hand, and by some which we ourselves hear or see. Now, we ought to be slow to believe what is told us. Many tell lies in order to deceive us, and many because they are themselves deceived. Some seek to win our favour by false accusations, and invent wrongs in order that they may appear angry at our having suffered them. One man lies out of spite, that he may set trusting friends at variance; some because they are suspicious, and wish to see sport, and watch from a safe distance those whom they have set by the ears.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: The best cure for anger is waiting. Ask your anger to give you time at first — not to forgive the offense, but to judge it fairly. If anger waits, it will fade away. Don't try to crush it all at once. The first rush of anger is fierce. Pull away its pieces and you'll remove the whole thing. Some things make us angry when we hear them secondhand. Others make us angry when we see or hear them ourselves. We should be slow to believe what people tell us. Many people lie to trick us. Many lie because they've been tricked themselves. Some people want to win our favor with false accusations. They make up wrongs so they can seem angry that we've been hurt. One person lies out of spite, hoping to turn trusting friends against each other. Some people are suspicious and want entertainment. They watch from a safe distance as they set people fighting.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: If you were about to give sentence in court about ever so small a sum of money, you would take nothing as proved without a witness, and a witness would count for nothing except on his oath. You would allow both sides to be heard: you would allow them time: you would not despatch the matter at one sitting, because the oftener it is handled the more distinctly the truth appears. And do you condemn your friend off-hand? Are you angry with him before you hear his story, before you have cross-examined him, before he can know either who is his accuser or with what he is charged.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: If you were judging a court case over even a small amount of money, you wouldn't accept anything as fact without a witness. And you wouldn't trust a witness unless they swore an oath. You would listen to both sides. You would give them time. You wouldn't rush through the case in one session, because the more you examine it, the clearer the truth becomes. So why do you condemn your friend immediately? Why get angry with him before you hear his side, before you question him, before he even knows who accused him or what the charge is?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Why then, just now, in the case which you just tried, did you hear what was said on both sides? This very man who has informed against your friend, will say no more if he be obliged to prove what he says. "You need not," says he, "bring me forward as a witness; if I am brought forward I shall deny what I have said; unless you excuse me from appearing I shall never tell you anything." At the same time he spurs you on and withdraws himself from the strife and battle. The man who will tell you nothing save in secret hardly tells you anything at all. What can be more unjust than to believe in secret, and to be angry openly?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: So why didn't you hear both sides in the case you just decided? The person who accused your friend won't say more if you make him prove it. He'll tell you, "Don't call me as a witness. If you do, I'll deny everything I said. Unless you promise I won't have to testify, I'll never tell you anything again." He pushes you to act, then backs away from the fight. Someone who only speaks in secret barely tells you anything at all. What could be more unfair than believing secret accusations and showing your anger publicly?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Some offences we ourselves witness: in these cases let us
examine the disposition and purpose of the offender. Perhaps he is
a child; let us pardon his youth, he knows not whether he is doing
wrong: or he is a father; he has either rendered such great services,
as to have won the right even to wrong us—or perhaps this very act
which offends us is his chief merit: or a woman; well, she made a
mistake. The man did it because he was ordered to do it. Who but
an unjust person can be angry with what is done under compulsion?
You had hurt him: well, there is no wrong in suffering the pain
which you have been the first to inflict. Suppose that your opponent
is a judge; then you ought to take his opinion rather than your
own:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Sometimes we see the offense happen ourselves. When we do, let's examine why the person did it and what they intended. Maybe it's a child — we should forgive their youth. They don't know they're doing wrong. Maybe it's a father who has done so much for us that he's earned the right to hurt us sometimes. Or maybe this very thing that offends us is actually his greatest virtue. Maybe it's a woman who simply made a mistake. Maybe the person was just following orders. How can anyone fairly be angry at someone who was forced to act? Maybe you hurt him first — well, there's nothing wrong with suffering pain that you caused in the first place. Suppose your opponent is a judge — then you should trust his judgment over your own.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
or that he is a king; then, if he punishes the guilty, yield
to him because he is just, and if he punishes the innocent, yield
to him because he is powerful. Suppose that it is a dumb animal or
as stupid as a dumb animal: then, if you are angry with it, you
will make yourself like it. Suppose that it is a disease or a
misfortune; it will take less effect upon you if you bear it quietly:
or that it is a god; then you waste your time by being angry with
him as much as if you prayed him to be angry with some one
else. Is it a good man who has wronged you? do not believe it: is
it a bad one? do not be surprised at this; he will pay to some one
else the penalty which he owes to you—indeed, by his sin he has
already punished himself.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: If it is a king — whether he punishes the guilty or the innocent — yield to him either because he is just or because he is powerful. If it is a dumb animal or someone as stupid as a dumb animal, getting angry will only make you like them. If it is a disease or misfortune, you will suffer less if you bear it calmly. If it is a god, your anger is as pointless as praying for that god to be angry with someone else. If a good man has wronged you, don't believe it. If a bad man has wronged you, don't be surprised. He will pay someone else the penalty he owes you — in fact, by his sin he has already punished himself.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: There are, as I have stated, two cases which produce anger: first, when we appear to have received an injury, about which enough has been said, and, secondly, when we appear to have been treated unjustly: this must now be discussed. Men think some things unjust because they ought not to suffer them, and some because they did not expect to suffer them: we think what is unexpected is beneath our deserts. Consequently, we are especially excited at what befalls us contrary to our hope and expectation: and this is why we are irritated at the smallest trifles in our own domestic affairs, and why we call our friends' carelessness deliberate injury.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: As I said before, two things make us angry. First, when we think someone has hurt us — I've talked about that enough. Second, when we think someone has treated us unfairly. Let me explain this now. People think something is unfair for two reasons: either they believe they shouldn't have to suffer it, or they didn't expect it to happen. We think unexpected things are beneath what we deserve. That's why we get especially upset when things go against our hopes and expectations. And that's why we get so irritated by tiny problems at home, and why we assume our friends hurt us on purpose when they're just being careless.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: How is it, then, asks our opponent, that we are angered by the injuries inflicted by our enemies? It is because we did not expect those particular injuries, or, at any rate, not on so extensive a scale. This is caused by our excessive self-love: we think that we ought to remain uninjured even by our enemies: every man bears within his breast the mind of a despot, and is willing to commit excesses, but unwilling to submit to them. Thus it is either ignorance or arrogance that makes us angry: ignorance of common facts; for what is there to wonder at in bad men committing evil deeds? what novelty is there in your enemy hurting you, your friend quarrelling with you, your son going wrong, or your servant doing amiss?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "But wait," someone asks, "why do we get angry when our enemies hurt us?" It's because we didn't expect that specific injury, or at least not on such a large scale. This happens because we love ourselves too much. We think we should stay unharmed even by our enemies. Every person has the mind of a tyrant inside — willing to dish it out but unwilling to take it. So anger comes from either ignorance or arrogance. Ignorance of basic facts. What's so surprising about bad people doing bad things? What's new about your enemy hurting you, your friend fighting with you, your son messing up, or your servant making mistakes?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Fabius was wont to say that the most shameful excuse a general could make was "I did not think." I think it the most shameful excuse that a man can make. Think of everything, expect everything: even with men of good character something queer will crop up; human nature produces minds that are treacherous, ungrateful, greedy, and impious: when you are considering what any man's morals may be, think what those of mankind are. When you are especially enjoying yourself, be especially on your guard: when everything seems to you to be peaceful, be sure that mischief is not absent, but only asleep. Always believe that something will occur to offend you. A pilot never spreads all his canvas abroad so confidently as not to keep his tackle for shortening sail ready for use.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: General Fabius used to say that the most shameful excuse a commander could make was "I didn't think." I believe that's the most shameful excuse any person can make. Think about everything. Expect everything. Even good people will surprise you with something strange. Human nature creates minds that betray, show no gratitude, grab what they can, and ignore what's sacred. When you're judging what one person might do, remember what people in general are capable of. When you're having the most fun, be extra careful. When everything seems calm, remember that trouble isn't gone — it's just sleeping. Always believe that something will happen to upset you. A ship captain never puts up full sail without keeping his gear ready to bring the sails down quickly.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Think, above all, how base and hateful is the power of doing mischief, and how unnatural in man, by whose kindness even fierce animals are rendered tame. See how bulls yield their necks to the yoke, how elephants allow boys and women to dance on their backs unhurt, how snakes glide harmlessly over our bosoms and among our drinking-cups, how within their dens bears and lions submit to be handled with complacent mouths, and wild beasts fawn upon their master: let us blush to have exchanged habits with wild beasts. It is a crime to injure one's country: so it is, therefore, to injure any of our countrymen, for he is a part of our country; if the whole be sacred, the parts must be sacred too. Therefore it is also a crime to injure any man: for he is your fellow-citizen in a larger state. What, if the hands were to wish to hurt the feet?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Think about how ugly and hateful it is to hurt other people. It goes against human nature. Even wild animals can be tamed by human kindness. Look at how bulls let us put yokes on their necks. Elephants let children and women dance on their backs without hurting them. Snakes slide harmlessly across our chests and around our cups. Bears and lions in their dens let us pet them with gentle mouths. Wild beasts show affection to their masters. We should be ashamed that we've become worse than wild animals. It's a crime to hurt your country. So it's also a crime to hurt any of your fellow citizens, because each person is part of your country. If the whole country is sacred, then each part must be sacred too. And it's a crime to hurt any human being at all — because in the larger community of humanity, every person is your fellow citizen. What if your hands decided to hurt your feet?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: or the eyes to hurt the hands? As all the limbs act in unison, because it is the interest of the whole body to keep each one of them safe, so men should spare one another, because they are born for society. The bond of society, however, cannot exist unless it guards and loves all its members. We should not even destroy vipers and water-snakes and other creatures whose teeth and claws are dangerous, if we were able to tame them as we do other animals, or to prevent their being a peril to us: neither ought we, therefore, to hurt a man because he has done wrong, but lest he should do wrong, and our punishment should always look to the future, and never to the past, because it is inflicted in a spirit of precaution, not of anger: for if everyone who has a crooked and vicious disposition were to be punished, no one would escape punishment.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: What if your hands wanted to hurt your feet? Or your eyes wanted to hurt your hands? All your body parts work together because the whole body needs each part to stay safe. In the same way, people should protect each other because we're born to live together. Society only works when it guards and loves all its members. We wouldn't even kill poisonous snakes and other dangerous creatures if we could tame them like other animals or keep them from harming us. So we shouldn't hurt someone just because they did wrong. We should only act to prevent future wrongs. Our punishments should look forward, not backward. We should act from caution, not anger. If we punished everyone with a twisted and corrupt nature, no one would escape punishment.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“But anger possesses a certain pleasure of its own, and it
is sweet to pay back the pain you have suffered.” Not at all; it
is not honourable to requite injuries by injuries, in the same way
as it is to repay benefits by benefits. In the latter case it is a
shame to be conquered; in the former it is a shame to conquer.
Revenge and retaliation are words which men use and even think to
be righteous, yet they do not greatly differ from wrong-doing,
except in the order in which they are done: he who renders pain for
pain has more excuse for his sin; that is all. Some one who did not
know Marcus Cato struck him in the public bath in his ignorance,
for who would knowingly have done him an injury?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "But anger has its own pleasure. It feels sweet to pay back the pain you've suffered." Not at all. It's not honorable to return injuries with injuries, just as it is honorable to return favors with favors. With favors, it's shameful to be outdone. With injuries, it's shameful to win. Revenge and retaliation are words people use and think are righteous. But they're barely different from wrongdoing — just done in reverse order. The person who inflicts pain for pain has more excuse for his sin, but that's all. Someone who didn't know Marcus Cato once struck him at the public bath out of ignorance. After all, who would knowingly hurt him?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Afterwards when
he was apologizing, Cato replied, “I do not remember being struck.”
He thought it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it. You
ask, “Did no harm befall that man for his insolence?” No, but rather
much good; he made the acquaintance of Cato. It is the part of a
great mind to despise wrongs done to it; the most contemptuous form
of revenge is not to deem one’s adversary worth taking vengeance
upon. Many have taken small injuries much more seriously to heart
than they need, by revenging them: that man is great and noble who
like a large wild animal hears unmoved the tiny curs that bark at
him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: When the man later apologized, Cato replied, "I don't remember being struck." He thought it was better to ignore the insult than to get revenge. You ask, "Didn't that man face any consequences for his rudeness?" No, but he got something much better — he met Cato. It takes a great mind to ignore wrongs done against it. The most dismissive form of revenge is deciding your enemy isn't even worth striking back at. Many people have made small injuries much worse by seeking revenge. A truly great and noble person is like a large wild animal that doesn't even flinch when tiny dogs bark at him.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“We are treated,” says our opponent, “with more respect if
we revenge our injuries.” If we make use of revenge merely as a
remedy, let us use it without anger, and not regard revenge as
pleasant, but as useful: yet often it is better to pretend not to
have received an injury than to avenge it. The wrongs of the powerful
must not only be borne, but borne with a cheerful countenance: they
will repeat the wrong if they think they have inflicted it. This
is the worst trait of minds rendered arrogant by prosperity,
they hate those whom they have injured. Every one knows the saying
of the old courtier, who, when some one asked him how he had achieved
the rare distinction of living at court till he reached old age,
replied, “By receiving wrongs and returning thanks for them.”
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "People respect us more if we get revenge for injuries," our opponent argues. If we use revenge only as medicine, let's use it without anger. Don't see revenge as pleasant — see it as useful. But often it's better to pretend you weren't hurt at all than to get revenge. You must not only endure wrongs from powerful people, but endure them with a smile. If they think they've hurt you, they'll do it again. This is the worst trait of minds made arrogant by success: they hate the people they've wronged. Everyone knows the saying of that old courtier. When someone asked how he managed to survive at court until old age, he replied: "By taking abuse and saying thank you for it."

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
It
is often so far from expedient to avenge our wrongs, that it will
not do even to admit them. Gaius Caesar, offended at the smart
clothes and well-dressed hair of the son of Pastor, a distinguished
Roman knight, sent him to prison. When the father begged that his
son might suffer no harm, Caius, as if reminded by this to put him
to death, ordered him to be executed, yet, in order to mitigate his
brutality to the father, invited him that very day to dinner. Pastor
came with a countenance which betrayed no illwill. Caesar pledged
him in a glass of wine, and set a man to watch him. The wretched
creature went through his part, feeling as though he were drinking
his son’s blood: the emperor sent him some perfume and a garland,
and gave orders to watch whether he used them:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Sometimes revenge is not just unwise — it's dangerous to even acknowledge you've been wronged. Emperor Caligula was annoyed by the fancy clothes and styled hair of a young man whose father, Pastor, was a respected Roman knight. So Caligula threw the son in prison. When Pastor begged for his son's life, Caligula — as if reminded by the plea — ordered the young man executed instead. Then, to soften this cruelty toward the father, he invited Pastor to dinner that very same day. Pastor came, showing no anger or hatred on his face. Caesar offered him wine and had someone watch his reaction. The miserable man played his part, feeling as though he were drinking his own son's blood. The emperor even sent him perfume and a garland, ordering his men to watch whether Pastor would use them.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
he did so. On the
very day on which he had buried, nay, on which he had not even
buried his son, he sat down as one of a hundred guests, and, old
and gouty as he was, drank to an extent which would have been hardly
decent on a child’s birthday; he shed no tear the while; he did not
permit his grief to betray itself by the slightest sign; he dined
just as though his entreaties had gained his son’s life. You ask
me why he did so? he had another son. What did Priam do in the
Iliad? Did he not conceal his wrath and embrace the knees of Achilles?
did he not raise to his lips that death-dealing hand, stained with
the blood of his son, and sup with his slayer? True!
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Pastor used the perfume and wore the garland. On the very day he had buried his son — or rather, on the day when he hadn't even been allowed to bury his son — he sat down as one of a hundred dinner guests. Though he was old and suffered from gout, he drank heavily. It would have been too much even at a child's birthday party. He shed no tears. He didn't let his grief show by even the smallest sign. He ate dinner as if his pleading had actually saved his son's life. You ask why he did this? He had another son. What did Priam do in the Iliad? Didn't he hide his anger and kneel before Achilles? Didn't he kiss that deadly hand, still stained with his son's blood, and eat dinner with his son's killer? Exactly!

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
but there were
no perfumes and garlands, and his fierce enemy encouraged him with
many soothing words to eat, not to drain huge goblets with a guard
standing over him to see that he did it. Had he only feared for
himself, the father would have treated the tyrant with scorn:
but love for his son quenched his anger: he deserved the emperor’s
permission to leave the banquet and gather up the bones of his son:
but, meanwhile, that kindly and polite youth the emperor would not
even permit him to do this, but tormented the old man with frequent
invitations to drink, advising him thereby to lighten his sorrows.
He, on the other hand, appeared to be in good spirits, and to have
forgotten what had been done that day: he would have lost his second
son had he proved an unacceptable guest to the murderer of his
eldest.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: But there were no fancy perfumes or flowers at that dinner. And Priam's fierce enemy spoke kindly to him, urging him to eat. He didn't have to drain huge cups while a guard watched to make sure he did it. If the father had only feared for himself, he would have scorned the tyrant. But his love for his son crushed his anger. He had earned the emperor's permission to leave the banquet and collect his son's bones. But meanwhile, that gracious and polite young emperor wouldn't even let him do this. Instead, he tormented the old man with repeated invitations to drink, telling him it would ease his grief. The father, on the other hand, seemed cheerful and acted as if he had forgotten what happened that day. He would have lost his second son if he had been an unwelcome guest to his first son's murderer.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
We must, therefore, refrain from anger, whether he who
provokes us be on a level with ourselves, or above us, or below us.
A contest with one’s equal is of uncertain issue, with one’s superior
is folly, and with one’s inferior is contemptible. It is the part
of a mean and wretched man to turn and bite one’s biter: even mice
and ants show their teeth if you put your hand to them, and all
feeble creatures think that they are hurt if they are touched. It
will make us milder tempered to call to mind any services which he
with whom we are angry may have done us, and to let his deserts
balance his offence. Let us also reflect, how much credit the tale
of our forgiveness will confer upon us, how many men may be made
into valuable friends by forgiveness. One of the lessons which
Sulla’s cruelty teaches us is not to be angry with the children of
our enemies, whether they be public or private; for he drove the
sons of the proscribed into exile. Nothing is more unjust than that
any one should inherit the quarrels of his father.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We must avoid anger whether the person who provokes us is our equal, our superior, or our inferior. Fighting an equal could go either way. Fighting a superior is foolish. Fighting an inferior is beneath us. It's the mark of a petty, miserable person to bite back at someone who has bitten you. Even mice and ants show their teeth when you touch them — all weak creatures think they're being hurt when they're just being touched. We'll be calmer if we remember any good things the person we're angry at has done for us. Let their good deeds balance out their offense. We should also think about how much respect we'll earn by forgiving them, and how many enemies we could turn into valuable friends through forgiveness. Sulla's cruelty teaches us one lesson: don't be angry with the children of our enemies, whether public or private. He drove the sons of the condemned into exile. Nothing is more unfair than making someone inherit their father's quarrels.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Whenever we are
loth to pardon any one, let us think whether it would be to our
advantage that all men should be inexorable. He who refuses to
pardon, how often has he begged it for himself? how often has he
grovelled at the feet of those whom he spurns from his own? How can
we gain more glory than by turning anger into friendship?
what more faithful allies has the Roman people than those who have
been its most unyielding enemies? where would the empire be to-day,
had not a wise foresight united the conquered and the conquerors?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: When you don't want to forgive someone, ask yourself this: would it help you if everyone refused to forgive anyone? The person who won't forgive others — how many times has he begged for forgiveness himself? How often has he crawled at the feet of people he now pushes away? What brings more honor than turning an enemy into a friend? Who are Rome's most loyal allies? The nations that once fought us most fiercely. Where would our empire be today if we hadn't been wise enough to unite the conquered with the conquerors?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
If any one is angry with you, meet his anger by returning benefits
for it: a quarrel which is only taken up on one side falls to the
ground: it takes two men to fight. But[14] suppose that there is
an angry struggle on both sides, even then, he is the better man
who first gives way; the winner is the real loser. He struck you;
well then, do you fall back: if you strike him in turn you will
give him both an opportunity and an excuse for striking you again:
you will not be able to withdraw yourself from the struggle when
you please.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: If someone is angry with you, respond by being kind to them. A fight needs two people — if only one person is fighting, there's no fight at all. But suppose you both get angry and struggle against each other. Even then, whoever backs down first is the better person. The winner is actually the real loser. He hit you? Then step back. If you hit him back, you'll just give him a reason and chance to hit you again. Once you're in the fight, you won't be able to get out when you want to.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Does any one wish to strike his enemy so hard, as to leave
his own hand in the wound, and not to be able to recover his balance
after the blow? yet such a weapon is anger: it is scarcely possible
to draw it back. We are careful to choose for ourselves light
weapons, handy and manageable swords: shall we not avoid these
clumsy, unwieldy,[15] and never-to-be-recalled impulses of the mind?
The only swiftness of which men approve is that which, when bidden,
checks itself and proceeds no further, and which can be guided, and
reduced from a run to a walk: we know that the sinews are diseased
when they move against our will. A man must be either aged or weakly
who runs when he wants to walk:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Would anyone want to hit their enemy so hard that their hand gets stuck in the wound? Would they want to lose their balance and fall down from their own blow? Yet that's exactly what anger is like. Once you use it, you can hardly pull it back. We carefully choose light weapons — swords that are easy to handle and control. So why don't we avoid these clumsy, heavy impulses of the mind that we can never take back? The only kind of speed people respect is the kind that can stop when told to. Speed that can be guided and slowed from a run to a walk. We know our muscles are sick when they move without our permission. A person must be old or weak if they run when they meant to walk.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
let us think that those are the
most powerful and the soundest operations of our minds, which act
under our own control, not at their own caprice. Nothing, however,
will be of so much service as to consider, first, the hideousness,
and, secondly, the danger of anger. No passion bears a more troubled
aspect: it befouls the fairest face, makes fierce the expression
which before was peaceful. From the angry “all grace has fled;”
though their clothing may be fashionable, they will trail it
on the ground and take no heed of their appearance; though their
hair be smoothed down in a comely manner by nature or art, yet it
will bristle up in sympathy with their mind. The veins become
swollen, the breast will be shaken by quick breathing, the man’s
neck will be swelled as he roars forth his frantic talk:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We should think that our minds are strongest and healthiest when we control them — not when they control us. But nothing will help more than understanding two things about anger. First, how ugly it makes us look. Second, how dangerous it is. No emotion ruins your appearance worse than anger. It turns the most beautiful face hideous. It makes a peaceful expression look savage. When people are angry, "all grace has fled." Even if their clothes are stylish, they'll drag them on the ground and stop caring how they look. Even if their hair is perfectly styled, it will stick up wildly to match their wild mind. Their veins bulge. Their chest heaves from rapid breathing. Their neck swells as they scream out their crazy words.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
then, too,
his limbs will tremble, his hands will be restless, his whole body
will sway hither and thither. What, think you, must be the state
of his mind within him, when its appearance without is so shocking?
how far more dreadful a countenance he bears within his own breast,
how far keener pride, how much more violent rage, which will burst
him unless it finds some vent? Let us paint anger looking like those
who are dripping with the blood of foemen or savage beasts, or those
who are just about to slaughter them—like those monsters of the
nether world fabled by the poet to be girt with serpents and breathing
flame, when they sally forth from hell, most frightful to behold,
in order that they may kindle wars, stir up strife between nations,
and overthrow peace;
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Then his whole body starts shaking. His hands won't stay still. He sways back and forth. What do you think is happening inside his mind when the outside looks this terrible? The face he wears inside his chest is far more hideous. His pride cuts deeper. His rage burns hotter. It will tear him apart unless he finds some way to let it out. Picture anger looking like warriors dripping with enemy blood, or like savage beasts about to kill. Think of those mythical monsters from hell that poets describe — wrapped in snakes, breathing fire. They come up from the underworld looking absolutely terrifying, ready to start wars, turn nations against each other, and destroy peace.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
let us paint her eyes glowing with fire, her
voice hissing, roaring, grating, and making worse sounds if worse
there be, while she brandishes weapons in both hands, for she cares
not to protect herself, gloomy, stained with blood, covered with
scars and livid with her own blows, reeling like a maniac, wrapped
in a thick cloud, dashing hither and thither, spreading desolation
and panic, loathed by every one and by herself above all, willing,
if otherwise she cannot hurt her foe, to overthrow alike earth,
sea, and heaven, harmful and hateful at the same time. Or, if we
are to see her, let her be such as our poets have described her—
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Picture anger with eyes blazing like fire. Her voice hisses, roars, and grates — making sounds worse than anything you can imagine. She waves weapons in both hands, not caring about protecting herself. She's gloomy, stained with blood, covered with scars and bruises from hitting herself. She staggers like a madwoman, wrapped in thick clouds, charging back and forth, spreading destruction and terror. Everyone hates her — and she hates herself most of all. If she can't hurt her enemy any other way, she's willing to destroy the earth, sea, and sky all at once. She's both harmful and hateful. Or if we want to see what anger looks like, let her be exactly as our poets have described her —

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“There with her blood-stained scourge Bellona fights. And
Discord in her riven robe delights,”[16]

or, if possible, let some even more dreadful aspect be invented
for this dreadful passion.
