on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "There with her blood-stained whip, Bellona fights. And Discord delights in her torn robe," or, if possible, let someone invent an even more terrible image for this terrible passion.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Some angry people, as Sextius remarks, have been benefited
by looking at the glass: they have been struck by so great an
alteration in their own appearance: they have been, as it were,
brought into their own presence and have not recognized themselves:
yet how small a part of the real hideousness of anger did that
reflected image in the mirror reproduce? Could the mind be displayed
or made to appear through any substance, we should be confounded
when we beheld how black and stained, how agitated, distorted, and
swollen it looked: even at present it is very ugly when seen through
all the screens of blood, bones, and so forth: what would it be,
were it displayed uncovered? You say, that you do not believe that
any one was ever scared out of anger by a mirror:
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Some angry people have been helped by looking in a mirror, as Sextius points out. They were shocked by how much their appearance had changed. It was like meeting themselves for the first time — they didn't recognize who they had become. But even that reflected image showed only a tiny part of anger's true ugliness. If we could see the mind itself — if it could be displayed through some material — we would be horrified. We would see how black and stained it looks, how agitated and twisted and swollen. Even now, hidden behind blood and bones and flesh, the angry mind is very ugly. What would it look like if we could see it completely uncovered? You might say that you don't believe anyone was ever scared out of anger by looking in a mirror.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
and why not?
Because when he came to the mirror to change his mind, he had changed
it already: to angry men no face looks fairer than one that is
fierce and savage and such as they wish to look like. We ought
rather to consider, how many men anger itself has injured. Some in
their excessive heat have burst their veins; some by straining their
voices beyond their strength have vomited blood, or have injured
their sight by too violently injecting humours into their eyes, and
have fallen sick when the fit passed off. No way leads more swiftly
to madness: many have, consequently, remained always in the frenzy
of anger, and, having once lost their reason, have never recovered
it.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: And why not? Because when someone comes to the mirror to change their mind, they've already changed it. To angry people, no face looks better than one that is fierce and wild — exactly how they want to look. We should think about how many people anger itself has actually hurt. Some people get so heated that they burst their blood vessels. Others strain their voices so hard they cough up blood. Some damage their eyesight by forcing too much pressure into their eyes. They get sick when the anger passes. No path leads to madness faster than this one. Many people have stayed trapped in angry rage forever. Once they lost their minds to it, they never got them back.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Ajax was driven mad by anger, and driven to suicide by madness.
Men, frantic with rage, call upon heaven to slay their children,
to reduce themselves to poverty, and to ruin their houses, and yet
declare that they are not either angry or insane. Enemies to their
best friends, dangerous to their nearest and dearest, regardless
of the laws save where they injure, swayed by the smallest trifles,
unwilling to lend their ears to the advice or the services
of their friends, they do everything by main force, and are ready
either to fight with their swords or to throw themselves upon them,
for the greatest of all evils, and one which surpasses all vices,
has gained possession of them.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Ajax was driven mad by anger, and his madness drove him to kill himself. People in wild rage call on the gods to kill their children, make them poor, and destroy their homes. Yet they insist they are not angry or crazy. They become enemies to their best friends. They become dangerous to the people they love most. They ignore all laws except when breaking them hurts others. The smallest things set them off. They refuse to listen to advice or help from friends. They use brute force for everything. They are ready to fight with swords or fall on them. The greatest evil of all has taken control of them — one that is worse than any other vice.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Other passions gain a footing in the
mind by slow degrees: anger’s conquest is sudden and complete, and,
moreover, it makes all other passions subservient to itself. It
conquers the warmest love: men have thrust swords through the bodies
of those whom they loved, and have slain those in whose arms they
have lain. Avarice, that sternest and most rigid of passions, is
trampled underfoot by anger, which forces it to squander its carefully
collected wealth and set fire to its house and all its property in
one heap. Why, has not even the ambitious man been known to fling
away the most highly valued ensigns of rank, and to refuse high
office when it was offered to him? There is no passion over which
anger does not bear absolute rule.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Other emotions creep into your mind slowly. But anger conquers you all at once, completely. And once it takes over, it forces every other emotion to serve it. Anger defeats even the strongest love. Men have stabbed people they loved deeply. They have killed those they once held in their arms. Greed — that hardest and most stubborn passion — gets trampled by anger. Anger makes greedy people throw away fortunes they spent years collecting. It makes them burn down their own houses with everything inside. Even ambitious people, driven by rage, have thrown away honors they treasured most. They have refused high positions when offered. There is no passion that anger cannot completely control.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: We will now, my Novatus, attempt to do that which you so especially long to do, that is, to drive out anger from our minds, or at all events to curb it and restrain its impulses. This may sometimes be done openly and without concealment, when we are only suffering from a slight attack of this mischief, and at other times it must be done secretly, when our anger is excessively hot, and when every obstacle thrown in its way increases it and makes it blaze higher. It is important to know how great and how fresh its strength may be, and whether it can be driven forcibly back and suppressed, or whether we must give way to it until its first storm blow over, lest it sweep away with it our remedies themselves.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Now, Novatus, we'll try to do what you most want to do: drive anger out of our minds. Or at least control it and hold back its impulses. Sometimes we can do this openly when we're only dealing with a mild case of this problem. Other times we must work in secret, when our anger burns white-hot and any obstacle we put in its path only feeds the flames and makes it blaze higher. We need to know how strong and fresh our anger is. Can we force it down and suppress it? Or should we wait until the first storm passes, so it doesn't sweep away our remedies along with everything else?

on-anger_book-3.originalText: We must deal with each case according to each man's character: some yield to entreaties, others are rendered arrogant and masterful by submission: we may frighten some men out of their anger, while some may be turned from their purpose by reproaches, some by acknowledging oneself to be in the wrong, some by shame, and some by delay, a tardy remedy for a hasty disorder, which we ought only to use when all others have failed: for other passions admit of having their case put off, and may be healed at a later time; but the eager and self-destructive violence of anger does not grow up by slow degrees, but reaches its full height as soon as it begins.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: We must handle each person based on their character. Some people calm down when you ask nicely. Others become more arrogant and controlling when you give in to them. You can frighten some people out of their anger. Others respond to criticism, or to admitting you were wrong, or to shame. Some need time to cool off — though delay is a slow cure for a quick problem. You should only use delay when nothing else works. Other emotions can wait and be dealt with later. But anger is eager and self-destructive. It doesn't build up slowly. It reaches full strength the moment it starts.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Nor does it, like other vices, merely disturb men's minds, but it takes them away, and torments them till they are incapable of restraining themselves and eager for the common ruin of all men, nor does it rage merely against its object, but against every obstacle which it encounters on its way. The other vices move our minds; anger hurls them headlong. If we are not able to withstand our passions, yet at any rate our passions ought to stand firm: but anger grows more and more powerful, like lightning flashes or hurricanes, or any other things which cannot stop themselves because they do not proceed along, but fall from above.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Unlike other vices that simply disturb our minds, anger takes complete control of us. It torments us until we can't hold back anymore. We become eager to destroy everything around us. Anger doesn't just rage against the person who upset us — it attacks every obstacle in its path. Other vices move our minds around. Anger hurls them off a cliff. Even when we can't resist our other passions, at least those passions stay steady. But anger keeps growing stronger and stronger. It's like lightning or hurricanes — things that can't stop themselves because they don't move forward step by step. They fall from above with crushing force.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Other vices affect our judgment, anger affects our sanity: others come in mild attacks and grow unnoticed, but men's minds plunge abruptly into anger. There is no passion that is more frantic, more destructive to its own self; it is arrogant if successful, and frantic if it fails. Even when defeated it does not grow weary, but if chance places its foe beyond its reach, it turns its teeth against itself. Its intensity is in no way regulated by its origin: for it rises to the greatest heights from the most trivial beginnings.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Other vices mess with your judgment. Anger messes with your sanity. Other vices sneak up on you gradually. But anger? Your mind crashes straight into it. No other emotion is more wild or more destructive. When anger wins, it becomes arrogant. When it loses, it goes completely mad. Even when it's beaten, it never gets tired. If it can't reach its target, it attacks itself instead. The size of what started it doesn't matter at all. Anger can explode into a massive rage over the tiniest things.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: It passes over no time of life; no race of men is exempt from it: some nations have been saved from the knowledge of luxury by the blessing of poverty; some through their active and wandering habits have escaped from sloth; those whose manners are unpolished and whose life is rustic know not chicanery and fraud and all the evils to which the courts of law give birth: but there is no race which is not excited by anger, which is equally powerful with Greeks and barbarians, and is just as ruinous among law-abiding folk as among those whose only law is that of the stronger. Finally, the other passions seize upon individuals; anger is the only one which sometimes possesses a whole state. No entire people ever fell madly in love with a woman, nor did any nation ever set its affections altogether upon gain and profit.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Anger spares no age and no people. Some nations have avoided luxury because they were poor. Others escaped laziness through their active, wandering lives. People with rough manners and simple rural lives don't know trickery, fraud, and all the evils that come from courtrooms. But no race escapes anger. It has equal power over Greeks and barbarians. It destroys law-abiding people just as much as those who live by force alone. Finally, other passions attack individuals. Anger is the only one that can possess an entire nation. No whole people ever fell madly in love with one woman. No nation ever devoted itself completely to money and profit.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Ambition attacks single individuals; ungovernable rage is the only passion that affects nations. People often fly into a passion by troops; men and women, old men and boys, princes and populace all act alike, and the whole multitude, after being excited by a very few words, outdoes even its exciter: men betake themselves straightway to fire and sword, and proclaim a war against their neighbours or wage one against their countrymen. Whole houses are burned with the entire families which they contain, and he who but lately was honoured for his popular eloquence now finds that his speech moves people to rage. Legions aim their darts at their commander; the whole populace quarrels with the nobles; the senate, without waiting for troops to be levied or appointing a general, hastily chooses leaders, for its anger chases well-born men through the houses of Rome, and puts them to death with its own hand.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Ambition targets individuals one at a time. But uncontrolled rage is the only passion that can take over entire nations. People often explode into fury in groups. Men and women, old and young, rulers and common people — they all act the same way. A whole crowd gets worked up by just a few words and becomes even more extreme than whoever stirred them up. They immediately grab fire and weapons. They declare war on their neighbors or fight their own people. Entire families get burned alive in their houses. A speaker who was recently praised for his inspiring words now finds that same voice drives people into a frenzy. Soldiers turn their spears on their own commanders. The whole population fights with the nobles. The senate doesn't wait to raise troops or appoint a general. Instead, anger picks its own leaders and hunts down aristocrats through the streets of Rome, killing them with its bare hands.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Ambassadors are outraged, the law of nations violated, and an unnatural madness seizes the state. Without allowing time for the general excitement to subside, fleets are straightway launched and laden with a hastily enrolled soldiery. Without organization, without taking any auspices, the populace rushes into the field guided only by its own anger, snatches up whatever comes first to hand by way of arms, and then atones by a great defeat for the reckless audacity of its anger. This is usually the fate of savage nations when they plunge into war: as soon as their easily excited minds are roused by the appearance of wrong having been done them, they straightway hasten forth, and, guided only by their wounded feelings, fall like an avalanche upon our legions, without either discipline, fear, or precaution, and wilfully seeking for danger. They delight in being struck, in pressing forward to meet the blow, writhing their bodies along the weapon, and perishing by a wound which they themselves make.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Ambassadors are attacked, and international laws are broken. An unnatural madness takes hold of the entire nation. Without waiting for the rage to cool down, they launch ships right away and fill them with soldiers who were recruited in a hurry. Without proper organization or consulting the gods for guidance, the people rush into battle driven only by their anger. They grab whatever weapons they can find and then pay for their reckless fury with crushing defeat. This is what usually happens to savage nations when they go to war. As soon as their easily stirred emotions are aroused by some perceived injustice, they immediately rush out to fight. Guided only by their hurt feelings, they fall on our legions like an avalanche — without discipline, without fear, without caution. They actually seek out danger on purpose. They enjoy being struck and pushing forward to meet the blow. They twist their bodies along the weapon and die from wounds they create themselves.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
“No doubt,” you say, “anger is very powerful and ruinous: point
out, therefore, how it may be cured.” Yet, as I stated in my former
books, Aristotle stands forth in defence of anger, and forbids it
to be uprooted, saying that it is the spur of virtue, and that when
it is taken away, our minds become weaponless, and slow to attempt
great exploits. It is therefore essential to prove its unseemliness
and ferocity, and to place distinctly before our eyes how monstrous
a thing it is that one man should rage against another, with what
frantic violence he rushes to destroy alike himself and his foe,
and overthrows those very things whose fall he himself must share.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: "You're right," you say. "Anger is powerful and destructive. So show me how to cure it." But as I mentioned in my earlier books, Aristotle defends anger. He says we shouldn't get rid of it completely. He argues that anger drives virtue forward, and that without it, our minds become defenseless and slow to attempt great things. So I need to prove how ugly and savage anger really is. I need to show you clearly what a monstrous thing it is when one person rages against another. Look at the frantic violence — how someone rushes to destroy both himself and his enemy, toppling the very things that will crush him too when they fall.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
What, then? can any one call this man sane, who, as though caught
up by a hurricane, does not go but is driven, and is the slave of
a senseless disorder? He does not commit to another the duty of
revenging him, but himself exacts it, raging alike in thought and
deed, butchering those who are dearest to him, and for whose loss
he himself will ere long weep. Will any one give this passion as
an assistant and companion to virtue, although it disturbs calm
reason, without which virtue can do nothing?
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: So what do you think? Can anyone call this person sane? He's like someone caught in a hurricane — he doesn't walk anywhere, he gets thrown around. He's enslaved by mindless fury. He won't let anyone else handle his revenge. He has to do it himself, wild with rage in both mind and body. He slaughters the people he loves most — the same people he'll soon be crying over when they're gone. Would anyone really want this passion as virtue's helper and friend? Anger destroys calm thinking, and virtue can't do anything without that.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
The strength which a
sick man owes to a paroxysm of disease is neither lasting nor
wholesome, and is strong only to its own destruction. You need not,
therefore, imagine that I am wasting time over a useless task in
defaming anger, as though men had not made up their minds about it,
when there is some one, and he, too, an illustrious philosopher,
who assigns it services to perform, and speaks of it as useful and
supplying energy for battles, for the management of business, and
indeed for everything which requires to be conducted with spirit.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: A sick man might feel strong during a fever, but that strength won't last and it's not healthy. It's only strong enough to destroy itself. So don't think I'm wasting time attacking anger when everyone has already made up their minds about it. There's actually a famous philosopher who thinks anger has its uses. He says it gives us energy for battles, for handling business, and for anything that needs to be done with spirit.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
Lest it should delude any one into thinking that on certain occasions
and in certain positions it may be useful, we must show its
unbridled and frenzied madness, we must restore to it its attributes,
the rack, the cord, the dungeon, and the cross, the fires lighted
round men’s buried bodies, the hook[1] that drags both living men
and corpses, the different kinds of fetters, and of punishments,
the mutilations of limbs, the branding of the forehead, the dens
of savage beasts. Anger should be represented as standing among
these her instruments, growling in an ominous and terrible fashion,
herself more shocking than any of the means by which she gives vent
to her fury.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Some people might think anger can be useful in certain situations. To prevent this mistake, we must show anger's wild and crazy madness. We must remind them what anger really brings: torture racks, ropes, dungeons, and crosses. Fires lit around buried bodies. The hook that drags both living people and corpses. Different kinds of chains and punishments. Mutilated limbs. Brands burned into foreheads. Dens full of wild beasts. Picture anger standing among all these tools, growling in a threatening and terrible way. She is more horrifying than any of the methods she uses to release her fury.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
There may be some doubt about the others, but at any rate no
passion has a worse look. We have described the angry man’s appearance
in our former books, how sharp and keen he looks, at one time pale
as his blood is driven inwards and backwards, at another with all
the heat and fire of his body directed to his face, making it
reddish-coloured as if stained with blood, his eyes now restless
and starting out of his head, now set motionless in one fixed gaze.
Add to this his teeth, which gnash against one another, as though
he wished to eat somebody, with exactly the sound of a wild boar
sharpening his tusks: add also the cracking of his joints, the
involuntary wringing of his hands, the frequent slaps he deals
himself on the chest, his hurried breathing and deep-drawn sighs,
his reeling body, his abrupt broken speech, and his trembling lips,
which sometimes he draws tight as he hisses some curse through them.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: There might be debate about other emotions, but anger definitely has the worst appearance. In earlier books, I've described how an angry person looks — sharp and intense. Sometimes he turns pale as blood rushes away from his face. Other times all the heat in his body goes to his head, making his face red like it's stained with blood. His eyes either dart around wildly, bulging from his head, or lock in a cold, fixed stare. Add to this his grinding teeth — he gnashes them like he wants to devour someone, making the exact sound of a wild boar sharpening its tusks. Then there's the cracking of his joints, the way he wrings his hands without thinking, how he keeps slapping his own chest, his quick shallow breathing and heavy sighs, his swaying body, his choppy broken speech, and his trembling lips. Sometimes he pulls those lips tight to hiss curses through them.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
By Hercules, no wild beast, neither when tortured by hunger, or
with a weapon struck through its vitals, not even when it gathers
its last breath to bite its slayer, looks so shocking as a man
raging with anger. Listen, if you have leisure, to his words
and threats: how dreadful is the language of his agonized mind!
Would not every man wish to lay aside anger when he sees that it
begins by injuring himself? When men employ anger as the most
powerful of agents, consider it to be a proof of power, and reckon
a speedy revenge among the greatest blessings of great prosperity,
would you not wish me to warn them that he who is the slave of his
own anger is not powerful, nor even free? Would you not wish me to
warn all the more industrious and circumspect of men, that while
other evil passions assail the base, anger gradually obtains dominion
over the minds even of learned and in other respects sensible men?
So true is that, that some declare anger to be a proof of
straight-forwardness, and it is commonly believed that the best-natured
people are prone to it.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: By God, no wild beast looks as terrible as an angry man — not even when the animal is starving, or pierced through with a spear, or using its dying breath to bite its killer. If you have time, listen to an angry person's words and threats. The language that pours from their tortured mind is horrifying! Wouldn't everyone want to give up anger if they could see how it starts by hurting themselves first? Some people use anger as their most powerful tool. They think it proves their strength. They consider quick revenge one of the greatest rewards of success. But shouldn't I warn them that anyone enslaved by their own anger has no real power — and isn't even free? Shouldn't I especially warn the more careful and thoughtful people? Other evil emotions usually attack only bad people. But anger gradually takes control even of educated, sensible minds. This is so true that some people claim anger proves you're honest and straightforward. Most people believe that good-natured folks are naturally prone to anger.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: You ask me, whither does all this tend? To prove, I answer, that no one should imagine himself to be safe from anger, seeing that it rouses up even those who are naturally gentle and quiet to commit savage and violent acts. As strength of body and assiduous care of the health avail nothing against a pestilence, which attacks the strong and weak alike, so also steady and good-humoured people are just as liable to attacks of anger as those of unsettled character, and in the case of the former it is both more to be ashamed of and more to be feared, because it makes a greater alteration in their habits.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: You ask me, where is all this leading? Here's my point: no one should think they're safe from anger. It can drive even gentle, peaceful people to do brutal and violent things. Just as physical strength and careful health habits don't protect you from a plague that strikes everyone equally, steady and good-natured people are just as vulnerable to anger as unstable ones. In fact, it's more shameful and dangerous when it happens to them, because it represents such a dramatic change from who they usually are.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Now as the first thing is not to be angry, the second to lay aside our anger, and the third to be able to heal the anger of others as well as our own, I will set forth first how we may avoid falling into anger; next, how we may set ourselves free from it, and, lastly, how we may restrain an angry man, appease his wrath, and bring him back to his right mind. We shall succeed in avoiding anger, if from time to time we lay before our minds all the vices connected with anger, and estimate it at its real value: it must be prosecuted before us and convicted: its evils must be thoroughly investigated and exposed.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Since the first goal is to not get angry, the second is to let go of anger once we have it, and the third is to help calm angry people (including ourselves), I'll explain how to do each of these. First, how to avoid getting angry in the first place. Then, how to free ourselves from anger. And finally, how to calm an angry person, soothe their rage, and help them think clearly again. We can avoid anger by regularly reminding ourselves of all the problems anger causes. We need to see anger for what it really is. Put anger on trial and convict it. Investigate all its evils and expose them completely.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: That we may see what it is, let it be compared with the worst vices. Avarice scrapes together and amasses riches for some better man to use: anger spends money; few can indulge in it for nothing. How many slaves an angry master drives to run away or to commit suicide! how much more he loses by his anger than the value of what he originally became angry about! Anger brings grief to a father, divorce to a husband, hatred to a magistrate, failure to a candidate for office. It is worse than luxury, because luxury enjoys its own pleasure, while anger enjoys another's pain. It is worse than either spitefulness or envy; for they wish that some one may become unhappy, while anger wishes to make him so: they are pleased when evil befalls one by accident, but anger cannot wait upon Fortune; it desires to injure its victim personally, and is not satisfied merely with his being injured.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: To see what anger really is, let's compare it to the worst vices. Greed hoards wealth that someone else will eventually enjoy. But anger? It costs money. Few people can afford to be angry without paying for it. Think about how many slaves run away or kill themselves because of an angry master. His rage costs him far more than whatever originally made him mad. Anger brings grief to fathers, divorce to husbands, hatred to leaders, and failure to politicians. It's worse than luxury because luxury at least brings pleasure to the person indulging in it. Anger only enjoys other people's pain. It's worse than spite or envy. Those vices just hope someone becomes miserable. Anger actively tries to make them miserable. Spite and envy are happy when bad luck strikes someone. But anger won't wait for fate — it wants to hurt its victim personally and won't be satisfied unless it does the damage itself.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Nothing is more dangerous than jealousy: it is produced by anger. Nothing is more ruinous than war: it is the outcome of powerful men's anger; and even the anger of humble private persons, though without arms or armies, is nevertheless war. Moreover, even if we pass over its immediate consequences, such as heavy losses, treacherous plots, and the constant anxiety produced by strife, anger pays a penalty at the same moment that it exacts one: it forswears human feelings. The latter urge us to love, anger urges us to hatred: the latter bid us do men good, anger bids us do them harm. Add to this that, although its rage arises from an excessive self-respect and appears to show high spirit, it really is contemptible and mean: for a man must be inferior to one by whom he thinks himself despised, whereas the truly great mind, which takes a true estimate of its own value, does not revenge an insult because it does not feel it.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Nothing is more dangerous than jealousy — and anger creates it. Nothing is more destructive than war — and that comes from powerful people's anger. Even when ordinary people get angry, they may not have weapons or armies, but they're still waging war. And even if we ignore anger's immediate damage — financial losses, backstabbing, constant worry from conflict — anger punishes itself the moment it punishes others. It abandons human feelings. Our natural feelings tell us to love others. Anger tells us to hate them. Our nature says to help people. Anger says to harm them. Here's another thing: anger seems to come from self-respect and looks like strength, but it's actually pathetic and small. You can only feel insulted by someone you think is beneath you. But a truly great mind knows its own worth. It doesn't seek revenge for insults because it doesn't even feel them.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: As weapons rebound from a hard surface, and solid substances hurt those who strike them, so also no insult can make a really great mind sensible of its presence, being weaker than that against which it is aimed. How far more glorious is it to throw back all wrongs and insults from oneself, like one wearing armour of proof against all weapons, for revenge is an admission that we have been hurt. That cannot be a great mind which is disturbed by injury. He who has hurt you must be either stronger or weaker than yourself. If he be weaker, spare him: if he be stronger, spare yourself.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Think of weapons bouncing off armor, or how solid objects hurt the person who strikes them. Insults work the same way with a truly great mind. The insult is too weak to penetrate — it just bounces off harmlessly. How much more glorious it is to let all wrongs and insults bounce off you like armor that no weapon can pierce. When you seek revenge, you're admitting that someone actually hurt you. A great mind isn't disturbed by injury. The person who hurt you is either stronger or weaker than you. If he's weaker, show mercy. If he's stronger, protect yourself.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: There is no greater proof of magnanimity than that nothing which befalls you should be able to move you to anger. The higher region of the universe, being more excellently ordered and near to the stars, is never gathered into clouds, driven about by storms, or whirled round by cyclones: it is free from all disturbance: the lightnings flash in the region below it. In like manner a lofty mind, always placid and dwelling in a serene atmosphere, restraining within itself all the impulses from which anger springs, is modest, commands respect, and remains calm and collected: none of which qualities will you find in an angry man: for who, when under the influence of grief and rage, does not first get rid of bashfulness? who, when excited and confused and about to attack some one, does not fling away any habits of shamefacedness he may have possessed? what angry man attends to the number or routine of his duties? who uses moderate language? who keeps any part of his body quiet? who can guide himself when in full career?
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Nothing proves your strength of character more than staying calm when things go wrong. The highest part of the sky stays perfectly ordered and close to the stars. It never forms clouds or gets swept up in storms or whirlwinds. It's completely peaceful. Lightning strikes only in the lower regions below it. A great mind works the same way. It stays calm and peaceful, living in clear air. It controls all the urges that create anger. Such a mind is humble, earns respect, and stays composed. You won't find any of these qualities in an angry person. When someone is full of grief and rage, don't they first throw away their sense of shame? When they're worked up and confused and ready to attack someone, don't they abandon any modesty they once had? What angry person pays attention to their duties or follows their usual routine? Who speaks calmly when angry? Who keeps their body still? Who can control themselves when they're charging full speed ahead?

on-anger_book-3.originalText: We shall find much profit in that sound maxim of Democritus which defines peace of mind to consist in not labouring much, or too much for our strength, either in public or private matters. A man's day, if he is engaged in many various occupations, never passes so happily that no man or no thing should give rise to some offence which makes the mind ripe for anger. Just as when one hurries through the crowded parts of the city one cannot help jostling many people, and one cannot help slipping at one place, being hindered at another, and splashed at another, so when one's life is spent in disconnected pursuits and wanderings, one must meet with many troubles and many accusations.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: We can learn a lot from Democritus's wise saying. He said peace of mind comes from not taking on too much work — either in public life or private life. Don't push beyond your strength. When a person fills their day with too many different tasks, something always goes wrong. Someone offends them, or something irritates them, and they become ready to explode with anger. It's like rushing through busy city streets. You can't help bumping into people. You slip here, get blocked there, and get splashed somewhere else. When your life is scattered across too many disconnected activities, you're bound to run into troubles and complaints.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: One man deceives our hopes, another delays their fulfilment, another destroys them: our projects do not proceed according to our intention. No one is so favoured by Fortune as to find her always on his side if he tempts her often: and from this it follows that he who sees several enterprises turn out contrary to his wishes becomes dissatisfied with both men and things, and on the slightest provocation flies into a rage with people, with undertakings, with places, with fortune, or with himself. In order, therefore, that the mind may be at peace, it ought not to be hurried hither and thither, nor, as I said before, wearied by labour at great matters, or matters whose attainment is beyond its strength. It is easy to fit one's shoulder to a light burden, and to shift it from one side to the other without dropping it: but we have difficulty in bearing the burdens which others' hands lay upon us, and when overweighted by them we fling them off upon our neighbours. Even when we do stand upright under our load, we nevertheless reel beneath a weight which is beyond our strength.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: One person disappoints our hopes. Another delays what we want. Another destroys our plans completely. Nothing goes the way we planned it. No one is so lucky that Fortune always smiles on them — especially if they keep testing her patience. When several projects fail, we get angry at everyone and everything. The smallest thing sets us off. We rage at people, at our work, at places, at luck, at ourselves. If you want peace of mind, don't let yourself get pulled in every direction. Don't exhaust yourself with huge tasks or goals that are beyond your ability. It's easy to carry a light load on your shoulder and shift it from side to side without dropping it. But we struggle with burdens that others dump on us. When we're overloaded, we just throw the weight onto our neighbors. Even when we manage to stay upright, we still wobble under a load that's too heavy for us.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
Be assured that the same rule applies both to public and private
life: simple and manageable undertakings proceed according to the
pleasure of the person in charge of them, but enormous ones, beyond
his capacity to manage, are not easily undertaken. When he has got
them to administer, they hinder him, and press hard upon him, and
just as he thinks that success is within his grasp, they collapse,
and carry him with them: thus it comes about that a man’s wishes
are often disappointed if he does not apply himself to easy tasks,
yet wishes that the tasks which he undertakes may be easy.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: The same rule works for both public and private life: simple, manageable projects go according to plan when someone capable is in charge. But huge projects that are beyond a person's ability? Those are hard to even start. Once you're stuck managing them, they slow you down and weigh you down. Just when you think you're about to succeed, they collapse and drag you down with them. This is why people's wishes so often fail — they don't focus on easy tasks, but they wish the hard tasks they take on were easy.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
Whenever
you would attempt anything, first form an estimate both of
your own powers, of the extent of the matter which you are undertaking,
and of the means by which you are to accomplish it: for if you have
to abandon your work when it is half done, the disappointment will
sour your temper. In such cases, it makes a difference whether one
is of an ardent or of a cold and unenterprising temperament: for
failure will rouse a generous spirit to anger, and will move a
sluggish and dull one to sorrow. Let our undertakings, therefore,
be neither petty nor yet presumptuous and reckless: let our hopes
not range far from home: let us attempt nothing which if we succeed
will make us astonished at our success.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Before you try anything, think it through carefully. Look at your own abilities. Consider how big the task really is. Figure out what tools and resources you'll need to get it done. If you have to quit halfway through, the disappointment will make you angry. Your personality matters here too. If you're passionate and driven, failure will make you furious. If you're naturally calm and cautious, failure will just make you sad. So choose your projects wisely. Don't pick things that are too small and meaningless. But don't pick things that are reckless and way beyond you either. Keep your hopes realistic. Don't attempt anything so ambitious that you'd be shocked if you actually pulled it off.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Since we know not how to endure an injury, let us take care not to receive one: we should live with the quietest and easiest-tempered persons, not with anxious or with sullen ones: for our own habits are copied from those with whom we associate, and just as some bodily diseases are communicated by touch, so also the mind transfers its vices to its neighbours. A drunkard leads even those who reproach him to grow fond of wine: profligate society will, if permitted, impair the morals even of robust-minded men: avarice infects those nearest it with its poison. Virtues do the same thing in the opposite direction, and improve all those with whom they are brought in contact: it is as good for one of unsettled principles to associate with better men than himself as for an invalid to live in a warm country with a healthy climate.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Since we don't know how to handle injury well, let's try not to get injured in the first place. We should live with calm, even-tempered people — not anxious or moody ones. We copy the habits of the people we spend time with. Just as some diseases spread through touch, the mind passes its flaws to neighbors. A drunk will get even his critics to start liking wine. Bad company will corrupt even strong-minded people if you let it. Greed infects everyone nearby with its poison. Virtues work the same way, but in reverse — they improve everyone they touch. It's as good for someone with shaky principles to hang around better people as it is for a sick person to live somewhere warm and healthy.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: You will understand how much may be effected this way, if you observe how even wild beasts grow tame by dwelling among us, and how no animal, however ferocious, continues to be wild, if it has long been accustomed to human companionship: all its savageness becomes softened, and amid peaceful scenes is gradually forgotten. We must add to this, that the man who lives with quiet people is not only improved by their example, but also by the fact that he finds no reason for anger and does not practise his vice: it will, therefore, be his duty to avoid all those who he knows will excite his anger.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: You can see how powerful this approach is if you think about wild animals. Even they become gentle when they live with us. No matter how fierce an animal might be, it stops being wild after spending time around people. Its savage nature gets softer. In peaceful surroundings, it gradually forgets how to be wild. Here's another benefit: when you live with calm people, you improve not just from watching their example. You also improve because you have no reason to get angry. You don't get to practice your bad habit. So make it your goal to avoid anyone you know will make you angry.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: You ask, who these are: many will bring about the same thing by various means; a proud man will offend you by his disdain, a talkative man by his abuse, an impudent man by his insults, a spiteful man by his malice, a quarrelsome man by his wrangling, a braggart and liar by his vain-gloriousness: you will not endure to be feared by a suspicious man, conquered by an obstinate one, or scorned by an ultra-refined one: Choose straightforward, good-natured, steady people, who will not provoke your wrath, and will bear with it.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: You ask who these troublesome people are. Many different types will anger you in their own ways. A proud person will offend you with their arrogance. A chatty person will hurt you with their words. A rude person will insult you. A mean person will attack you out of spite. An argumentative person will pick fights. A show-off and liar will annoy you with their fake boasting. You won't want to be around a suspicious person who fears you, a stubborn person who tries to beat you, or a snobby person who looks down on you. Choose honest, kind, steady people instead. They won't make you angry, and they'll put up with you when you are.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Those whose dispositions are yielding, polite and suave, will be of even greater service, provided they do not flatter, for excessive obsequiousness irritates bad-tempered men. One of my own friends was a good man indeed, but too prone to anger, and it was as dangerous to flatter him as to curse him. Caelius the orator, it is well known, was the worst-tempered man possible. It is said that once he was dining in his own chamber with an especially long-suffering client, but had great difficulty when thrown thus into a man's society to avoid quarrelling with him. The other thought it best to agree to whatever he said, and to play second fiddle, but Caelius could not bear his obsequious agreement, and exclaimed, "Do contradict me in something, that there may be two of us!" Yet even he, who was angry at not being angry, soon recovered his temper, because he had no one to fight with.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: People who are flexible, polite, and smooth will help you even more — as long as they don't flatter you. Too much fawning irritates angry people. I had a friend who was a good man, but he got angry too easily. It was just as dangerous to compliment him as it was to insult him. Everyone knows that Caelius the orator had the worst temper imaginable. The story goes that he was once dining alone in his room with a very patient client. Even in private, Caelius could barely avoid picking a fight. His guest decided it was safest to agree with everything Caelius said and just go along with him. But Caelius couldn't stand all this obedient agreement. He finally burst out: "Argue with me about something, so there can be two of us in this conversation!" Even Caelius — who was actually angry about not being angry — soon calmed down, because he had no one to fight with.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: If, then, we are conscious of an irascible disposition, let us especially choose for our friends those who will look and speak as we do: they will pamper us and lead us into a bad habit of listening to nothing that does not please us, but it will be good to give our anger respite and repose. Even those who are naturally crabbed and wild will yield to caresses: no creature continues either angry or frightened if you pat him. Whenever a controversy seems likely to be longer or more keenly disputed than usual, let us check its first beginnings, before it gathers strength. A dispute nourishes itself as it proceeds, and takes hold of those who plunge too deeply into it: it is easier to stand aloof than to extricate oneself from a struggle.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: If you know you have a quick temper, you might want to choose friends who always agree with you. They will spoil you and get you used to hearing only what you want to hear. But this actually gives your anger a break and lets it rest. Even naturally cranky and harsh people soften when treated gently. No animal stays angry or scared if you pet it kindly. When an argument looks like it will drag on or get heated, stop it at the very start before it picks up steam. Arguments feed themselves as they continue. They grab hold of people who dive in too deep. It's much easier to stay out of a fight than to escape once you're in it.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
Irascible men ought not to meddle with the more serious class
of occupations, or, at any rate, ought to stop short of weariness
in the pursuit of them; their mind ought not to be engaged upon
hard subjects, but handed over to pleasing arts: let it be softened
by reading poetry, and interested by legendary history: let it be
treated with luxury and refinement. Pythagoras used to calm his
troubled spirit by playing upon the lyre: and who does not know
that trumpets and clarions are irritants, just as some airs are
lullabies and soothe the mind? Green is good for wearied eyes, and
some colours are grateful to weak sight, while the brightness of
others is painful to it. In the same way cheerful pursuits soothe
unhealthy minds. We must avoid law courts, pleadings, verdicts, and
everything else that aggravates our fault, and we ought no less to
avoid bodily weariness; for it exhausts all that is quiet and gentle
in us, and rouses bitterness.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: People who get angry easily shouldn't take on serious, demanding work. Or if they do, they should quit before they get exhausted. Their minds shouldn't wrestle with hard problems. Instead, give them pleasant activities. Let them read poetry and enjoy old stories. Treat them with luxury and care. Pythagoras used to calm his troubled spirit by playing the lyre. Everyone knows that trumpets and horns stir people up, while certain melodies put us to sleep and soothe the mind. Green is good for tired eyes. Some colors help weak sight, while bright ones hurt. In the same way, cheerful activities soothe unhealthy minds. We must avoid courtrooms, legal arguments, judgments, and anything else that makes our faults worse. We should also avoid physical exhaustion. It drains away everything calm and gentle in us, and brings out our bitter side.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
For this reason those who cannot trust
their digestion, when they are about to transact business of
importance always allay their bile with food, for it is peculiarly
irritated by fatigue, either because it draws the vital heat into
the middle of the body, and injures the blood and stops its circulation
by the clogging of the veins, or else because the worn-out and
weakened body reacts upon the mind: this is certainly the reason
why those who are broken by ill-health or age are more irascible
than other men. Hunger also and thirst should be avoided for the
same reason; they exasperate and irritate men’s minds: it is an old
saying that “a weary man is quarrelsome “: and so also is a hungry
or a thirsty man, or one who is suffering from any cause whatever:
for just as sores pain one at the slightest touch, and afterwards
even at the fear of being touched, so an unsound mind takes offence
at the slightest things, so that even a greeting, a letter,
a speech, or a question, provokes some men to anger.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: This is why people who don't trust their stomach always eat something before handling important business. Fatigue makes our bile especially irritable. Maybe it's because fatigue pulls our body heat inward and hurts our blood flow by clogging our veins. Or maybe it's because when our body gets worn down and weak, it affects our mind too. This certainly explains why people broken by sickness or old age get angrier than others. We should avoid hunger and thirst for the same reason. They make our minds sharp and irritable. There's an old saying: "a tired man picks fights." The same goes for someone who's hungry, thirsty, or suffering from anything else. Just like wounds hurt at the slightest touch — and then even hurt when we're afraid they might be touched — an unhealthy mind takes offense at the smallest things. Even a greeting, a letter, a speech, or a simple question can make some people angry.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
That which is diseased can never bear to be handled without
complaining: it is best, therefore, to apply remedies to oneself
as soon as we feel that anything is wrong, to allow oneself as
little licence as possible in speech, and to restrain one’s
impetuosity: now it is easy to detect the first growth of our
passions: the symptoms precede the disorder. Just as the signs of
storms and rain come before the storms themselves, so there are
certain forerunners of anger, love, and all the storms which torment
our minds. Those who suffer from epilepsy know that the fit is
coming on if their extremities become cold, their sight fails, their
sinews tremble, their memory deserts them, and their head swims:
they accordingly check the growing disorder by applying the usual
remedies: they try to prevent the loss of their senses by smelling
or tasting some drug; they battle against cold and stiffness of
limbs by hot fomentations;
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Anything diseased can't stand to be touched without causing pain. So it's best to treat yourself as soon as you notice something is wrong. Give yourself as little freedom as possible to speak, and hold back your impulses. It's easy to spot the first signs of our emotions — the symptoms come before the full disorder hits. Just as we see signs of storms and rain before the weather actually turns bad, there are warning signs before anger, love, and all the other storms that shake our minds. People who have epilepsy know a seizure is coming when their hands and feet get cold, their vision blurs, their muscles shake, their memory fails, and their head spins. So they fight the growing problem with their usual treatments. They try to prevent losing consciousness by smelling or tasting medicine. They fight the cold and stiff limbs with hot compresses.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
or, if all remedies fail, they retire
apart, and faint where no one sees them fall. It is useful for a
man to understand his disease, and to break its strength before it
becomes developed. Let us see what it is that especially irritates
us. Some men take offence at insulting words, others at deeds: one
wishes his pedigree, another his person, to be treated with respect.
This man wishes to be considered especially fashionable, that man
to be thought especially learned: one cannot bear pride, another
cannot bear obstinacy. One thinks it beneath him to be angry with
his slaves, another is cruel at home, but gentle abroad. One imagines
that he is proposed for office because he is unpopular, another
thinks himself insulted because he is not proposed. People do not
all take offence in the same way; you ought then to know what your
own weak point is, that you may guard it with especial care.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: When all else fails, people with epilepsy go somewhere private and faint where no one can see them. It helps to understand your own weakness and stop it before it takes over. Let's look at what makes different people angry. Some people get upset by insults. Others get upset by actions. One person wants respect for his family name. Another wants respect for his looks. This man wants to seem fashionable. That man wants to seem smart. One person can't stand pride. Another can't stand stubbornness. One thinks it's beneath him to get angry at his slaves. Another is cruel at home but gentle in public. One imagines he's nominated for office because people don't like him. Another thinks he's been insulted because he wasn't nominated. People don't all get offended the same way. You need to know your own weak spot so you can guard it carefully.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
It is better not to see or to hear everything: many causes of
offence may pass by us, most of which are disregarded by the
man who ignores them. Would you not be irascible? then be not
inquisitive. He who seeks to know what is said about him, who digs
up spiteful tales even if they were told in secret, is himself the
destroyer of his own peace of mind. Some stories may be so construed
as to appear to be insults: wherefore it is best to put some aside,
to laugh at others, and to pardon others. There are many ways in
which anger may be checked; most things may be turned into jest.
It is said that Socrates when he was given a box on the ear, merely
said that it was a pity a man could not tell when he ought to wear
his helmet out walking.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: It's better not to see or hear everything. Many things that could offend you will just pass by if you ignore them. Do you want to avoid getting angry? Then don't be so curious about what people are saying. If you go looking for gossip about yourself, or dig up mean stories that were told in private, you're destroying your own peace of mind. Some stories can be twisted to look like insults. So it's best to ignore some, laugh at others, and forgive the rest. There are many ways to stop anger before it starts. Most things can be turned into jokes. They say when Socrates got slapped in the face, he just said it was too bad a person couldn't tell when they should wear a helmet while walking around.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
It does not so much matter how an injury
is done, as how it is borne; and I do not see how moderation can
be hard to practise, when I know that even despots, though success
and impunity combine to swell their pride, have sometimes restrained
their natural ferocity. At any rate, tradition informs us that once,
when a guest in his cups bitterly reproached Pisistratus, the despot
of Athens, for his cruelty, many of those present offered to lay
hands on the traitor, and one said one thing and one another to
kindle his wrath, he bore it coolly, and replied to those who were
egging him on, that he was no more angry with the man than he should
be with one who ran against him blindfold.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish:
What matters isn't how someone wrongs you — it's how you handle it. And I don't see why self-control should be so difficult, especially when I know that even tyrants have sometimes held back their cruelty. Success and the ability to do whatever they want usually makes tyrants more arrogant. But they can still show restraint.

There's a story about Pisistratus, the tyrant of Athens. A drunk guest at his dinner party insulted him harshly, calling him cruel. Many people there offered to grab the traitor. They said different things to try to make Pisistratus angry. But he stayed calm. He told the people urging him to act that he was no more angry with this man than he would be with someone who bumped into him while wearing a blindfold.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: A large part of mankind manufacture their own grievances either by entertaining unfounded suspicions or by exaggerating trifles. Anger often comes to us, but we often go to it. It ought never to be sent for: even when it falls in our way it ought to be flung aside. No one says to himself, "I myself have done or might have done this very thing which I am angry with another for doing." No one considers the intention of the doer, but merely the thing done:
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Most people create their own problems. They build up groundless fears or turn small issues into big ones. Sometimes anger comes to us naturally. But more often, we chase after it. We should never invite anger in. Even when it shows up on its own, we should push it away. Nobody ever asks themselves: "Haven't I done this exact same thing I'm mad about? Or couldn't I have done it?" People don't think about why someone acted the way they did. They only focus on what that person did.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: yet we ought to think about him, and whether he did it intentionally or accidentally, under compulsion or under a mistake, whether he did it out of hatred for us, or to gain something for himself, whether he did it to please himself or to serve a friend. In some cases the age, in others the worldly fortunes of the culprit may render it humane or advantageous to bear with him and put up with what he has done. Let us put ourselves in the place of him with whom we are angry: at present an overweening conceit of our own importance makes us prone to anger, and we are quite willing to do to others what we cannot endure should be done to ourselves.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: We should think about the person who wronged us. Did they do it on purpose or by accident? Were they forced to do it or did they make a mistake? Did they act out of hatred for us, or to gain something for themselves? Were they trying to please themselves or help a friend? Sometimes the person's age matters. Sometimes their circumstances make it wise or kind to be patient with them and overlook what they did. We should put ourselves in their shoes. Right now, we think too highly of ourselves. This makes us quick to anger. We're happy to do things to others that we would never want done to us.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: No one will postpone his anger: yet delay is the best remedy for it, because it allows its first glow to subside, and gives time for the cloud which darkens the mind either to disperse or at any rate to become less dense. Of these wrongs which drive you frantic, some will grow lighter after an interval, not of a day, but even of an hour: some will vanish altogether. Even if you gain nothing by your adjournment, still what you do after it will appear to be the result of mature deliberation, not of anger. If you want to find out the truth about anything, commit the task to time: nothing can be accurately discerned at a time of disturbance.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: No one wants to delay their anger. But delay is the best cure for anger. It lets the first heat cool down. It gives time for the fog in your mind to clear up, or at least get thinner. Some of the wrongs that are driving you crazy will seem smaller after some time passes — not even a day, sometimes just an hour. Some will disappear completely. Even if waiting doesn't help, at least what you do afterward will look like you thought it through, not like you acted in anger. If you want to find out the truth about something, give it to time. You can't see anything clearly when you're upset.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: Plato, when angry with his slave, could not prevail upon himself to wait, but straightway ordered him to take off his shirt and present his shoulders to the blows which he meant to give him with his own hand: then, when he perceived that he was angry, he stopped the hand which he had raised in the air, and stood like one in act to strike. Being asked by a friend who happened to come in, what he was doing, he answered: "I am making an angry man expiate his crime." He retained the posture of one about to give way to passion, as if struck with astonishment at its being so degrading to a philosopher, forgetting the slave, because he had found another still more deserving of punishment.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Plato once got angry with his slave and couldn't make himself wait. He ordered the slave to take off his shirt and bare his shoulders for a beating that Plato planned to give with his own hands. But then Plato realized he was angry. He stopped his raised hand mid-air and stood frozen like a statue about to strike. A friend walked in and asked what he was doing. Plato answered: "I am making an angry man pay for his crime." He stayed in that position — hand raised, ready to hit — as if amazed that such behavior was so unworthy of a philosopher. He forgot all about the slave because he had found someone who deserved punishment even more.

on-anger_book-3.originalText: He therefore denied himself the exercise of authority over his own household, and once, being rather angry at some fault, said, "Speusippus, will you please to correct that slave with stripes; for I am in a rage." He would not strike him, for the very reason for which another man would have struck him. "I am in a rage," said he; "I should beat him more than I ought: I should take more pleasure than I ought in doing so: let not that slave fall into the power of one who is not in his own power." Can any one wish to grant the power of revenge to an angry man, when Plato himself gave up his own right to exercise it? While you are angry, you ought not to be allowed to do anything. "Why?" do you ask? Because when you are angry there is nothing that you do not wish to be allowed to do.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: So Plato denied himself authority over his own household. Once, when he was angry about something a slave had done wrong, he said, "Speusippus, please beat that slave for me — I'm too angry right now." He wouldn't strike the slave for the exact reason another person would have. "I'm furious," he said. "I'd beat him harder than I should. I'd enjoy it more than I should. Don't let that slave fall into the hands of someone who can't control himself." Does anyone really want to give an angry person the power of revenge, when even Plato gave up his own right to use it? When you're angry, you shouldn't be allowed to do anything. "Why?" you ask. Because when you're angry, there's nothing you don't want permission to do.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
Fight hard with yourself and if you cannot conquer anger, do
not let it conquer you: you have begun to get the better of it if
it does not show itself, if it is not given vent. Let us conceal
its symptoms, and as far as possible keep it secret and hidden. It
will give us great trouble to do this, for it is eager to burst
forth, to kindle our eyes and to transform our face; but if we allow
it to show itself in our outward appearance, it is our master. Let
it rather be locked in the innermost recesses of our breast, and
be borne by us, not bear us: nay, let us replace all its symptoms
by their opposites; let us make our countenance more composed than
usual, our voice milder, our step slower.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Fight hard against yourself. If you can't defeat anger completely, don't let it defeat you. You've started to win if anger stays hidden — if you don't let it show. We must hide its signs and keep it secret as much as possible. This will be hard work. Anger wants to burst out, light up our eyes, and twist our faces. But if we let it show on the outside, then anger becomes our master. Instead, lock it deep inside your chest. You should carry it — don't let it carry you. Better yet, do the opposite of what anger wants. Make your face calmer than usual. Make your voice gentler. Walk more slowly.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
Our inward thoughts
gradually become influenced by our outward demeanour. With Socrates
it was a sign of anger when he lowered his voice, and became sparing
of speech; it was evident at such times that he was exercising
restraint over himself. His friends, consequently, used to detect
him acting thus, and convict him of being angry; nor was he displeased
at being charged with concealment of anger; indeed, how could he
help being glad that many men should perceive his anger, yet that
none should feel it? they would however, have felt it had not he
granted to his friends the same right of criticizing his own conduct
which he himself assumed over theirs.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Our inner thoughts slowly change when we control how we act on the outside. With Socrates, you could tell he was angry when he lowered his voice and spoke less. It was clear he was holding himself back. His friends would catch him doing this and call him out for being angry. He didn't mind being accused of hiding his anger. After all, how could he not be happy that many people could see his anger, but nobody actually felt its effects? They would have felt it, though, if he hadn't given his friends the same right to criticize him that he used on them.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
How much more needful is it
for us to do this? let us beg all our best friends to give us their
opinion with the greatest freedom at the very time when we can bear
it least, and never to be compliant with us when we are angry.
While we are in our right senses, while we are under our own control,
let us call for help against so powerful an evil, and one which we
regard with such unjust favour. Those who cannot carry their wine
discreetly, and fear to be betrayed into some rash and insolent
act, give their slaves orders to take them away from the banquet
when they are drunk; those who know by experience how unreasonable
they are when sick give orders that no one is to obey them when
they are in ill health.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: How much more important is this for us? We should ask our best friends to speak honestly with us — especially when we least want to hear it. We should tell them never to give in to us when we're angry. While we're thinking clearly and have control over ourselves, let's ask for help against this powerful enemy that we foolishly favor. People who can't handle their wine and worry they'll do something rash or rude tell their servants to drag them away from dinner parties when they're drunk. People who know they make bad decisions when they're sick give orders that no one should obey them during illness.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
It is best to prepare obstacles beforehand
for vices which are known, and above all things so to tranquilize
our mind that it may bear the most sudden and violent shocks either
without feeling anger, or, if anger be provoked by the extent of
some unexpected wrong, that it may bury it deep, and not betray its
wound. That it is possible to do this will be seen, if I quote a
few of an abundance of examples, from which we may learn both how
much evil there is in anger, when it exercises entire dominion over
men in supreme power, and how completely it can control itself when
overawed by fear.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: It's best to set up barriers ahead of time against vices we know we have. Most importantly, we need to calm our minds so they can handle sudden, violent shocks. We should either feel no anger at all, or if we do get angry because of some unexpected wrong, we should bury it deep and not show our wound. You'll see that this is possible when I share some examples from many I could give. These stories will show you two things: how much damage anger causes when it controls people in power, and how well anger can control itself when it's scared.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
King Cambyses[2] was excessively addicted to wine. Praexaspes
was the only one of his closest friends who advised him to drink
more sparingly, pointing out how shameful a thing drunkenness was
in a king, upon whom all eyes and ears were fixed. Cambyses answered,
“That you may know that I never lose command of myself, I will
presently prove to you that both my eyes and my hands are fit for
service after I have been drinking.” Hereupon he drank more freely
than usual, using larger cups, and when heavy and besotted with
wine ordered his reprover’s son to go beyond the threshold and stand
there with his left hand raised above his head;
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: King Cambyses was a heavy drinker. Only one of his close friends, Praexaspes, had the courage to tell him to drink less. He pointed out how shameful it was for a king to be drunk when everyone was watching him. Cambyses replied, "I'll prove to you that I never lose control of myself. I'll show you that my eyes and hands work perfectly fine even after I've been drinking." Then he drank even more than usual, using bigger cups. When he was completely drunk, he ordered his critic's son to go stand just outside the door with his left hand raised above his head.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
then he bent his
bow and pierced the youth’s heart, at which he had said that he
aimed. He then had his breast cut open, showed the arrow
sticking exactly into the heart, and, looking at the boy’s father,
asked whether his hand was not steady enough. He replied, that
Apollo himself could not have taken better aim. God confound such
a man, a slave in mind, if not in station! He actually praised an
act which he ought not to have endured to witness. He thought that
the breast of his son being torn assunder, and his heart quivering
with its wound, gave him an opportunity of making a complimentary
speech.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Then Cambyses drew his bow and shot an arrow straight through the young man's heart — exactly where he said he would aim. He had the boy's chest cut open to show the arrow lodged perfectly in his heart. Looking at the boy's father, he asked whether his hand wasn't steady enough. The father replied that Apollo himself couldn't have aimed better. Damn such a man — a slave in his mind, if not in his position! He actually praised an act he should never have been able to watch. He thought his son's torn chest and pierced, quivering heart gave him a chance to pay a compliment.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
He ought to have raised a dispute with him about his success,
and have called for another shot, that the king might be pleased
to prove upon the person of the father that his hand was even
steadier than when he shot the son. What a savage king! what a
worthy mark for all his follower’s arrows! Yet though we curse him
for making his banquet end in cruelty and death, still it was worse
to praise that arrow-shot than to shoot it. We shall see hereafter
how a father ought to bear himself when standing over the corpse
of his son, whose murder he had both caused and witnessed: the
matter which we are now discussing, has been proved, I mean, that
anger can be suppressed.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: The father should have argued with the king about his aim. He should have demanded another shot, so the king could prove on the father himself that his hand was even steadier than when he killed the son. What a savage king! What a perfect target for all his soldiers' arrows! We curse him for ending his dinner party with cruelty and death. But it was worse to praise that arrow shot than to shoot it. Later we'll discuss how a father should act when standing over his son's corpse — a murder he both caused and witnessed. But for now, we've proven our point: anger can be controlled.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
He did not curse the king, he did not so
much as let fall a single inauspicious word, though he felt his own
heart as deeply wounded as that of his son. He may be said to have
done well in choking down his words; for though he might have spoken
as an angry man, yet he could not have expressed what he felt as a
father. He may, I repeat, be thought to have behaved with greater
wisdom on that occasion than when he tried to regulate the drink
of one who was better employed in drinking wine than in drinking
blood, and who granted men peace while his hands were busy with the
winecup. He, therefore, added one more to the number of those who
have shown to their bitter cost how little kings care for their
friends’ good advice.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: The father did not curse the king. He didn't even let slip a single harsh word, even though his heart was wounded as deeply as his son's body. You could say he was wise to hold back his words. If he had spoken in anger, he couldn't have said what he truly felt as a father. He may have shown more wisdom in that moment than when he tried to control the drinking of a man who was better off drinking wine than blood — a man who only granted peace when his hands were busy with his wine cup instead of weapons. So the father joined the long list of people who learned the hard way that kings don't care about their friends' good advice.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
I have no doubt that Harpagus must have given some such advice
to the king of the Persians and of himself, in anger at which the
king placed Harpagus’s own children before him on the dinner-table
for him to eat, and asked him from time to time, whether he liked
the seasoning. Then, when he saw that he was satiated with his own
misery, he ordered their heads to be brought to him, and asked him
how he liked his entertainment. The wretched man did not lose his
readiness of speech; his face did not change. “Every kind of dinner,”
said he, “is pleasant at the king’s table.” What did he gain by
this obsequiousness?
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: I'm sure Harpagus must have given similar advice to the Persian king. The king got angry about it and served Harpagus his own children for dinner. During the meal, the king kept asking if he liked how the food was prepared. When he saw that Harpagus was full of his own grief, the king had the children's heads brought out. He asked how Harpagus had enjoyed his meal. The poor man didn't lose his ability to speak. His expression never changed. "Any dinner is pleasant at the king's table," he said. What did he gain by being so submissive?

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
He avoided being invited a second time to
dinner, to eat what was left of them. I do not forbid a father to
blame the act of his king, or to seek for some revenge worthy of
so bloodthirsty a monster, but in the meanwhile I gather from the
tale this fact, that even the anger which arises from unheard of
outrages can be concealed, and forced into using language which is
the very reverse of its meaning. This way of curbing anger is
necessary, at least for those who have chosen this sort of life and
who are admitted to dine at a king’s table; this is how they must
eat and drink, this is how they must answer, and how they must laugh
at their own deaths.
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: He avoided getting invited to dinner again to eat what remained of his children. I'm not saying a father shouldn't condemn his king for such an act, or seek revenge against such a bloodthirsty monster. But I want to point out something from this story: even anger from the most horrible crimes can be hidden. You can force yourself to speak words that mean the exact opposite of what you feel. This kind of self-control over anger is necessary — at least for those who have chosen this kind of life and get invited to eat at a king's table. This is how they must eat and drink. This is how they must respond. This is how they must laugh at their own deaths.

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
Whether life is worth having at such a price,
we shall see hereafter; that is another question. Let us not console
so sorry a crew, or encourage them to submit to the orders of their
butchers; let us point out that however slavish a man’s condition
may be, there is always a path to liberty open to him, unless his
mind be diseased. It is a man’s own fault if he suffers, when by
putting an end to himself he can put an end to his misery. To him
whose king aimed arrows at the breasts of his friends, and to him
whose master gorged fathers with the hearts of their children, I
would say “Madman, why do you groan? for what are you waiting?
on-anger_book-3.plainEnglish: Whether life is worth living at such a price, we'll discuss later — that's a different question. Let's not comfort such miserable people or encourage them to obey their butchers. Let's show them that no matter how enslaved a person's situation may be, there's always a path to freedom open to him, unless his mind is sick. It's a man's own fault if he suffers, when he could end his misery by ending himself. To the person whose king shot arrows at his friends' chests, and to the person whose master forced fathers to eat their children's hearts, I would say: "You fool, why are you groaning? What are you waiting for?

on-anger_book-3.originalText:
for
some enemy to avenge you by the destruction of your entire
nation, or for some powerful king to arrive from a distant land?
Wherever you turn your eyes you may see an end to your woes. Do you
see that precipice? down that lies the road to liberty; do you see
